questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin for stroke prevention. His physician needs a laboratory test to guide dose adjustments. Which of the following tests is most appropriate for monitoring the degree of anticoagulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bleeding time

choices.label: C
choices.text: D-dimer assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: International normalized ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin time

explanation.summary: The INR (a standardized PT) measures the extrinsic and common pathways and is the preferred test for monitoring warfarin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warfarin interferes with gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X, most of which lie in the extrinsic and common pathways that the PT/INR measures. The INR standardizes the PT across laboratories, making it the best test to adjust warfarin dosing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The aPTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways and is used to monitor heparin, not warfarin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bleeding time assesses primary hemostasis (platelets and vessel wall), not the coagulation cascade affected by warfarin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D-dimer is a marker of fibrinolysis/thrombosis and does not reflect the degree of warfarin anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin time assesses only the fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion and is not used to monitor warfarin.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is admitted for a pulmonary embolism and started on a continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion. Which of the following laboratory tests is most appropriate to monitor her level of anticoagulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: International normalized ratio (INR)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prothrombin time (extrinsic pathway)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum fibrin degradation product assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standardized template bleeding time

explanation.summary: The aPTT measures the intrinsic and common pathways and is the standard test for monitoring unfractionated heparin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin activates antithrombin, which then inhibits many factors including IIa, IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa. In practice the aPTT is most useful for monitoring the intrinsic and common pathways, so it is used to follow heparin therapy (an anti-Xa assay is an alternative).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The INR is used to monitor warfarin, which affects the extrinsic and common pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways and is not the standard test for heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The FDP assay measures fibrinolysis products and is not used to monitor heparin dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bleeding time reflects primary hemostasis and does not track heparin effect.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man being evaluated for prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction is found to have a prolonged prothrombin time with a completely normal activated partial thromboplastin time. A deficiency of which of the following factors best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XI

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factor XII

explanation.summary: Factor VII is unique to the extrinsic pathway, which is assessed by the PT but not the aPTT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PT measures the activity of factor VII down through fibrin formation (extrinsic and common pathways). Because factor VII is not part of the intrinsic pathway, an isolated factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT while leaving the aPTT normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor IX is intrinsic; deficiency prolongs the aPTT rather than the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VIII is an intrinsic pathway factor; its deficiency prolongs the aPTT, not the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor XI is intrinsic; deficiency prolongs the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor XII is intrinsic; deficiency prolongs the aPTT (though it causes no clinical bleeding).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time and a normal prothrombin time. When his plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma, the aPTT corrects into the normal range both immediately and after incubation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A specific factor inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparin contamination of the sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lupus anticoagulant

explanation.summary: Correction of a prolonged aPTT with normal plasma indicates a clotting factor deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a mixing study, if the aPTT corrects after adding normal plasma, the missing ingredient was a coagulation factor supplied by the normal plasma. A boy with an isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects most likely has hemophilia (factor VIII deficiency), which can then be confirmed with a specific factor assay.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A specific factor inhibitor typically corrects immediately but becomes prolonged again after incubation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC produces prolonged PT and aPTT with low platelets and elevated D-dimer, not an isolated correcting aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin would not correct on mixing, since the drug remains in the mixture and blocks the reagent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lupus anticoagulant does not correct on mixing because it is an inhibitor, not a deficiency.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. A mixing study with normal plasma fails to correct the aPTT both immediately and after incubation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor VII deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lupus anticoagulant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: A prolonged aPTT that fails to correct on mixing, both immediately and after incubation, indicates a lupus anticoagulant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Failure to correct means a circulating inhibitor, not a missing factor, is present. A lupus anticoagulant (an antiphospholipid antibody) binds the phospholipid in the reagent and keeps the aPTT prolonged immediately and after incubation, matching the Case #3 mixing-study pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, not the aPTT, and is a deficiency that corrects on mixing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is a factor deficiency and would correct on mixing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency reduces factors II, VII, IX, X (a deficiency) and would correct on mixing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease chiefly affects platelet adhesion and factor VIII carriage and corrects on mixing.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops a deep venous thrombosis and is found to have a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time that does not correct on a mixing study; testing confirms a lupus anticoagulant. Which of the following best explains why her aPTT is prolonged despite her tendency to clot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hereditary deficiency of factor VIII in the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased hepatic synthesis of nearly all the coagulation factors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors from vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ongoing consumption of clotting factors by widespread microthrombi

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antibody binds and inactivates phospholipid in the assay reagent

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid antibodies prolong the aPTT in vitro as a lab artifact while promoting thrombosis in vivo.
explanation.whyCorrect: In vitro, antiphospholipid antibodies/lupus anticoagulant bind to and inactivate phospholipid-containing reagents used in the aPTT, leaving less reagent available and falsely prolonging the aPTT. This is a pure laboratory artifact; in vivo these antibodies actually increase thrombosis, putting patients at risk for DVT and pulmonary embolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A factor VIII deficiency would correct on mixing and does not cause thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired hepatic synthesis is a factor deficiency that corrects on mixing and causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin K deficiency reduces functional factors and prolongs the PT; it does not explain a non-correcting aPTT with thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Consumption of factors describes DIC, not the mechanism of a lupus anticoagulant, and would not fail to correct as an isolated finding.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man scheduled for elective hernia repair is found on routine testing to have an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. He has no personal or family history of abnormal bleeding and has previously undergone surgery without bleeding complications. A deficiency of which of the following factors best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor XI

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT in vitro but does not cause clinical bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factor XII deficiency prolongs clotting time in vitro (prolonged aPTT) because factor XII participates in the contact-activated intrinsic pathway of the assay. However, factor XII is not involved in physiologic coagulation, so its deficiency does not cause clinical bleeding, explaining this asymptomatic patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor IX deficiency (hemophilia B) prolongs the aPTT and causes clinical bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) prolongs the aPTT and causes significant clinical bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor XI deficiency prolongs the aPTT and can cause bleeding, unlike the asymptomatic picture here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding and typically a bleeding history, not an asymptomatic isolated aPTT prolongation.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit suddenly begins to ooze blood from his central venous line and surgical sites. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings would most support this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated platelet count with normal PT

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isolated low D-dimer with normal platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolated prolonged thrombin time with normal PT and aPTT

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal PT, normal aPTT, and normal D-dimer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged PT and aPTT with an elevated D-dimer

explanation.summary: DIC consumes clotting factors and platelets while generating clot breakdown, giving prolonged PT/aPTT with elevated D-dimer.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC, abnormal activation of the coagulation cascade produces widespread microthrombi and rapid consumption of clotting factors (prolonging PT/INR and aPTT), fibrin, and platelets (causing thrombocytopenia). Ongoing fibrinolysis of those clots raises the D-dimer, so prolonged PT and aPTT with an elevated D-dimer best supports DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DIC causes thrombocytopenia (low platelets) and a prolonged PT, not an elevated platelet count with a normal PT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC raises the D-dimer and lowers platelets, opposite to this choice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DIC produces global abnormalities, not an isolated prolonged thrombin time with otherwise normal tests.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entirely normal studies would argue against DIC, which produces multiple abnormalities.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with chest pain. Her vital signs, physical examination, and electrocardiogram are unremarkable, and clinical scoring places her at low probability for pulmonary embolism. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate and cost-effective choice to rule out a pulmonary embolism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding time

choices.label: B
choices.text: CT pulmonary angiography

choices.label: C
choices.text: D-dimer assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: International normalized ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin time

explanation.summary: A negative highly sensitive D-dimer in a low-probability patient effectively rules out pulmonary embolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: The D-dimer assay is very sensitive and is almost always elevated when a thrombus is present, making it excellent for ruling out clot. A negative result with such a sensitive test in a low-probability scenario effectively rules out pulmonary embolism, avoiding unnecessary imaging and cost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleeding time measures primary hemostasis and is unrelated to detecting a thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CT angiography is used to rule in a thrombus and is unnecessary imaging in a low-probability patient before a D-dimer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The INR monitors extrinsic/common pathway activity (e.g., warfarin) and cannot exclude a pulmonary embolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin time assesses fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion and does not rule out pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder arrives intoxicated with a protuberant abdomen after weeks of continuous drinking. Laboratory studies show a prolonged prothrombin time, prolonged partial thromboplastin time, and thrombocytopenia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the prolonged PT and PTT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An antibody against factor VII

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic kidney disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cirrhosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparin use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isolated factor VII deficiency

explanation.summary: The liver produces all coagulation factors, so advanced liver disease prolongs all coagulation assays.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient's chronic alcohol use and protuberant abdomen point to cirrhosis. Because all coagulation factors are produced in the liver, advanced liver disease decreases them all, prolonging the PT, PTT, and TT. Liver disease is the most common acquired cause of coagulation abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An antibody against factor VII would prolong the PT but not the PTT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic kidney disease causes uremic platelet dysfunction but does not directly reduce clotting factors to prolong PT and PTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The clinical picture fits cirrhosis; the patient is not receiving regular heparin injections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isolated factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT only, not the PTT.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a lifelong history of easy bruising is found to have a prolonged thrombin time despite a normal prothrombin time and normal activated partial thromboplastin time. The thrombin time most directly assesses which of the following steps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of the extrinsic pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet plug formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of factors

explanation.summary: The thrombin time isolates the final step of the common pathway: fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thrombin time is performed by adding thrombin to plasma and measuring the time to form fibrin, so it assesses conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. Because it sits at the very end of the common pathway, it is a specialized test most often used to detect fibrinogen deficiency or a fibrinogen functional mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The extrinsic pathway is assessed by the PT, not the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The intrinsic pathway is assessed by the aPTT, not the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet plug formation is primary hemostasis, evaluated by platelet tests, not the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation relates to factor synthesis and is reflected in the PT/INR, not the thrombin time.

questions.stem: A laboratory technician draws blood for coagulation testing into a light-blue-top vacutainer tube that contains citrate. Which of the following best explains why citrate is required for the sample to be usable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates the intrinsic pathway for the assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: It adds thrombin to standardize fibrin formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides a phospholipid surface to accelerate clotting

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes calcium to prevent the blood from clotting

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies tissue factor needed for the prothrombin time

explanation.summary: Citrate chelates calcium, preventing clotting in the tube so timed coagulation tests can be run.
explanation.whyCorrect: The light-blue-top tube contains citrate, which removes calcium from the blood. Because calcium binds the phospholipids exposed during platelet activation and provides a surface for assembly of some coagulation factors, removing it prevents clotting in the tube. Calcium is then added back during the actual assay so the timed test can be performed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intrinsic pathway activators (silica, kaolin) are reagents used in the aPTT, not the anticoagulant in the tube.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thrombin is added only in the specific thrombin time assay, not by the collection tube.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phospholipid and calcium are added later during the assay; citrate does not provide a clotting surface.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor (thromboplastin) is a PT reagent added in the lab, not the citrate in the collection tube.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing how a stable clot forms at a site of vascular injury. Sealing of the platelet plug with fibrin through the steps of the coagulation cascade is best termed which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact phase activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinolysis of the clot

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow thrombopoiesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary platelet hemostasis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary hemostasis

explanation.summary: Fibrin formation through the coagulation cascade is secondary hemostasis; the platelet plug itself is primary hemostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Making a clot requires two things: forming a platelet plug and sealing that plug with fibrin. Fibrin formation, which occurs through the steps of the coagulation cascade, is called secondary hemostasis. Defects in this step lead to poor clot formation and excessive bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Contact activation describes how reagents such as silica start the intrinsic pathway in vitro, not the overall fibrin-forming step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinolysis is the breakdown of fibrin once a clot has formed, the opposite of clot formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombopoiesis is the production of platelets in the marrow and is unrelated to fibrin formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary hemostasis refers to formation of the platelet plug itself, not the fibrin that seals it.

questions.stem: A prothrombin time is being performed on a patient's citrated plasma sample. Which of the following is added to the plasma to carry out this assay?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Additional citrate, to chelate calcium remaining in the sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phospholipid and calcium, with no tissue factor-like substance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Silica or kaolin as a contact activator, together with calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombin, which acts directly on the fibrinogen in the sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thromboplastin reagent with phospholipid and tissue factor, plus calcium

explanation.summary: The PT is run by adding thromboplastin reagent (phospholipid plus a tissue factor-like substance) and calcium to plasma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PT is determined by taking the patient's plasma, adding thromboplastin reagent containing phospholipid and a tissue factor-like substance along with calcium, and measuring the seconds to fibrin formation. Tissue factor combines with factor VIIa to activate factor X, so this reagent triggers the extrinsic pathway that the PT measures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrate is the anticoagulant already in the collection tube; more citrate would prevent, not permit, the timed test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phospholipid and calcium without a tissue factor-like substance is the PTT reagent; no extrinsic activation occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Silica or kaolin is the chemical activator used in the PTT/aPTT to start the intrinsic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding thrombin directly to plasma is the thrombin time, which measures only fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a lifelong bleeding tendency has a prothrombin time of 13 seconds. A deficiency of which of the following factors would be missed by this normal result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor I

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factor X

explanation.summary: The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways only and does not assess factors XI, IX, or VIII.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PT is a measurement of the activity of factor VII on down through fibrin formation. It will not measure the activities of factors XI, IX, and VIII, which are all part of the intrinsic pathway. A factor VIII deficiency therefore leaves the PT normal and shows up instead as a prolonged aPTT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor I (fibrinogen) is in the common pathway, so its deficiency would prolong the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor II (prothrombin) is in the common pathway and its deficiency would prolong the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VII is the extrinsic factor the PT is designed to assess, so a deficiency would prolong the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor X is in the common pathway and a deficiency would prolong the PT.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient has an activated partial thromboplastin time reported. Which of the following is the normal reference range for this test?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 11 to 15 seconds

choices.label: C
choices.text: 12 to 14 seconds

choices.label: D
choices.text: 25 to 40 seconds

choices.label: E
choices.text: 60 to 90 seconds

explanation.summary: The normal range of the aPTT is 25 to 40 seconds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aPTT adds an activator to the PTT assay, which speeds clot formation and yields a narrower reference range than the PTT. Its normal range is 25 to 40 seconds, and values above that range suggest a problem in the intrinsic or common pathway, an anticoagulant drug, or an inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.8 to 1.2 is the normal range for the INR, which is a ratio rather than a time in seconds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 11 to 15 seconds is the typical normal range for the prothrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 12 to 14 seconds is the normal range for the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 60 to 90 seconds is well above the reference range and would represent a markedly prolonged aPTT.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on a stable warfarin dose is transferred between hospitals. His prothrombin time in seconds differs noticeably from the value reported at the first hospital, although his anticoagulation has not changed. Which of the following best explains this discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium is added to the assay at only some laboratories

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incubation times for the assay are not standardized

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet counts differ between the two specimens

choices.label: D
choices.text: The intrinsic pathway contributes variably to the PT

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thromboplastin reagents vary widely among manufacturers

explanation.summary: PT values fluctuate between hospitals because thromboplastin reagents differ by manufacturer, which is why the INR was created.
explanation.whyCorrect: The problem with the raw PT is that values can fluctuate between hospitals because thromboplastin reagents vary a lot from manufacturer to manufacturer. The INR was developed to standardize the measurement: it is derived from a formula using the ratio of the patient's PT to the PT done in serum with normal clotting, so a patient's INR value will be similar at any hospital.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium is a required component of the PT assay everywhere, not an optional ingredient that varies by site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Incubation intervals are part of the mixing study protocol, not a source of PT variability between hospitals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PT is performed on plasma after centrifugation and does not depend on the patient's platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PT assesses the extrinsic and common pathways; the intrinsic factors XI, IX, and VIII are not measured by it.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory switches from reporting the partial thromboplastin time to reporting the activated partial thromboplastin time. Which of the following best describes how the aPTT differs from the PTT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An activator is added, speeding clot formation and narrowing the range

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium is omitted, so the specimen cannot clot prematurely

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal plasma is added, so factor deficiencies are corrected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombin is added, so fibrinogen conversion is measured directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor is added, so the extrinsic pathway is also assessed

explanation.summary: The aPTT adds an activator to the PTT assay, speeding clot formation, narrowing the reference range, and improving sensitivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the aPTT, an activator is added to the PTT assay. This helps speed up clot formation and results in a narrower reference range, and the aPTT is considered more sensitive than the PTT. For these reasons the aPTT is the version more commonly used in clinical practice.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium is added back during the assay in both the PTT and aPTT; it is citrate in the tube that prevents premature clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adding normal plasma describes a mixing study, a separate test performed when the PTT is prolonged.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding thrombin to measure fibrinogen conversion describes the thrombin time, not the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No tissue factor-like substance is present in the PTT or aPTT; only the phospholipid portion of the reagent is used, so the extrinsic pathway is not activated.

questions.stem: An anticoagulation committee is revising the protocol for monitoring unfractionated heparin infusions and wants to adopt the assay that is gaining popularity over the aPTT for this purpose. Which of the following tests are they most likely adopting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-Xa assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bleeding time

choices.label: C
choices.text: D-dimer assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: International normalized ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin time

explanation.summary: An anti-Xa assay is increasingly used in place of the aPTT for monitoring heparin therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin has traditionally been monitored with the aPTT because heparin-activated antithrombin acts on factors of the intrinsic and common pathways. An anti-Xa assay is now beginning to gain popularity over the aPTT for monitoring heparin therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bleeding time evaluates primary hemostasis and has largely been abandoned for poor reproducibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The D-dimer assay detects degradation of cross-linked fibrin and is used to evaluate clotting, not drug levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The INR measures the extrinsic and common pathways and is the test used to follow warfarin, not heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin time assesses fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion and is used mainly for fibrinogen problems.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is started on intravenous unfractionated heparin for a deep venous thrombosis. The anticoagulant effect of this drug is produced primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of antithrombin, which then inhibits IIa, IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of phospholipid in the thromboplastin reagent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chelation of the calcium needed for factor assembly on phospholipid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degradation of cross-linked fibrin within formed clots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interference with gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent factors

explanation.summary: Heparin works by activating antithrombin, which then inhibits multiple activated factors of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin acts through antithrombin. Once antithrombin is activated, it works on many factors of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, including IIa, VIIa, IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa. Because the aPTT is much more useful for monitoring the intrinsic and common pathways, it is the assay used to follow heparin therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding phospholipid in the reagent describes the in vitro effect of antiphospholipid antibodies, not heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chelating calcium is what citrate does in the collection tube; it is not how heparin acts in a patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Degradation of cross-linked fibrin is performed by plasmin and generates D-dimers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors is the mechanism of warfarin, monitored by the INR.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man develops new large soft-tissue hematomas and has a prolonged partial thromboplastin time. On a mixing study with normal plasma, the PTT corrects immediately but is prolonged again at 1 hour and 2 hours of incubation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A specific factor inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin contamination of the specimen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lupus anticoagulant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency

explanation.summary: Immediate correction followed by prolongation on incubation is the mixing-study signature of a specific factor inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the new PTT corrects into the normal range after mixing but then becomes prolonged with incubation, a specific factor inhibitor is present. This time-dependent pattern (corrects immediately, prolongs at 1 and 2 hours) is Case #2 in the mixing-study table and reflects an antibody that needs time to inactivate the added factor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is a factor deficiency: the PTT corrects at every time point once normal plasma supplies factor VIII.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heparin in the sample blocks the reagent and does not correct at any time point after mixing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lupus anticoagulant fails to correct immediately and stays prolonged at 1 and 2 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency is a deficiency state that corrects on mixing and principally prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has an unexplained prolonged partial thromboplastin time, and a mixing study is ordered. Which of the following best describes how this study is performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Silica is added to the patient's plasma and the PTT is repeated

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient's plasma is diluted with saline and the PTT is repeated

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patient's plasma is incubated with thrombin and the clotting time is measured

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient's plasma is mixed with normal plasma and the PTT is repeated

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's serum is assayed for fibrin degradation products

explanation.summary: A mixing study is performed by mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma and rerunning the PTT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mixing study is done by mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma and then running the PTT again. If the new PTT is normal, a factor that was missing has been supplied and the patient likely has a clotting factor deficiency; if it remains prolonged, something in the patient's blood, such as a drug or an antibody, is binding up the reagent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Silica is the intrinsic-pathway activator routinely used in the PTT itself, not the basis of a mixing study.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Saline dilution adds no clotting factors and would not distinguish a deficiency from an inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incubating plasma with thrombin and timing clot formation is the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Measuring fibrin degradation products in serum is the FDP assay, used to assess fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a suspected thrombotic disorder has a markedly elevated fibrin degradation product level. This result most directly indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An antibody is inhibiting the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clots are being broken down in the body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic synthesis of clotting factors has fallen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet adhesion to the vessel wall is impaired

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation is blocked

explanation.summary: Elevated FDPs signal fibrinolysis, implying that clot is present and being broken down.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrin degradation products are substances released into the serum as a clot dissolves, specifically as fibrin is degraded by plasmin. Elevated FDPs therefore indicate that fibrinolysis is occurring in the body, implying that many clots are present, which is why the assay is used to evaluate thrombotic disorders such as DVT, pulmonary embolism, and DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inhibitory antibody is suggested by a PTT that fails to correct on mixing, not by elevated FDPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced hepatic factor synthesis prolongs the PT, PTT, and TT rather than raising FDP levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired platelet adhesion is a problem of primary hemostasis, detected by bleeding time or platelet function tests.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocked gamma-carboxylation (as with warfarin) is reflected in the INR, not in the FDP assay.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man being evaluated for possible thrombosis has an elevated fibrin degradation product level. His physician notes that this assay is less specific for the presence of a clot than the D-dimer assay. Which of the following best explains that lower specificity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FDPs appear only after factor XIII has cross-linked fibrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: FDPs are cleared by the liver and accumulate in cirrhosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: FDPs are measured in plasma rather than in serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: FDPs rise only when thrombin generation is impaired

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fibrinogen, which is not part of a clot, is also degraded to FDPs

explanation.summary: FDPs can arise from degradation of fibrinogen, a precursor that is not part of any clot, which limits the assay's specificity.
explanation.whyCorrect: FDP can also form from the degradation of fibrinogen by plasmin, which is generated from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator. Fibrinogen is the precursor of fibrin and is not a component of clots, so an elevated FDP does not necessarily mean a clot was broken down. The D-dimer, which comes only from cross-linked fibrin, is more specific for actual clot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Requiring factor XIII cross-linking describes the D-dimer, the more specific of the two assays.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Poor specificity is attributed to the source of the fragments measured, not to impaired hepatic clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FDPs are measured in serum; the specimen type is not the reason for the assay's poor specificity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FDPs rise when fibrinolysis is active, which follows thrombin-driven clot formation rather than impaired thrombin generation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with suspected deep venous thrombosis has a D-dimer assay ordered. The fragments measured by this assay are produced when plasmin degrades which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cross-linked fibrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasminogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prothrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor

explanation.summary: A D-dimer is the fibrin degradation product generated specifically from plasmin digestion of cross-linked fibrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: A D-dimer is a particular type of FDP that forms when cross-linked fibrin is degraded by plasmin. Because cross-linking occurs only within a formed clot, the D-dimer assay measures only chunks of fibrin that have been cross-linked in a clot, making it more specific for actual clot than the general FDP assay.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasmin digestion of fibrinogen yields general FDPs, not D-dimers, because fibrinogen is never cross-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasminogen is the inactive precursor converted to plasmin by tPA, not the substrate that yields D-dimers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by the common pathway and is not a plasmin substrate measured here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic pathway with factor VIIa and is not degraded into D-dimers.

questions.stem: A patient's clot is broken down in the days after an episode of thrombosis. Which of the following best describes the role of tissue plasminogen activator in this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates antithrombin to inhibit factor Xa

choices.label: B
choices.text: It combines with factor VIIa to activate factor X

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts plasminogen to plasmin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cross-links fibrin strands into a stable clot

choices.label: E
choices.text: It degrades cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers

explanation.summary: Tissue plasminogen activator catalyzes the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, the enzyme that degrades fibrin and fibrinogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin in a reaction catalyzed by tissue plasminogen activator. Plasmin then degrades fibrinogen and fibrin into fibrin degradation products, and degrades cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation of antithrombin is the mechanism of heparin and has no role in fibrinolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Combining with factor VIIa to activate factor X is the role of tissue factor in the extrinsic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cross-linking of fibrin is performed by factor XIII acting on fibrin, not by tPA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Degradation of cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers is carried out by plasmin, the product of tPA activity.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with unilateral leg swelling has a positive D-dimer result. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine whether a pathologic thrombus is actually present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obtain ultrasound imaging of the leg

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order a fibrin degradation product assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order a mixing study

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order a thrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the D-dimer assay in 24 hours

explanation.summary: A positive D-dimer lacks specificity, so imaging such as ultrasound or angiography is needed to confirm a thrombus.
explanation.whyCorrect: D-dimer and FDP assays are hypersensitive and can be elevated simply as a result of normal clotting, so they are not useful for ruling in a pathologic thrombus. If the test is positive, the patient may or may not have a pathologic thrombus and needs more testing, usually imaging such as ultrasound or angiography.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The FDP assay is even less specific than the D-dimer and cannot confirm a clot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixing studies investigate a prolonged PTT, distinguishing factor deficiency from an inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thrombin time evaluates fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion and cannot demonstrate a thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeating a test that lacks specificity provides no additional diagnostic certainty.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with recurrent nosebleeds and heavy menses has a prolonged bleeding time, a normal prothrombin time, and a normal activated partial thromboplastin time. Which of the following best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor VII deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor XII deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Von Willebrand disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin therapy

explanation.summary: A prolonged bleeding time with normal PT and aPTT points to a problem of primary hemostasis such as Von Willebrand disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleeding time is measured by making a standardized incision on the forearm and timing how long bleeding takes to stop. Causes of a prolonged bleeding time include thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, Von Willebrand disease, and vessel wall defects, none of which need to disturb the coagulation cascade assays.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT rather than the bleeding time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT in vitro and causes no clinical bleeding at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heparin prolongs the aPTT through antithrombin activation rather than prolonging the bleeding time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin prolongs the PT/INR by reducing the vitamin K-dependent factors.

questions.stem: A hematology laboratory has replaced bleeding time with platelet function testing, although bleeding time still appears on national board examinations. Which of the following is the best reason this test fell out of favor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be performed in a patient receiving heparin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has poor accuracy and reproducibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is prolonged only in coagulation factor deficiencies

choices.label: D
choices.text: It measures the same process as the prothrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires a citrated specimen that is difficult to obtain

explanation.summary: Bleeding time has largely been replaced by other assays because it has poor accuracy and reproducibility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleeding time involves making a standardized forearm incision and timing how long bleeding lasts. This test has largely been replaced by other assays, including platelet function tests, because bleeding time has poor accuracy and reproducibility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its decline is due to measurement quality, not to any restriction about anticoagulated patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bleeding time is prolonged in platelet and vessel wall disorders, not in coagulation factor deficiencies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways, an entirely different process from primary hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bleeding time is performed directly on the patient's skin and requires no collection tube at all.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a lifelong bleeding tendency has a normal prothrombin time and a normal activated partial thromboplastin time. A thrombin time is ordered and returns at 26 seconds. This result most likely indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A circulating lupus anticoagulant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acquired vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrinogen deficiency or dysfunction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary factor VII deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hereditary factor VIII deficiency

explanation.summary: A prolonged thrombin time, whose normal range is 12 to 14 seconds, points to a fibrinogen deficiency or functional mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thrombin time is at the very end of the common pathway and has much more limited use than the PT and PTT. It is a specialized test most often used to determine whether a patient has a fibrinogen deficiency or a fibrinogen functional mutation; the normal range is 12 to 14 seconds, so 26 seconds is clearly prolonged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT by binding phospholipid reagent and is associated with thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin K deficiency reduces factors II, VII, IX, and X, prolonging the PT rather than the thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, which is normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the aPTT and leaves the thrombin time normal.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with chronic malnutrition has a prolonged prothrombin time attributed to vitamin K deficiency. Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of which of the following groups of clotting factors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factors I, II, V, and X

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factors V, VIII, XI, and XII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII

explanation.summary: Factors II, VII, IX, and X are the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, and most of them lie in the extrinsic and common pathways measured by the PT.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X requires vitamin K; this is the same step that warfarin interferes with. Because most of these factors are components of the extrinsic and common pathways, deficiency of vitamin K prolongs the PT/INR, and vitamin K deficiency is listed among the acquired coagulation deficiencies detected by the PT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factors I and V are not vitamin K-dependent, so this group is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII do not require vitamin K-dependent carboxylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factors V, VIII, XI, and XII are not the vitamin K-dependent group, and several are purely intrinsic factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only factor IX in this list is vitamin K-dependent; VIII, XI, and XII are not.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with gram-negative sepsis develops oozing from venipuncture sites together with digital ischemia. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is diagnosed. Which of the following best describes the underlying process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An antibody that binds phospholipid in coagulation reagents

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficient cross-linking of fibrin strands by factor XIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of hepatic synthesis of all coagulation factors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolated destruction of circulating platelets by autoantibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widespread microthrombi with consumption of factors and platelets

explanation.summary: DIC is abnormal activation of the coagulation cascade producing widespread microthrombi and rapid consumption of factors and platelets, so hemorrhage and thrombosis occur together.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC there is abnormal activation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in widespread microthrombi throughout the vessels. This activation leads to rapid consumption of clotting factors (prolonging the INR and aPTT), fibrin, and platelets (causing thrombocytopenia), so both hemorrhage and thrombosis occur simultaneously, as seen here with oozing plus digital ischemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An antiphospholipid antibody prolongs the PTT as an in vitro artifact and causes thrombosis without factor consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deficient fibrin cross-linking would impair clot stability rather than generate widespread microthrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of hepatic factor synthesis describes liver disease, which prolongs assays without widespread thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isolated immune platelet destruction lowers platelets but does not consume clotting factors or produce microthrombi.

questions.stem: Before an elective operation, a surgeon wants to know how well a patient can form a clot. Which of the following pairs of components should be evaluated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic transaminase levels and serum albumin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelets (number and function) and the coagulation cascade

choices.label: C
choices.text: Total red blood cell mass and measured plasma viscosity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total white blood cell count and serum calcium level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vessel wall thickness and systemic arterial blood pressure

explanation.summary: Assessing clot formation means assessing platelets (number and function) and the coagulation cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a patient presents with unexplained bleeding, or if we simply want to assess how well a patient can clot before surgery, the two main things to evaluate are the platelets (number and function) and the coagulation cascade. This is because forming a clot requires making a platelet plug and then sealing it with fibrin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic enzymes reflect liver injury; the coagulation assays, not transaminases, measure clotting capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell mass and plasma viscosity describe oxygen carrying and flow properties, not clot formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: White cell count and serum calcium do not assess platelet function or cascade activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vessel wall thickness and blood pressure are hemodynamic measures, not tests of hemostasis.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist collects a coagulation sample into a plain tube with no additive and carries it to the laboratory 30 minutes later. Which of the following best describes the resulting problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Plasma cannot be separated from the cells by centrifugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood clots in the tube, so the timed assays cannot be run

choices.label: C
choices.text: The specimen contains excess calcium, falsely prolonging the aPTT

choices.label: D
choices.text: The specimen hemolyzes, falsely shortening the prothrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin in the tube degrades fibrinogen before testing

explanation.summary: Without citrate to remove calcium, blood clots in the tube before it reaches the laboratory, making timed coagulation tests impossible.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coagulation samples are drawn into a citrate tube because citrate removes calcium and prevents clotting. If blood is drawn into a regular test tube and left sitting, it will clot before it gets back to the lab and the timed tests cannot be run. In the lab the specimen is centrifuged and the plasma layer is collected for testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Centrifugation still separates layers; the specimen is unusable because fibrin has already formed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The calcium is native to the specimen rather than excess, and the problem is clotting, not a falsely prolonged aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolysis is not the issue described here; the specimen fails because it clots.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin is added deliberately only in the thrombin time assay and is not present in a collection tube.

questions.stem: A technologist performing a partial thromboplastin time adds a chemical activator of the intrinsic pathway to the patient's plasma. Which of the following substances serves this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kaolin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thromboplastin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor

explanation.summary: The PTT uses a chemical contact activator such as silica, kaolin, or celite to initiate the intrinsic pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PTT is done by adding a specific chemical activator of the intrinsic pathway, for example silica, kaolin, or celite, along with phospholipid and calcium. The test then measures the activity of the intrinsic and common pathways, that is, all the clotting factors except VII.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citrate is the anticoagulant in the collection tube; it removes calcium and prevents clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombin is added in the thrombin time to measure conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thromboplastin is the PT reagent and contains a tissue factor-like substance that triggers the extrinsic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor activates the extrinsic pathway with factor VIIa and is deliberately absent from the PTT reagent.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman taking no anticoagulant medication has coagulation studies drawn as part of a preoperative evaluation. Which of the following INR values falls within the normal reference range?

explanation.summary: The normal reference range for the INR is 0.8 to 1.2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The INR is derived from a formula using the ratio of the patient's PT to the PT done in serum with normal clotting, so the value is comparable at any hospital. Its normal range is 0.8 to 1.2, and a value of 1.1 falls within that range in a patient taking no anticoagulant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.2 lies far below the normal range of 0.8 to 1.2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.5 is below the lower limit of the normal INR range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 1.8 is above the upper limit of 1.2 and suggests impaired extrinsic or common pathway activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2.6 is well above the normal range and would be typical of a patient on warfarin therapy.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with acute onset of right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Imaging confirms an acute ischemic stroke, and he is given a thrombolytic agent that restores blood flow by breaking down the occluding clot. Which of the following molecules is directly responsible for dissolving the already-formed clot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasmin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasminogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin

explanation.summary: Plasmin is the active enzyme of fibrinolysis that degrades fibrin and dissolves clots.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clots are broken down through fibrinolysis, and the main actor is the enzyme plasmin, which cleaves the fibrin surrounding a clot into small fragments that wash away. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) generates plasmin from plasminogen and is used clinically to dissolve clots after strokes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin stops the formation of new fibrin by inhibiting thrombin, but it does not dissolve fibrin that has already formed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen is the inactive precursor that is converted into fibrin to build a clot, not to break one down.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasminogen is the inactive zymogen precursor; it must be activated to plasmin before it can degrade fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin promotes clotting by converting fibrinogen to fibrin, the opposite of clot dissolution.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman reports frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, heavy menstrual periods, and gum bleeding when she brushes her teeth. Her platelet count, PT, and aPTT are near normal, and specialized testing shows reduced activity of a protein secreted by endothelial cells. Which of the following best describes the normal function of this protein in primary hemostasis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates thrombin from prothrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It aids platelet adhesion

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts fibrinogen to fibrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cross-links fibrin strands

choices.label: E
choices.text: It dissolves fibrin clots

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand factor acts as a molecular glue that mediates platelet adhesion to the subendothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Von Willebrand factor is secreted by endothelial cells and binds both exposed subendothelial collagen and platelet glycoprotein Ib receptors, anchoring platelets to the damaged wall during platelet adhesion. Its deficiency causes von Willebrand disease, the most common hereditary bleeding disorder, with mucocutaneous bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prothrombin is activated to thrombin by activated Factor X in the common pathway, not by von Willebrand factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin is catalyzed by thrombin, part of secondary hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cross-linking of fibrin is performed by Factor XIII during secondary hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dissolving fibrin is the job of plasmin during fibrinolysis, not von Willebrand factor.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin, an anticoagulant that blocks the recycling of vitamin K. Which of the following best describes the role of vitamin K in normal coagulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates plasminogen to plasmin during fibrinolysis of a clot

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds calcium ions directly to cross-link fibrin into a clot

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly cleaves prothrombin into thrombin at the start of the common pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of Factors II, VII, IX, and X

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is required for hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factor XIII

explanation.summary: Vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on Factors II, VII, IX, and X so they can bind calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin K is a cofactor in the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting Factors II, VII, IX, and X (and proteins C and S), a modification that lets these factors bind calcium and become functional. Warfarin inhibits the enzyme that recycles vitamin K, reducing functional levels of these factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tPA, not by vitamin K.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin K does not bind calcium itself; it enables the clotting factors to bind calcium after they are carboxylated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prothrombin is cleaved to thrombin by activated Factor X in the common pathway, not by vitamin K.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrinogen synthesis occurs in the liver and is not vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for a swollen, painful knee that developed after minimal activity. He has a history of prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. Laboratory testing shows a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and normal platelet count. A deficiency of which of the following factors most likely explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor V

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XIII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Hemophilia A is an X-linked Factor VIII deficiency affecting the intrinsic pathway, causing hemarthroses with prolonged aPTT and normal PT.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia A is caused by Factor VIII deficiency, an X-linked recessive disorder that mainly affects males and presents with muscle, joint, and deep tissue bleeding such as hemarthrosis. Because Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, the aPTT is prolonged while the PT (extrinsic pathway) remains normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor V is part of the common pathway, and its involvement would prolong both PT and aPTT; it is better known for the Factor V Leiden thrombophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor VII deficiency affects the extrinsic pathway and would prolong the PT, not selectively the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin; its deficiency does not prolong the aPTT because standard tests still form an initial clot.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease usually has a normal or only mildly prolonged aPTT and features mucocutaneous rather than deep joint bleeding.

questions.stem: Immediately after a small arteriole is lacerated, a series of events begins to limit blood loss. Which of the following is the first event in primary hemostasis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Generation of active thrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood vessel constriction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of fibrin strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet adhesion to collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aggregation of platelets

explanation.summary: Vessel constriction is the first step of primary hemostasis, reducing blood flow to the injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Almost immediately after a vessel is damaged, regional small arterioles constrict, driven by endothelin released from endothelial cells. This vasoconstriction reduces blood loss and brings platelets and clotting factors into closer contact with the injured wall before the plug forms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombin activation occurs during secondary hemostasis, well after the initial vascular response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin formation stabilizes the plug during secondary hemostasis, not at the outset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet adhesion occurs after constriction, once platelets contact exposed collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet aggregation is a later step that forms the soft platelet plug.

questions.stem: A patient sustains a deep laceration, and clotting factors in the blood are exposed to a substance released from the damaged vessel wall that sits at the top of the extrinsic pathway. Which of the following substances triggers the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor XII (Hageman factor)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Tissue factor (Factor III) released by damaged tissue initiates the extrinsic pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The extrinsic pathway is triggered by tissue factor (TF, Factor III), which is normally hidden from the bloodstream until vessel cells are damaged. Once released, it activates Factor VII and initiates coagulation along the extrinsic arm, which then proceeds through the common pathway starting at Factor X.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exposed collagen and other negatively charged surfaces activate the intrinsic pathway, not the extrinsic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor XII begins the intrinsic pathway in vitro and, notably, is not required for physiologic clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombin acts within the cascade to amplify clotting and loops back to the intrinsic pathway; it does not initiate the extrinsic arm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand factor functions in platelet adhesion during primary hemostasis, not in triggering the extrinsic pathway.

questions.stem: In the coagulation cascade, the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at a single point that begins the common pathway. Which of the following factors is the convergence point where both pathways meet?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor X

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factor XII

explanation.summary: Factor X is the convergence point of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways and starts the common pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways activate Factor X to Xa, which is the start of the common pathway. From there, the common pathway (Factors X, V, II, and I) generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin to form a stable clot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor IX is an intrinsic pathway factor upstream of Factor X.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor VII belongs to the extrinsic pathway only and acts upstream of the convergence point.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway and does not represent the point of convergence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor XII initiates the intrinsic pathway in vitro and is not the shared convergence point.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman admitted with a deep vein thrombosis is started on heparin. Heparin produces its anticoagulant effect by enhancing the activity of which of the following naturally occurring molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plasmin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Heparin enhances antithrombin, which inhibits thrombin and amplification of the cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antithrombin is a natural inhibitor of thrombin, and its activity is enhanced by heparin. Because thrombin amplifies the clotting cascade, boosting antithrombin damps both the intrinsic and common pathways. Heparin-like molecules on endothelial cells naturally augment antithrombin at the vessel wall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasmin dissolves existing clots during fibrinolysis and is not the target enhanced by heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein C is activated by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex with protein S, a pathway independent of heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor switches off the extrinsic arm but is not potentiated by heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand factor promotes platelet adhesion and is unrelated to heparin's mechanism.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman of European descent has had two unprovoked deep vein thromboses. Workup reveals a mutation in Factor V that renders it resistant to cleavage by activated protein C. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor V Leiden

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Factor V Leiden is a mutation making Factor V resistant to activated protein C, the most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Factor V Leiden, mutated Factor V is not degraded by activated protein C, so the anticoagulant brake fails and clotting continues unchecked. It is the most common inherited thrombophilia (hypercoagulability) in Caucasian populations of European descent and predisposes to venous thromboses.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is a Factor VIII deficiency that causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Liver failure reduces clotting factor synthesis and tends to cause bleeding rather than clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency impairs Factors II, VII, IX, and X and causes bleeding, not a hypercoagulable state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder from deficient von Willebrand factor, the opposite of a clotting tendency.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man taking warfarin needs periodic monitoring to keep his dose in the correct range. Which laboratory test, which primarily assesses the extrinsic and common pathways, is most appropriate for monitoring his warfarin therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bleeding time

choices.label: C
choices.text: D-dimer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prothrombin time (PT/INR)

explanation.summary: The PT/INR assesses the extrinsic and common pathways and is used to monitor warfarin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prothrombin time assesses the extrinsic pathway and, by extension, the common pathway (Factors I, II, V, VII, and X). The INR standardizes the PT so clotting times can be compared between labs, making PT/INR the standard test to adjust warfarin dosing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The aPTT assesses the intrinsic and common pathways and is used to monitor heparin rather than warfarin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bleeding time reflects platelet function and vessel response, not the vitamin K-dependent factors affected by warfarin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D-dimer is a marker of fibrin breakdown used to evaluate thrombosis, not to monitor anticoagulant dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet count measures platelet number and is unaffected by warfarin's action on clotting factors.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man undergoing preoperative screening is found to have an isolated prolonged aPTT with a normal PT. He has never had abnormal bleeding, even after prior dental extractions, and further testing reveals a deficiency of Factor XII (Hageman factor). Which of the following best explains why he does not have a clinical bleeding tendency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor XII activates plasmin to prevent bleeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor XII deficiency is compensated by increased platelet counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor XII is not involved in physiologic in vivo coagulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XII is only needed for fibrinolysis, not clotting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factor XII is replaced by vitamin K in the liver

explanation.summary: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT in vitro but does not cause bleeding because Factor XII is not needed for physiologic clotting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although Factor XII deficiency prolongs clotting time in vitro (a longer aPTT), it does not cause clinical bleeding because Factor XII is not involved in physiologic coagulation. In the body, the tissue factor pathway generates thrombin that loops back to amplify the intrinsic pathway, so the cascade proceeds without Factor XII.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor XII does not activate plasmin to prevent bleeding; its absence is tolerated because it is dispensable in vivo.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bleeding protection here is not due to platelet numbers; Factor XII deficiency simply lacks physiologic relevance to clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor XII is classically an intrinsic-pathway (clotting) factor in vitro, not a dedicated fibrinolytic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K supports carboxylation of Factors II, VII, IX, and X and does not replace Factor XII.

questions.stem: A blood bank collects a unit of whole blood into a tube containing citrate to keep it from clotting during storage. Citrate prevents coagulation by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chelating calcium ions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleaving fibrin into D-dimers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Converting plasminogen to plasmin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibiting vitamin K recycling

explanation.summary: Citrate and EDTA block clotting by chelating calcium, which is required at multiple steps of the cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcium is required at numerous points in the coagulation cascade to bind and activate clotting factors. Chelating calcium with citrate or EDTA blocks these steps, which is why citrate is used in blood banking and blood is collected in EDTA tubes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is potentiated by heparin, not by citrate, and this is not how citrate anticoagulates a specimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleaving fibrin into D-dimers is the action of plasmin during fibrinolysis, unrelated to citrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Converting plasminogen to plasmin is done by tissue plasminogen activator, not by citrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting vitamin K recycling is the mechanism of warfarin, not citrate.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has a laceration of the forearm. At the injury site, von Willebrand factor binds platelet glycoprotein Ib, and the activated platelets produce thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 then activates a second platelet surface receptor that allows the platelets to bind one another. Which of the following receptors is activated by thromboxane A2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelin receptor, which binds tissue factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib, the von Willebrand factor receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombomodulin, the thrombin-binding receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor, the Factor VIIa receptor

explanation.summary: Thromboxane A2 activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor that mediates platelet aggregation.
explanation.whyCorrect: During platelet activation, thromboxane A2 activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor on the platelet surface. In the next step, activated platelets bind fibrinogen through this receptor, linking platelets into the loose soft platelet plug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endothelin is a cytokine that causes vessel constriction; it is not a platelet receptor for tissue factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycoprotein Ib binds von Willebrand factor during adhesion and acts upstream of thromboxane A2 production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombomodulin sits on endothelial cells and binds thrombin to activate protein C, not on platelets for aggregation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor is a plasma anticoagulant that switches off the extrinsic arm, not a platelet receptor.

questions.stem: A researcher studies a platelet surface receptor that anchors circulating platelets to the exposed subendothelial matrix of a damaged vessel by binding von Willebrand factor. Which of the following receptors is being studied?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein S

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombomodulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor

explanation.summary: Glycoprotein Ib is the activated platelet receptor that von Willebrand factor binds during adhesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adhesion is the step in which platelets stick to exposed collagen and subendothelial matrix. Von Willebrand factor acts as a molecular glue by binding both the exposed collagen and platelet glycoprotein Ib receptors, and this binding also activates the platelet.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen during aggregation and is activated later, by thromboxane A2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein S is a plasma cofactor for activated protein C and has no role in anchoring platelets to the wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombomodulin is an endothelial surface protein that binds thrombin to activate protein C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor is released by damaged tissue to trigger the extrinsic pathway, not to bind platelets to collagen.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has a molar extracted. Bleeding stops promptly at the end of the procedure, but several hours later he returns with steady bleeding from the socket. His platelet count and bleeding time are normal. Failure of which of the following steps best explains this pattern of delayed bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adhesion of platelets to exposed collagen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aggregation of platelets into a soft plug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Constriction of the injured arteriole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degradation of fibrin by circulating plasmin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilization of the platelet plug by fibrin

explanation.summary: Patients with clotting factor deficiencies achieve temporary hemostasis but rebleed later because the platelet plug is never stabilized by fibrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The soft platelet plug of primary hemostasis covers the hole but is not stable and quickly falls apart. Patients with deficient clotting factors can form that plug and stop bleeding right after injury, but because secondary hemostasis does not stabilize the clot with fibrin, they bleed excessively hours after a procedure such as dental surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defective adhesion impairs the initial plug, so bleeding would not have stopped promptly after the extraction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective aggregation also prevents the initial plug from forming, giving immediate rather than delayed bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed vessel constriction would produce immediate brisk bleeding at the time of injury, not a delayed rebleed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasmin degradation of fibrin is a normal clot-removal process, not the step whose failure causes rebleeding here.

questions.stem: Thrombin has converted fibrinogen to fibrin at a wound site, and one additional factor now acts on the fibrin meshwork to stabilize the clot. Which of the following factors performs this final stabilizing step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor V

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XIII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor

explanation.summary: Factor XIII, produced by platelets, stabilizes the fibrin clot into a crosslinked fibrin clot.
explanation.whyCorrect: After thrombin converts fibrinogen (Factor I) to fibrin, Factor XIII, which is produced by platelets, acts on the fibrin to stabilize the clot. The end product of the common pathway is therefore the crosslinked fibrin clot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is a natural anticoagulant that inhibits thrombin and thus opposes clot formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor IX is an intrinsic pathway factor that acts well upstream of fibrin formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor V acts in the common pathway upstream, contributing to thrombin generation rather than stabilizing fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor sits at the top of the extrinsic pathway and initiates, rather than finishes, the cascade.

questions.stem: The intrinsic and extrinsic arms of the coagulation cascade converge on a shared final segment that ends in a stable fibrin clot. Which of the following groups of factors makes up this common pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factors IX, VII, and III

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factors VII, III, and XI

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factors X, V, II, and I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factors XII, VIII, and VII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII

explanation.summary: The common pathway consists of Factors X, V, II (prothrombin), and I (fibrinogen).
explanation.whyCorrect: The common pathway is the convergence point of the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways and involves Factors X, V, II (prothrombin), and I (fibrinogen). Activated Factor X leads to thrombin production, and thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a stable clot.
