whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor IX is intrinsic while Factor VII and tissue factor are extrinsic, so this group is not the common pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor VII with tissue factor (Factor III) belongs to the extrinsic arm, and Factor XI is intrinsic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are intrinsic and extrinsic factors listed together and do not describe the shared final segment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII make up the intrinsic pathway, the arm activated by negatively charged surfaces.

questions.stem: In physiologic coagulation, tissue factor released at a site of vascular injury generates only a small quantity of thrombin. Which of the following best describes what this small amount of thrombin accomplishes next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds tissue factor pathway inhibitor to prolong the extrinsic arm

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carboxylates glutamate residues on Factors II, VII, IX, and X

choices.label: C
choices.text: It chelates calcium so downstream factors can be carboxylated

choices.label: D
choices.text: It converts plasminogen to plasmin to remodel the new clot

choices.label: E
choices.text: It loops back to the intrinsic pathway to begin the amplification phase

explanation.summary: The tissue factor arm is the initiation phase; the small amount of thrombin it makes loops back to the intrinsic pathway to amplify clotting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Physiologically, the tissue factor pathway represents the initiation phase of coagulation, generating only a small amount of thrombin. That thrombin loops back to the intrinsic pathway to activate other clotting factors and initiate the amplification phase, boosting fibrin production so the platelet plug can be glued together.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor switches the extrinsic arm off almost immediately; thrombin does not prolong it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gamma-carboxylation of those factors requires vitamin K as a cofactor and occurs during factor synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chelating calcium blocks coagulation, as with citrate or EDTA, and is not an action of thrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tissue plasminogen activator, which dissolves clots rather than building them.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with long-standing hyperlipidemia is counseled that his elevated circulating lipoproteins contribute to atherosclerosis in part through their effect on coagulation. Which of the following best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipoproteins degrade thrombomodulin, preventing protein C activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipoproteins inactivate antithrombin, removing inhibition of thrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipoproteins inhibit plasmin, preventing breakdown of formed fibrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipoproteins provide negatively charged surfaces that trigger the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lipoproteins release tissue factor into plasma, initiating the extrinsic pathway

explanation.summary: Circulating lipoproteins are one of the negatively charged surfaces that activate the intrinsic pathway, linking hyperlipidemia to atherosclerosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The intrinsic pathway is triggered by exposure to negatively charged surfaces, including bacterial infiltration, phospholipids, and circulating lipoproteins. This last trigger is the reason hyperlipidemia contributes to atherosclerosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombomodulin on endothelial cells binds thrombin to activate protein C and is not degraded by lipoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antithrombin activity is enhanced by heparin and heparin-like molecules; lipoproteins are not described as inactivating it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Free circulating plasmin is rapidly inhibited by alpha 2-plasmin, not by lipoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor is normally hidden from the bloodstream and is released by damaged vessel cells, not by lipoproteins.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered at term is given an intramuscular injection in the delivery room to prevent a bleeding disorder, including intracranial hemorrhage, that occurs because the infant's gut has not yet been colonized by the bacteria that normally supply it. Which of the following is being administered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue plasminogen activator

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K

explanation.summary: Newborns lack vitamin K-producing gut bacteria and receive a vitamin K injection to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the fetus and newborn.
explanation.whyCorrect: Newborns lack vitamin K-producing gut bacteria at birth, which predisposes them to hemorrhagic disease of the fetus and newborn with serious bleeding risks, especially intracranial hemorrhage. To prevent this, newborns routinely receive a vitamin K injection in the delivery room.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is a natural anticoagulant; giving it would promote bleeding rather than prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heparin enhances antithrombin activity and is an anticoagulant, the opposite of what a bleeding newborn needs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein C is an anticoagulant that inactivates Factors VIIIa and Va and would not correct this deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tissue plasminogen activator dissolves clots and would worsen a bleeding tendency.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is started on warfarin. In addition to reducing functional levels of procoagulant Factors II, VII, IX, and X, warfarin lowers the level of two vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulants. Which of the following pairs is affected in this way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin and thrombomodulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen and Factor XIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasmin and plasminogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein C and protein S

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor and prostacyclin

explanation.summary: Vitamin K is required for the synthesis of anticoagulant proteins C and S as well as Factors II, VII, IX, and X.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warfarin works by competitively inhibiting the effects of vitamin K, preventing its activation and depleting its functional levels. Vitamin K is important for the synthesis of the clotting factors and of the anticoagulant proteins C and S, so both groups fall on warfarin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is potentiated by heparin and thrombomodulin is an endothelial surface protein; neither depends on vitamin K.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen is synthesized in the liver without vitamin K, and Factor XIII is produced by platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasminogen and plasmin belong to the fibrinolytic system and are not vitamin K-dependent proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor and prostacyclin are endothelial products not described as vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: Seconds after the extrinsic pathway is switched on at a damaged vessel wall, a plasma substance produced by endothelial cells shuts it back down. Which of the following substances performs this function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated protein C with protein S

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha 2-plasmin, the plasmin inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antithrombin potentiated by heparin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thromboxane A2 from activated platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor

explanation.summary: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor is an endothelial product that switches off the extrinsic arm almost immediately after it is switched on.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) is a substance produced by endothelial cells and found in plasma that switches off the extrinsic arm almost immediately after the pathway is switched on. It is one of the natural anticoagulants, along with antithrombin and proteins C and S, that keep the cascade in check.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activated protein C with protein S inactivates Factors VIIIa and Va, not the tissue factor arm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha 2-plasmin inhibits free circulating plasmin and belongs to the fibrinolytic system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and therefore acts on the intrinsic and final common pathways rather than shutting off the extrinsic arm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thromboxane A2 is a platelet mediator that promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction, not an anticoagulant.

questions.stem: A plasma glycoprotein binds thrombomodulin on the endothelial cell surface and is activated by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex. Once activated, it partners with a second protein to cleave and inactivate two activated clotting factors. Which of the following pairs of factors is inactivated by this complex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factors VIIa and IXa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factors VIIIa and Va

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factors Xa and IIa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factors XIIa and XIa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factors XIIIa and Ia

explanation.summary: Activated protein C, with protein S, cleaves and inactivates Factors VIIIa and Va.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protein C is a plasma glycoprotein that binds thrombomodulin on the endothelial cell surface. When activated by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex, activated protein C binds protein S, and together they cleave and inactivate Factors VIIIa and Va. Factor V Leiden is the mutation that makes Factor V resistant to this cleavage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIIa is inhibited through the tissue factor pathway inhibitor arm, and Factor IXa is not this complex's target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor Xa and thrombin (IIa) are inhibited by antithrombin, whose activity is enhanced by heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factors XIIa and XIa sit at the top of the intrinsic arm and are not the targets of activated protein C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor XIIIa stabilizes the clot and fibrin is the end product; neither is cleaved by activated protein C.

questions.stem: Intact endothelial cells release two substances that inhibit platelet binding, secretion, and activation, helping keep blood fluid in an undamaged vessel. Which of the following pairs of substances provides this antiplatelet activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelin and thromboxane A2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasmin and D-dimer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prostacyclin and nitric oxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin and tissue factor

explanation.summary: Endothelial cells produce prostacyclin and nitric oxide, which inhibit platelet binding, secretion, and activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endothelial cells have many antithrombotic effects. They produce substances that inhibit platelet binding, secretion, and activation, namely prostacyclin and nitric oxide, and they also produce anticoagulant heparin-like molecules such as heparan sulfate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endothelin causes vessel constriction and thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation, so both favor hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen links platelets during aggregation and von Willebrand factor anchors them to the wall, both prothrombotic roles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasmin dissolves fibrin and D-dimer is a degradation product; neither is an endothelial antiplatelet substance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombin and tissue factor drive the coagulation cascade rather than inhibiting platelets.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea after a long flight. A blood test is ordered that measures a degradation product released when plasmin digests crosslinked fibrin. Which of the following is this test measuring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: D-dimer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrinogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasminogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prothrombin

explanation.summary: Plasmin digestion of crosslinked fibrin releases D-dimers, sensitive markers used to evaluate DVT and pulmonary embolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasmin cleaves the fibrin surrounding a clot, and its digestion of crosslinked fibrin releases D-dimers. D-dimers are sensitive markers of blood clot formation and are used to help diagnose deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is a natural inhibitor of thrombin and is not produced by plasmin cleaving fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinogen is the soluble precursor that thrombin converts to fibrin, not a breakdown product of a formed clot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasminogen is the inactive zymogen incorporated into clots; it is not generated by fibrin digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prothrombin is the Factor II precursor of thrombin and is unrelated to fibrin degradation products.

questions.stem: During fibrinolysis, a small amount of plasmin escapes the clot and enters the circulation, where it is rapidly neutralized so that widespread fibrin breakdown does not occur. Which of the following inhibits free circulating plasmin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha 2-plasmin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antithrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein S

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombomodulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor

explanation.summary: Any free plasmin circulating in the blood is rapidly inhibited by alpha 2-plasmin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasmin acts on fibrin within the clot, where plasminogen was incorporated as the clot formed. Any free plasmin circulating in the blood is rapidly inhibited by alpha 2-plasmin, which confines fibrinolysis to the clot itself.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and thus limits fibrin formation; it does not neutralize plasmin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein S serves as the partner of activated protein C in inactivating Factors VIIIa and Va.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombomodulin binds thrombin on endothelial cells to activate protein C, an anticoagulant step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor switches off the extrinsic arm of coagulation and has no role in fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: The zymogen precursor of plasmin is already present inside a thrombus at the moment the thrombus is formed, rather than having to diffuse in afterward. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds fibrinogen and fibrin and is incorporated as the clot forms

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is cleaved from Factor XIII as the clot is stabilized

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is gamma-carboxylated so that calcium anchors it to the clot

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is produced locally by endothelial cells at the injury site

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is stored in platelet granules and released during activation

explanation.summary: Plasminogen binds fibrinogen and fibrin, so it is built into the clot as the clot forms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasminogen, the precursor of plasmin, binds to fibrinogen and fibrin and is thus incorporated into clots as they form. Tissue plasminogen activator later converts this trapped plasminogen into active plasmin, which cleaves the fibrin surrounding the clot into fragments that wash away.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor XIII stabilizes the fibrin clot and is not the source of plasminogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gamma-carboxylation with calcium binding applies to Factors II, VII, IX, and X, not to plasminogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endothelial cells secrete tissue plasminogen activator, the activator, rather than the plasminogen itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet granules release substances such as ADP and calcium during activation; plasminogen is not described among them.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive develops a calf deep vein thrombosis after a period of immobilization. Her physician reviews the three broad categories of clotting risk that explain her presentation. Which of the following sets of risk factors is being reviewed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor VIII deficiency, Factor IX deficiency, and low von Willebrand factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolonged PT, prolonged aPTT, and elevated D-dimer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency, liver failure, and malabsorption

explanation.summary: Virchow's triad of clotting risk factors is stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Virchow's triad comprises stasis (slow or stagnant blood flow), hypercoagulability (increased tendency of the blood to clot), and endothelial injury (damage to the inner lining of blood vessels). Oral estrogen in contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy predisposes to clots through hypercoagulability, and leg clots may dislodge and travel to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These factor deficiencies define hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and von Willebrand disease, all bleeding disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are laboratory results used to assess clotting, not the categories of risk that predispose to thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are blood count abnormalities; thrombocytopenia in particular causes bleeding rather than clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency, liver failure, and malabsorption are causes of acquired bleeding disorders, not thrombosis.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient receiving heparin has an activated partial thromboplastin time drawn. Which of the following is the normal range for clot formation in the aPTT test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 to 5 seconds

choices.label: B
choices.text: 11 to 14 seconds

choices.label: C
choices.text: 25 to 35 seconds

choices.label: D
choices.text: 45 to 60 seconds

choices.label: E
choices.text: 70 to 90 seconds

explanation.summary: The normal range for clot formation in the aPTT test is 25 to 35 seconds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The activated partial thromboplastin time assesses the intrinsic and, by extension, the common pathway. The normal range for the formation of a clot in the aPTT test is 25 to 35 seconds.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No standard coagulation test forms a clot this quickly; this is far below the reported aPTT range.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 11 to 14 seconds is the time normally required for the prothrombin time to form fibrin, not the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 45 to 60 seconds exceeds the normal aPTT range and would suggest a prolonged intrinsic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 70 to 90 seconds is markedly prolonged rather than normal for this assay.

questions.stem: Two clotting-time assays are performed in a laboratory. One uses a mixture of phospholipid, a tissue factor-like substance, and calcium; the other uses a phospholipid agent that provides a negative surface. Which of the following best describes the assay that uses the negative surface?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It assesses only the extrinsic pathway, excluding the common pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects fibrin degradation products released by plasmin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the aPTT, in which no extrinsic pathway activation occurs

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the prothrombin time, which is standardized as the INR

choices.label: E
choices.text: It measures platelet function rather than clotting factor activity

explanation.summary: The aPTT uses a phospholipid negative surface, so no extrinsic pathway activation occurs, unlike the PT/INR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The activated partial thromboplastin time uses a phospholipid agent that acts as a negative surface, and therefore no activation of the extrinsic pathway occurs as it does for the PT and INR. Standardizing that activation process made the aPTT more precise and reproducible, and it has replaced the original PTT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The extrinsic pathway is assessed by the PT, and both assays also reflect the common pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin degradation products are measured by the D-dimer assay, which is not a clotting-time test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prothrombin time is the assay that uses the tissue factor-like substance, and the INR standardizes that test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet function is reflected by tests such as the bleeding time, not by a phospholipid-activated clotting assay.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with heavy menses, frequent nosebleeds, and bleeding gums is told she has the most common hereditary bleeding disorder, the same one her mother has. Which of the following best characterizes the inheritance and frequency of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired rather than inherited, arising from vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Typically autosomal dominant, occurring in about 1 in 10,000 males

choices.label: C
choices.text: Typically autosomal dominant, occurring in about 1 in 100 people

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive, affecting about 1 in 100 people

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive, so females are carriers and males are affected

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder, occurring in about 1 in 100 people and typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: Von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder, occurring in about 1 in 100 people, many of whom are totally asymptomatic. It is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, although it can also be autosomal recessive, unlike the hemophilias. Symptoms are mucocutaneous: nosebleeds, easy bruising, petechiae, heavy menstrual bleeding, and gum bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin K deficiency is an acquired cause of bleeding, whereas this patient has an inherited disorder shared with her mother.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The dominant pattern is right, but the disorder is far more common than this and is not limited to males.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The frequency is correct but the pattern is not; X-linked recessive inheritance describes the hemophilias.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked recessive transmission with carrier females and affected males applies to hemophilia A and B.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is being evaluated for suspected von Willebrand disease before an elective cholecystectomy. Her platelet count, PT, and aPTT are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculate the INR to standardize her prothrombin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measure Factor IX activity to identify the deficient factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order a D-dimer level to assess for excess fibrin turnover

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order a von Willebrand factor antigen test and an activity test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the aPTT, which reliably excludes the disorder when normal

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand disease is confirmed with vWF antigen testing (quantification) and vWF activity testing (function), since routine coagulation studies are usually normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In von Willebrand disease the PT and platelet count are usually normal, and although the aPTT may be prolonged because von Willebrand factor stabilizes Factor VIII, it is not a reliable screening test. Testing options are the vWF antigen test, which quantifies the factor, and the vWF activity test, which assesses its function; confirmation typically also involves hematology consultation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The INR standardizes the prothrombin time for warfarin monitoring and adds nothing when the PT is already normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor IX deficiency defines hemophilia B, which causes deep tissue and joint bleeding in males, not this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown and is used to evaluate thrombosis, not a mucocutaneous bleeding disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The aPTT is explicitly unreliable for screening in this disorder, so a normal result does not exclude it.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with a family history of an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder has deep muscle bleeding and a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT. Testing shows normal Factor VIII activity and markedly reduced activity of a different intrinsic pathway factor. Which of the following factors is deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor V

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor X

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factor XIII

explanation.summary: Hemophilia B is an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor IX, an intrinsic pathway factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII) and hemophilia B (Factor IX) are inherited factor deficiencies presenting with muscle, joint, and deep tissue bleeding. Both are X-linked recessive and affect the intrinsic pathway, so the aPTT is increased while the PT/INR remains normal. With normal Factor VIII activity, the deficiency here is Factor IX.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor V is a common pathway factor, so a deficiency would affect both the PT and the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VII is the extrinsic pathway factor, and its deficiency prolongs the PT rather than the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor X is the convergence point of the common pathway and would likewise prolong both clotting times.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor XIII stabilizes the formed fibrin clot and its deficiency does not prolong the aPTT.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with hemophilia has recurrent bleeding into his knee after minimal or no trauma, while a child with an isolated extrinsic pathway problem rarely bleeds into joints. Which of the following best explains why joint spaces are particularly vulnerable in disorders of the intrinsic pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Joint capillaries release large amounts of tissue factor pathway inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Joint spaces are shielded from calcium needed for clotting factors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Synovial fluid contains high concentrations of plasmin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synovial joint spaces naturally have low levels of tissue factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synovial membranes lack von Willebrand factor for adhesion

explanation.summary: Synovial joint spaces have naturally low tissue factor, so the extrinsic pathway cannot compensate when the intrinsic pathway is deficient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemarthroses, bleeding into joints, are particularly common with the hemophilias. Since synovial joint spaces naturally have low levels of tissue factor, the extrinsic clotting pathway is less able to compensate in patients with disorders of the intrinsic pathway, and joint bleeding can occur with minimal to no trauma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor is an endothelial anticoagulant and is not described as concentrated in joints.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium is released near sites of injury and is not selectively excluded from joint spaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excess plasmin in synovial fluid is not the described mechanism; the issue is the local scarcity of tissue factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemophilia is a clotting factor deficiency of secondary hemostasis, and von Willebrand factor levels are normal in it.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis has easy bruising and bleeding from a small laceration. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most consistent with his liver disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated PT, elevated PTT, and thrombocytopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated PT, normal PTT, and an elevated platelet count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, and an elevated platelet count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, and normal platelet count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal PT, prolonged PTT, and normal platelet count

explanation.summary: Liver failure reduces hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, giving elevated PT and PTT together with thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liver failure, as in cirrhosis, leads to a lack of hepatic synthesis of the coagulation factors made in the liver, with reduced factor levels and increased bleeding. Laboratory analysis can show elevated PT and PTT together with thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver failure lowers rather than raises the platelet count, and it prolongs both clotting times.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal clotting times with a high platelet count would not account for his bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entirely normal studies would not explain a bleeding tendency due to impaired factor synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An isolated prolonged PTT with normal platelets suggests an intrinsic factor deficiency such as hemophilia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has bleeding gums, heavy menstrual periods, and scattered petechiae and purpura on her legs. Her PT and aPTT are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor IX deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor V Leiden mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor XII deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia produces mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae and purpura while clotting times remain normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombocytopenia, a decreased platelet count caused by a variety of conditions, may lead to mucocutaneous bleeding such as bleeding gums, heavy menstrual periods, and petechiae and purpura on the skin. Because the clotting factors themselves are unaffected, the PT and aPTT are normal, and a decreased platelet count on the CBC makes the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor IX deficiency likewise prolongs the aPTT and presents with deep tissue and joint bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor V Leiden is a hypercoagulable state that predisposes to thrombosis, not to mucocutaneous bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the aPTT and causes muscle, joint, and deep tissue bleeding rather than petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the aPTT in vitro yet causes no clinical bleeding at all.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman in the ICU is receiving a transfusion of packed red blood cells. A few minutes into the transfusion she develops chills, a temperature of 102.4 F, back pain, and dark red urine. Her blood pressure falls to 76/52 mm Hg. The blood bank later determines that her unit was mislabeled. Which of the following best explains her reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial contamination of the stored donor unit causing sepsis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking the recipient's tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recipient antibodies against ABO antigens on the donor red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recipient antibodies against HLA class I antigens on the donor leukocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 1 hypersensitivity to soluble allergens in the donor plasma

explanation.summary: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are caused by recipient anti-ABO antibodies binding mismatched donor RBCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: A mislabeled unit leading to ABO-incompatible transfusion causes an acute hemolytic reaction. Recipient antibodies against ABO antigens on the donor RBCs trigger fever/chills (the most common presenting symptom), back pain, hemoglobinuria, kidney failure, DIC, and hypotension/shock. The direct antiglobulin (DAT) test is positive in the post-transfusion sample.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial contamination can cause septic shock, but the mislabeled ABO-incompatible unit and hemoglobinuria point specifically to an acute hemolytic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor T lymphocytes attacking host tissue causes transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which presents with fever, rash, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly 7-10 days later, not within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against donor leukocyte HLA antigens cause a febrile nonhemolytic reaction, which presents with fever and flushing without hemoglobinuria or shock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A type 1 hypersensitivity (allergic) reaction presents with urticaria, itching, and wheezing rather than back pain and hemoglobinuria.

questions.stem: A trauma patient with unknown blood type is exsanguinating, and there is no time to complete blood typing. The blood bank issues emergency red blood cells that can be given to any recipient. Which of the following blood types are these units?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-negative

choices.label: B
choices.text: AB-negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: AB-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: O-negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: O-positive

explanation.summary: O-negative is the universal red cell donor because its RBCs carry no A, B, or D antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The universal RBC donor is type O-negative. Because there are no A, B, or D antigens on the surface of these red cells, they will not prompt an anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D response in any recipient. Emergency blood release therefore typically uses O-negative units.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A-negative RBCs carry the A antigen, so they would be attacked by anti-A antibodies in type B and type O recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AB-negative RBCs carry A and B antigens, which would react with anti-A and anti-B in most recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AB-positive is the universal recipient (can receive any blood), not the universal donor; its RBCs carry A, B, and D antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: O-positive RBCs carry the D antigen and could sensitize or react in Rh-negative recipients, so they are not truly universal.

questions.stem: A patient is described as a "universal recipient" who can safely receive red blood cells of any ABO and Rh type. Which of the following is this patient's blood type?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: AB-positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: B-negative

choices.label: D
choices.text: O-negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: O-positive

explanation.summary: AB-positive patients have no anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D antibodies, so they can receive any blood type.
explanation.whyCorrect: An AB-positive patient carries the A, B, and D antigens on their RBCs and therefore makes no antibodies against these antigens. With no anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D antibodies in their plasma, they can receive any type of blood, making them the universal recipient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A-positive patients have anti-B antibodies and cannot receive B or AB blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B-negative patients have anti-A (and possibly anti-D) antibodies and cannot receive A, AB, or Rh-positive blood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: O-negative patients have anti-A, anti-B, and (if exposed) anti-D antibodies, so they can receive only O-negative blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: O-positive patients have anti-A and anti-B antibodies, limiting them to O-positive or O-negative blood.

questions.stem: A blood bank technologist notes that a particular patient's plasma may contain both anti-A antibodies and anti-Rh (anti-D) antibodies. Which of the following blood types is most consistent with this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-negative

choices.label: B
choices.text: A-positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: AB-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: B-negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: B-positive

explanation.summary: A B-negative person lacks the A antigen and the D antigen, so they can form anti-A (naturally) and anti-D (after exposure).
explanation.whyCorrect: B-negative red cells carry only the B antigen (no A, no D). Anti-A antibodies are naturally occurring in anyone who lacks the A antigen. Anti-Rh (anti-D) antibodies are not naturally occurring but can develop after an Rh-negative person is exposed to Rh-positive blood. A B-negative patient can therefore have both anti-A and anti-D antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An A-negative patient has the A antigen and would not make anti-A; they could make anti-D only if exposed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An A-positive patient has the A and D antigens, so they make neither anti-A nor anti-D antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An AB-positive patient has A, B, and D antigens and makes no ABO or anti-D antibodies at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A B-positive patient has the D antigen and would not make anti-D antibodies.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative woman is pregnant with her first child. Her physician plans to give an injection of anti-D antibody (RhoGAM) during pregnancy and again immediately after delivery. Which of the following best describes how this injection prevents harm in future pregnancies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds fetal Rh-positive red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It converts the mother's blood type to Rh-positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: It crosses the placenta to protect the fetal red cells directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the fetal red cells destroyed by maternal antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses production of naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies

explanation.summary: RhoGAM is an anti-D antibody that masks fetal Rh-positive cells so the mother never becomes sensitized to the D antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: If fetal Rh-positive RBCs enter the Rh-negative mother's circulation, the RhoGAM anti-D antibodies bind those cells and prevent the mother's immune system from "seeing" the Rh antigen. This blocks formation of maternal anti-D antibodies. It is given both during pregnancy and immediately after delivery because fetal blood may enter maternal circulation at any time.

whyWrongByChoice.B: RhoGAM does not change the mother's blood type; she remains Rh-negative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RhoGAM (like the anti-D antibody used) does not cross the placenta; that property is what makes it safe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RhoGAM does not replace red cells; it prevents maternal sensitization to the D antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RhoGAM targets the D (Rh) antigen only and has no effect on naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative woman with an Rh-positive fetus received no anti-D prophylaxis during her first pregnancy, which was uncomplicated. During a later pregnancy with a second Rh-positive fetus, the fetus develops severe hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Which of the following best explains why the first fetus was spared but the second was affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-Rh antibodies are naturally occurring and take years to reach high levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal red cells only enter maternal circulation during a second pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first fetus was Rh-negative and the second was Rh-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mother developed anti-A antibodies rather than anti-Rh antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mother's initial anti-Rh antibodies were IgM and too large to cross the placenta

explanation.summary: In hemolytic disease of the newborn, the first-pregnancy anti-Rh response is IgM (cannot cross placenta), while later IgG antibodies do cross and attack the fetus.
explanation.whyCorrect: When fetal Rh-positive cells first sensitize the Rh-negative mother, the initial anti-Rh antibodies are IgM, which are too big to cross the placenta, so there is usually no harm in the current pregnancy. Over time these antibodies become IgG, which can cross the placenta. In a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, maternal IgG anti-Rh antibodies cross and hemolyze the fetal red cells, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-Rh antibodies are not naturally occurring; they form only after exposure to Rh-positive blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fetal red cells can enter maternal circulation during the first delivery (and sometimes pregnancy), which is what sensitizes the mother.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem specifies both fetuses were Rh-positive, so a change in fetal Rh type does not explain the difference.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The disease is caused by anti-Rh (anti-D) antibodies, not anti-A antibodies.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding is being prepared for an urgent transfusion. As part of pre-transfusion testing, his serum is combined with the actual red blood cells from the unit to be transfused, and the sample is observed for agglutination or hemolysis. Which of the following steps is being performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ABO forward typing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody screen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-matching

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse typing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rh (D antigen) typing

explanation.summary: The cross-match is the only pre-transfusion step that mixes recipient serum with the actual donor red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cross-matching is like a mini-transfusion: the patient's serum is combined with the specific donor RBCs. If agglutination or hemolysis occurs, the patient has an antibody against an antigen on those donor cells and the unit must not be transfused. It is the only step that uses the actual donated red cells and is done immediately before transfusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Forward typing uses the patient's own RBCs and known anti-A/anti-B reagents, not donor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The antibody screen tests patient serum against a manufactured panel of reagent RBCs, not the specific donor unit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse typing tests patient serum against known type A and type B reagent cells to confirm ABO type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rh typing detects the D antigen on the patient's own red cells using anti-D reagent.

questions.stem: A patient with active bleeding is found to have a very low fibrinogen level (fibrinogen < 100 mg/dL). Which of the following blood products is the most appropriate choice to correct this deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate is the concentrated source of fibrinogen and is preferred for bleeding with low fibrinogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor and is indicated for bleeding emergencies in patients with fibrinogen deficiency (fibrinogen < 100). It is made by thawing fresh frozen plasma and collecting the precipitate, concentrating the fibrinogen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma does contain fibrinogen, but it is diluted in a large volume of plasma, making it less efficient for correcting isolated low fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulocytes are used for uncontrolled infection with a very low neutrophil count, not for bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed RBCs are used for severe symptomatic anemia and do not contain clotting factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets treat bleeding due to thrombocytopenia and would not correct low fibrinogen.

questions.stem: A patient with symptomatic anemia and a hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL is transfused one unit of packed red blood cells. Which of the following best describes the expected effect of this single unit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It corrects a low fibrinogen level

choices.label: B
choices.text: It provides white blood cells to fight infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It raises the hemoglobin by approximately 1 g/dL

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises the platelet count by 30,000-50,000/mm3

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replaces all of the patient's coagulation factors

explanation.summary: Packed RBCs are given for severe symptomatic anemia; one unit raises hemoglobin by roughly 1 g/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Packed red blood cells are indicated for severe anemia (hemoglobin < 7 g/dL, or < 8 g/dL with symptoms) to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. One unit of packed RBCs raises the hemoglobin by approximately 1 g/dL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correcting low fibrinogen is the role of cryoprecipitate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulocyte transfusions provide white blood cells; packed RBCs contain concentrated red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Raising the platelet count by 30,000-50,000/mm3 describes a unit of apheresis platelets, not packed RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fresh frozen plasma, not packed RBCs, contains the coagulation factors.

questions.stem: Several minutes after starting a transfusion of packed red blood cells, a patient becomes hypotensive and short of breath and develops hives all over her body. She does not have a fever. Which of the following types of transfusion reaction is she most likely experiencing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allergic transfusion reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion-related acute lung injury

explanation.summary: An allergic (IgE-mediated) transfusion reaction presents with urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension without fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient is experiencing difficulty breathing and hypotension from mast cell and histamine activation, causing vasodilation and urticaria, all consistent with an anaphylactic (allergic, type 1 hypersensitivity) reaction to allergens in the donor blood. Dyspnea plus hives plus hypotension points to an IgE-mediated reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute hemolytic reactions present with fever, back pain, and hemoglobinuria, not urticaria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delayed hemolytic reactions occur roughly a week or more after transfusion, not within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Febrile nonhemolytic reactions present with fever and flushing, and this patient has no fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion-related acute lung injury causes hypoxia and respiratory failure but not the hives seen here, and the dyspnea-plus-hives-plus-hypotension picture is classic for an IgE-mediated reaction.

questions.stem: A severely immunocompromised transplant recipient receives a packed red blood cell transfusion. About 8 days later he develops fever, a diffuse rash, watery diarrhea, and hepatomegaly, and his condition rapidly deteriorates. Which of the following would most likely have prevented this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Irradiation of the blood product before transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leukoreduction to remove donor leukocytes to reduce febrile reactions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Premedication with antihistamines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pretreatment with antipyretics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use of O-negative red cells

explanation.summary: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease is caused by donor T lymphocytes and is prevented by irradiating blood products.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fever, rash, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly appearing 7-10 days after transfusion in an immunocompromised patient describe transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, in which donor T lymphocytes attack the host's tissues. It is 80-90% fatal, and prevention is achieved by irradiating the blood product to disable donor lymphocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukoreduction reduces febrile reactions and CMV transmission but does not reliably prevent graft-versus-host disease, which requires irradiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines are used for allergic reactions, not graft-versus-host disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antipyretics treat fever symptomatically and do not prevent graft-versus-host disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Using O-negative cells addresses ABO/Rh compatibility, not donor lymphocyte-mediated disease.

questions.stem: A patient receiving a red blood cell transfusion develops fever and flushing but no hypotension, back pain, hemoglobinuria, or urticaria. The reaction is attributed to recipient antibodies directed against HLA antigens on donor leukocytes. Which of the following interventions would most reduce the incidence of this type of reaction in the future?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Giving only O-negative units

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irradiation of the blood product

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukoreduction of the blood product

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premedication with epinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusing cryoprecipitate instead

explanation.summary: Febrile nonhemolytic reactions result from antibodies against donor leukocytes and are reduced by leukoreduction.
explanation.whyCorrect: A febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction is caused by recipient antibodies against HLA antigens on donor leukocytes and presents with fever and flushing. Removing the white blood cells from the product (leukoreduction) reduces the incidence of these reactions; antipyretic premedication may also be used.

whyWrongByChoice.A: O-negative units address ABO/Rh compatibility and do not target leukocyte-related febrile reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, not febrile nonhemolytic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine is used to treat anaphylaxis from allergic reactions, not to prevent febrile reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cryoprecipitate is a specific product for fibrinogen deficiency and is unrelated to preventing febrile reactions.

questions.stem: A researcher studying the biochemistry of the ABO blood group finds a precursor antigen on the surface of red blood cells from every donor she samples, including donors typed as group O. Inherited enzymes add specific sugars to this precursor to create the A and B antigens. Which of the following antigens is she describing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: B antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both A and B antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: D antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: H antigen

explanation.summary: The H antigen is the precursor antigen on all red blood cells onto which sugars are added to form A and B antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are three antigens in the ABO system: A, B, and H. The H antigen is the precursor antigen present on the surface of all RBCs. Based on inherited alleles, enzymes may add specific sugars to the H antigen, producing the A and B antigens. Type O red cells still carry the H antigen even though it is not mentioned in the blood type.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The A antigen is a product of adding a sugar to the precursor, not the precursor itself, and it is absent on type B and type O cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The B antigen is likewise a modified form of the precursor and is absent on type A and type O cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells carrying both A and B antigens are type AB; this combination is not present on every donor's red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The D antigen belongs to the Rh system, not the ABO system, and is absent in Rh-negative people.

questions.stem: Genetic testing of a healthy 24-year-old blood donor reveals an ABO genotype of BO. Which of the following antigens is expressed on this donor's red blood cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A antigen only

choices.label: B
choices.text: B antigen only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both A and B antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: H antigen only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither A nor B antigen

explanation.summary: We inherit one ABO allele from each parent and express both, so genotype BO produces the B antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: One allele (A, B, or O) is inherited from each parent and both alleles are expressed, giving six possible genotypes: AA, AO, BB, BO, AB, and OO. The O allele contributes no A or B antigen, so the BO genotype expresses the B antigen, the same antigen expressed by the BB genotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The A antigen requires inheritance of an A allele, which this donor does not carry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both A and B antigens are expressed only by the AB genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Expressing only the precursor H antigen without A or B corresponds to the OO genotype, not BO.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither A nor B antigen is expressed by the OO genotype, in which both inherited alleles are O.

questions.stem: A medical student learns that the Rh blood group system contains three antigens, but that only one of them is clinically important in transfusion practice and in hemolytic disease of the newborn. Which of the following is that antigen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: B antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: D antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: H antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: HLA antigen

explanation.summary: Within the Rh system, only the D antigen is clinically important, and it is what determines Rh-positive versus Rh-negative status.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Rh system contains three antigens, but the only clinically important one is the D antigen, which is also called the Rh antigen because it was first described in Rhesus monkeys. Red cells carrying the D antigen are Rh-positive; red cells lacking it are Rh-negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The A antigen is part of the ABO system, not the Rh system.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The B antigen is also an ABO system antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The H antigen is the ABO precursor antigen present on all red cells and is not part of the Rh system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA antigens are found on leukocytes and are implicated in febrile nonhemolytic reactions, not in Rh typing.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman who has never been pregnant and has never received a blood transfusion has a type and screen performed before elective surgery. Her red blood cells carry the A antigen and the D antigen. Which of the following antibodies is expected in her plasma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-A and anti-B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anti-D

choices.label: E
choices.text: No ABO or Rh antibodies

explanation.summary: Anti-A and anti-B antibodies are naturally occurring against whichever ABO antigen a person lacks, while anti-D forms only after exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient is A-positive. Antibodies against the A and B antigens are naturally occurring, meaning they are made automatically without antigen exposure, directed at whichever antigen the person's own red cells lack. She lacks the B antigen, so she has anti-B. Because she carries the D antigen, she cannot form anti-D.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-A would attack her own red cells, which carry the A antigen, so it is not produced.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-A is absent because her own red cells express the A antigen; only anti-B is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-D is not naturally occurring and forms only in an Rh-negative person exposed to Rh-positive blood; she is Rh-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Having no ABO antibodies at all describes the AB-positive patient, who lacks both anti-A and anti-B.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who types as blood group AB and lacks the D antigen requires red blood cell transfusion, but the blood bank has no units of his own type in stock. Which of the following units may be safely transfused into this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A-positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: AB-positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: B-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: O-negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: O-positive

explanation.summary: AB-negative patients may receive AB-negative, A-negative, B-negative, or O-negative red cells, but never Rh-positive units.
explanation.whyCorrect: An AB-negative patient has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so the ABO type of the donor unit is not limiting. However, he lacks the D antigen and may have anti-D if previously exposed, so Rh-negative blood must be given to this Rh-negative patient. Of the options, only the O-negative unit is Rh-negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A-positive units carry the D antigen, and Rh-positive blood should not be given to an Rh-negative recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AB-positive units are ABO-compatible but Rh-positive, which is the problem for an Rh-negative recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B-positive units also carry the D antigen and are therefore unsuitable for this Rh-negative patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: O-positive units lack A and B antigens but carry the D antigen, so they are not appropriate here.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative woman asks her obstetrician what determines whether her baby could develop hemolytic disease of the newborn. Which of the following conditions must be met for her fetus to be at risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The father must be Rh-negative

choices.label: B
choices.text: The father must be Rh-positive

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mother must be blood type O

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mother must have anti-A antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mother must have received Rh-negative blood previously

explanation.summary: Hemolytic disease of the newborn requires an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus, which is possible only if the father is Rh-positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemolytic disease of the newborn occurs when an Rh-negative mother makes anti-Rh antibodies against the red cells of an Rh-positive fetus. An Rh-negative mother can only give birth to an Rh-positive baby if the father was Rh-positive, since she has no D antigen to contribute.

whyWrongByChoice.A: If the father were Rh-negative, the fetus could not be Rh-positive and there would be no D antigen for maternal antibodies to attack.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mother's ABO type is not what drives this disease; the relevant antigen is the D (Rh) antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-A antibodies target the ABO system; hemolytic disease of the newborn here results from maternal anti-Rh antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exposure to Rh-negative blood would provide no D antigen and therefore could not sensitize her.

questions.stem: During pre-transfusion testing, a patient's red blood cells agglutinate when mixed with anti-A reagent and do not agglutinate when mixed with anti-B reagent. Reverse typing is then performed on the same patient. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination with both reagent type A cells and reagent type B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agglutination with reagent type A cells and hemolysis of reagent type B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agglutination with reagent type A cells but not reagent type B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Agglutination with reagent type B cells but not reagent type A cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: No agglutination with either reagent type A cells or reagent type B cells

explanation.summary: Reverse typing confirms forward typing by showing that the patient's serum agglutinates reagent cells bearing the antigen the patient lacks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Forward typing here shows A antigen present and B antigen absent, so the patient is group A. Reverse typing tests the patient's serum against known reagent type A and type B red cells. A group A patient has naturally occurring anti-B antibodies, so the serum agglutinates reagent type B cells and leaves reagent type A cells unagglutinated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Agglutination of both reagent cell types indicates anti-A plus anti-B, the pattern of a group O patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This pattern reverses the expected result, since it implies anti-A antibodies are present in a group A patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Agglutination of reagent type A cells would indicate anti-A antibodies, which a group A patient does not make against her own antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Agglutination of neither reagent cell type indicates no ABO antibodies, the pattern of a group AB patient.

questions.stem: As part of a type and screen, a blood bank technologist performs the screening step on a patient's sample. Against which of the following is the patient's serum tested during this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A purchased panel of red cells bearing various non-ABO/Rh antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Commercially prepared anti-A and anti-B antibody reagents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pooled plasma collected from several screened volunteer donors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red cells drawn from the specific donor unit selected for transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's own washed red cells resuspended in normal saline

explanation.summary: The antibody screen tests patient serum against a manufactured panel of reagent red cells carrying various non-ABO/Rh antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: After blood typing, a screen is performed in which the patient's serum is tested against a small panel of RBCs displaying various non-ABO/Rh RBC antigens. These reagent cells are purchased from a manufacturer, and the test determines whether the patient's serum contains antibodies against other blood group antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-A and anti-B reagents are combined with the patient's red cells during forward typing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor plasma is not used in the screen; the assay looks for recipient antibodies against red cell antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testing patient serum against the actual donor unit's red cells is the cross-match, the separate second part of pre-transfusion testing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient's own red cells are used in forward typing, not in the antibody screen.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man arrives in the trauma bay exsanguinating from a gunshot wound. Because a cross-match typically takes about 45 minutes and can take 1 to 2 hours or longer, the hospital activates emergency blood release and O-negative units are issued. Which of the following best describes how long emergency-release units are typically continued?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For the rest of the hospitalization, because the patient is now sensitized to D antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Until a retrospective cross-match on those same units is reported as negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Until an antibody screen performed on the donor's serum returns negative

choices.label: D
choices.text: Until the patient's hemoglobin has risen by at least 1 g/dL per unit given

choices.label: E
choices.text: Until the patient's own blood type is established and type-specific units can be issued

explanation.summary: Because O-negative units are precious and in short supply, emergency release is continued only until the patient's own type is known.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emergency blood release lets the blood bank issue products immediately, bypassing standard testing, when a patient's life is at risk, and it typically uses O-negative red cells because they are compatible with any patient. Since O-negative units are precious and can be in short supply, emergency release is typically continued only until the patient's blood type can be established and type-specific units can be given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Emergency release is a temporary measure, and continuing scarce O-negative units for an entire hospitalization is not the practice described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The point of emergency release is that the patient cannot wait for cross-match results; the switch is driven by establishing the type, not by a completed cross-match.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibody screen is performed on the recipient's serum as part of the type and screen, not on donor serum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin response guides how many units a patient needs, not whether uncrossmatched O-negative units continue to be used.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision with large-volume traumatic hemorrhage. Which of the following blood products is specifically indicated for this scenario?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole blood

explanation.summary: Whole blood is the product indicated for large-volume traumatic hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Donated whole blood is usually separated by centrifuge into red blood cells, platelets, and plasma, but whole blood itself remains among the commonly transfused products, and its stated indication is large-volume traumatic hemorrhage such as this patient's.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate is used for bleeding emergencies in patients with fibrinogen deficiency, with fibrinogen less than 100.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma is used for abnormal bleeding from coagulation factor deficiencies, warfarin over-anticoagulation, liver failure, and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulocytes are indicated for uncontrolled infection with a very low absolute neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets are indicated for medically significant bleeding related to thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A blood bank is selecting an apheresis platelet unit for a patient. Which of the following best describes the blood group antigens found on the surface of transfused platelets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ABO antigens are present, but Rh antigens are absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both ABO and Rh antigens are present

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither ABO nor Rh antigens are present

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the precursor H antigen is present

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rh antigens are present, but ABO antigens are absent

explanation.summary: Platelets carry ABO antigens on their surface but lack Rh antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelets have ABO antigens on their surface, but they lack Rh antigens. Each unit of apheresis platelets should raise the platelet count by 30,000-50,000/mm3, and platelets are crucial to primary hemostasis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cells carry both ABO and Rh antigens, but platelets do not carry Rh antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelets are not antigen-free; their ABO antigens are present on the platelet surface.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The H antigen is the ABO precursor described on red blood cells, not the only antigen expressed by platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the actual pattern; it is the Rh antigens, not the ABO antigens, that platelets lack.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy is scheduled for a major abdominal operation. His hematologist notes that different platelet count cut-offs apply depending on the clinical indication. Below which platelet count is transfusion commonly indicated before major surgery?

explanation.summary: For major surgery, a platelet count below 50,000/mm3 is the commonly cited threshold for platelet transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelets are transfused for medically significant bleeding related to thrombocytopenia, and different platelet count cut-offs are used depending on the clinical indication, with less than 50,000 cited for major surgery. Each unit of apheresis platelets should raise the count by 30,000-50,000/mm3.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 10,000/mm3 is lower than the threshold given for the major-surgery indication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 20,000/mm3 is also below the cut-off applied when a patient is going to major surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 100,000/mm3 is above the stated major-surgery threshold and would lead to unnecessary transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 150,000/mm3 falls within the normal range and is not a transfusion trigger.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman receiving induction chemotherapy for leukemia has an absolute neutrophil count of 200/mm3 and a bloodstream infection that is not responding to broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following blood products is indicated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets

explanation.summary: Granulocyte transfusion is indicated for uncontrolled infection with an absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulocytes are transfused for uncontrolled infection in a patient with a very low absolute neutrophil count, specified as less than 500/mm3. This patient's count of 200/mm3 with an infection failing to respond to antibiotics fits that indication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate is used for bleeding emergencies in patients with fibrinogen deficiency, not for neutropenic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma replaces coagulation factors and has no role in treating neutropenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells are given for severe symptomatic anemia to increase oxygen-carrying capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are given for medically significant bleeding related to thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with hematemesis and a markedly supratherapeutic INR. He is actively bleeding and needs rapid replacement of his coagulation factors. Which of the following products is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets

explanation.summary: Fresh frozen plasma contains all coagulation factors and is indicated for bleeding from warfarin over-anticoagulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fresh frozen plasma is indicated for abnormal bleeding with coagulation factor deficiencies, warfarin over-anticoagulation, liver failure, and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. It contains all of the coagulation factors, which is what this over-anticoagulated bleeding patient needs replaced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor and is reserved for fibrinogen deficiency with bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulocytes are used for uncontrolled infection with a very low absolute neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity in severe anemia but contain no coagulation factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets address bleeding caused by thrombocytopenia, which is not the problem in warfarin over-anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow reviews how cryoprecipitate is manufactured, noting that it is produced by thawing fresh frozen plasma and collecting the precipitate by centrifugation. In addition to fibrinogen, this product is a concentrated source of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin and immunoglobulins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor IX and antithrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets and granulocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The complete set of coagulation factors

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryoprecipitate is made by thawing fresh frozen plasma and collecting the precipitate by centrifugation, which concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor. This is why it is the preferred product for bleeding emergencies in patients with fibrinogen deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin and immunoglobulins are plasma proteins that are not what cryoprecipitate is used to supply.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor IX and antithrombin are not the components attributed to cryoprecipitate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets and granulocytes are separate cellular products and are not present in cryoprecipitate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Containing all coagulation factors describes fresh frozen plasma, the starting material rather than the precipitate.

questions.stem: A quality committee is standardizing terminology for the blood bank. Although several definitions exist, which of the following is a common threshold for labeling a patient's care as a massive transfusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More than 2 units of blood products in 24 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: More than 4 units of blood products in 24 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: More than 10 units of blood products in 24 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: More than 25 units of blood products in 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 50 units of blood products in 24 hours

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion is commonly defined as more than 10 units in 24 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Massive transfusion refers to any situation in which a patient is receiving a large number of blood transfusions. Different definitions exist, with a common one being more than 10 units in 24 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two units in a day is an ordinary transfusion episode and falls far short of the cited definition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Four units in a day is still below the commonly used threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25 units in a day exceeds the commonly cited threshold and would exclude many genuinely massive transfusions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 50 units in a day is far above the number used in the common definition.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a placental abruption develops hemorrhagic shock, and the team activates the massive transfusion protocol. Which of the following best describes how blood products are administered under this protocol?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least 6 units of packed red cells given rapidly in fixed 1:1:1 ratios with other products

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate given first, followed by packed red cells in a fixed 2:1 ratio

choices.label: C
choices.text: Packed red cells alone until the hemoglobin exceeds 10 g/dL, then plasma is added

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma alone in a fixed 1:1 ratio with crystalloid until the cross-match returns

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole blood alone, with platelets withheld until the bleeding has stopped

explanation.summary: A massive transfusion protocol delivers large amounts of blood products rapidly in fixed 1:1:1 ratios for hemorrhagic shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: The massive transfusion protocol refers to rapid administration of large amounts of blood products, at least 6 units of packed red blood cells, in fixed ratios that are usually 1:1:1, for the management of hemorrhagic shock. It is activated in settings such as traumatic or obstetric hemorrhage, or when the pattern of product usage and response to treatment suggests more than 6 to 10 units will be needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryoprecipitate is a fibrinogen product for specific deficiency, and a 2:1 cryoprecipitate-first scheme is not the protocol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Withholding plasma until a hemoglobin target is reached contradicts the fixed-ratio design of the protocol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma paired with crystalloid does not deliver the red cells needed for hemorrhagic shock, and the protocol exists precisely to bypass waiting for testing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole blood is indicated for large-volume traumatic hemorrhage, but the protocol described uses packed red cells in fixed ratios with other products.

questions.stem: A patient in a United States hospital refuses a medically indicated transfusion because she is afraid of contracting HIV from donated blood. Which of the following best represents the current risk of HIV transmission from blood transfusion in developed countries?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Approximately 1 in 1,000 patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Approximately 1 in 10,000 patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately 1 in 100 patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: Approximately 1 in 100,000 patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Less than 1 in 1,000,000 patients

explanation.summary: In developed countries, HIV transmission from transfusion is now less than 1 in 1,000,000 patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transfusion recipients can become infected with pathogens in donated blood, but this is increasingly rare in developed countries, where HIV transmission from blood transfusion is now less than 1 in 1,000,000 patients. Screening may be less rigorous and the risk much higher in developing countries.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1 in 1,000 risk is orders of magnitude higher than the current figure in developed countries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 1 in 10,000 risk still greatly exceeds what modern donor screening achieves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 1 in 100 risk vastly overstates the danger and would make transfusion unusable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 1 in 100,000 risk remains ten times higher than the cited figure.

questions.stem: A premature infant requires transfusion, and no units from cytomegalovirus-negative donors are available. The blood bank offers leukoreduced units, which it describes as "CMV-safe" and equivalent to units from CMV-negative donors. Which of the following best explains this equivalence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leukoreduction concentrates red cells so that fewer units are needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leukoreduction inactivates free virus circulating in the donor plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukoreduction lowers the storage temperature enough to kill the virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leukoreduction removes donor antibodies that would reactivate the virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leukoreduction removes the white blood cells in which the virus lies latent

explanation.summary: CMV remains latent inside donor white blood cells, so removing those cells makes a product CMV-safe.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like the herpes or varicella viruses, CMV remains dormant in the body after the initial infection resolves, and an otherwise healthy donor's blood can carry latent CMV that reactivates and causes disease in the recipient. Universal leukoreduction removes the white blood cells that could contain the virus, and the resulting "CMV-safe" products are considered equivalent to products collected from CMV-negative donors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Concentrating red cells to reduce the number of units transfused does not address latent virus in the product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukoreduction is a cell-removal step, not an inactivation step aimed at virus free in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukoreduction does not change storage temperature, and temperature is not how the CMV risk is addressed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The risk comes from latent virus in donor leukocytes, not from donor antibodies triggering reactivation.

questions.stem: A hospital transfusion committee is reviewing several cases of transfusion-transmitted bacteremia. Which of the following products carries the higher risk of transmitting bacterial pathogens, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate, because it is produced by centrifugation

choices.label: B
