choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma, because it is thawed before administration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocytes, because they contain living white blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells, because they are refrigerated during storage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets, because they are stored at room temperature

explanation.summary: Platelet transfusions carry a higher risk of bacterial contamination because platelets are stored at room temperature.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood products can be contaminated with bacteria from the donor's blood, the donor's skin, the phlebotomist's skin, or the environment during production or packaging. Platelet transfusions have a higher risk of carrying bacterial pathogens because they are stored at room temperature, and contamination is extremely dangerous because it can progress rapidly to bacteremia and septic shock if not recognized and treated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Centrifugation is simply how cryoprecipitate is collected from thawed plasma and is not the stated risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thawing plasma before administration is not identified as the driver of higher bacterial risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The presence of living white cells in granulocyte products relates to cellular immune complications rather than to bacterial growth in storage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Refrigerated storage of packed red cells restrains bacterial growth rather than promoting it.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman who received 2 units of packed red blood cells 9 days ago returns with fatigue, mild jaundice, and a low-grade fever. Her hemoglobin has drifted down, and her antibody screen before the transfusion had been negative. Which of the following best explains her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A type 1 hypersensitivity response to allergens in the donor plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor T lymphocytes attacking the recipient's tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recipient antibodies against ABO antigens on the donor red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recipient antibodies against HLA antigens on donor leukocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recipient antibodies against minor non-ABO antigens on the donor red cells

explanation.summary: A delayed hemolytic reaction reflects an antibody to a minor non-ABO antigen that had faded below detection and was re-stimulated by transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions are caused by recipient antibodies against minor (non-ABO) antigens on donor RBCs. Typically the antibody fades from detection over time, which is why the pre-transfusion screen was negative, and the patient is re-exposed to the antigen on a future transfusion. The picture is mild anemia or fever, with or without jaundice, occurring about a week or more after transfusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A type 1 hypersensitivity reaction produces urticaria, itching, and wheezing within minutes of the transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor T lymphocytes attacking host tissue cause transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, with rash, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly, and it is 80-90% fatal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies against ABO antigens cause an acute hemolytic reaction with fever, back pain, hemoglobinuria, and shock within minutes, not a mild picture 9 days later.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against HLA antigens on donor leukocytes cause a febrile nonhemolytic reaction with fever and flushing during transfusion.

questions.stem: A patient develops fever, back pain, and dark urine minutes into a red cell transfusion, and an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is suspected. Which of the following laboratory findings would support this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A negative antibody screen on the pre-transfusion sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive antibody screen performed on the donor's plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: A positive direct antiglobulin test on the post-transfusion sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rise in hemoglobin of approximately 1 g/dL per unit transfused

choices.label: E
choices.text: Agglutination of the patient's red cells with anti-A and anti-B reagents

explanation.summary: In an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, the direct antiglobulin test is positive on the post-transfusion sample.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are caused by recipient antibodies against ABO antigens on donor red cells, and the direct antiglobulin (DAT) test is positive in the post-transfusion sample because recipient antibody is coating the transfused cells. The clinical picture includes fever and chills as the most common presenting symptom, back pain, hemoglobinuria, kidney failure, DIC, and hypotension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A negative pre-transfusion screen is a routine result and does not confirm that hemolysis is occurring now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The antibody screen tests the recipient's serum for antibodies against red cell antigens, not the donor's plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 1 g/dL rise per unit is the expected effect of packed red cells and would argue against ongoing destruction of the transfused cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Agglutination of the patient's own cells with anti-A and anti-B reagents is forward typing showing group AB and says nothing about hemolysis.

questions.stem: A patient receiving an ABO-incompatible unit develops fever, back pain, hemoglobinuria, and a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg. The transfusion is stopped immediately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next set of interventions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antihistamines, with epinephrine and steroids if symptoms progress

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antipyretics and observation, with transfusion resumed once afebrile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous hydration, blood pressure support, and diuresis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irradiation of all subsequent blood products for this patient

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leukoreduction of all subsequent blood products for this patient

explanation.summary: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are managed with IV hydration, blood pressure support, and diuresis.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from recipient antibodies against ABO antigens on the donor red cells, and it threatens kidney failure, DIC, and shock. Treatment consists of IV hydration, blood pressure support, and diuresis, which protect the kidneys from the free hemoglobin load and support the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines, epinephrine, and steroids are the treatment for an allergic transfusion reaction with urticaria and wheezing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antipyretics and resuming the transfusion would be dangerous here, since the fever reflects ongoing intravascular hemolysis of incompatible cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease and does nothing for hemolysis already underway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leukoreduction reduces the incidence of febrile nonhemolytic reactions and would not treat this reaction.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man becomes hypoxic and hypotensive during a transfusion and progresses to respiratory failure. He has no urticaria, no back pain, and no hemoglobinuria, and transfusion-related acute lung injury is diagnosed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-D immune globulin to prevent further sensitization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antihistamines and epinephrine for an IgE-mediated reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunosuppression to blunt donor lymphocyte activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous hydration and diuresis to protect the kidneys

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supportive care, including intubation if needed

explanation.summary: Transfusion-related acute lung injury is treated supportively, and intubation may be required.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mechanism of transfusion-related acute lung injury is uncertain and may involve donor antibodies attacking recipient cells. It presents with hypoxia, hypotension, and respiratory failure, and treatment is supportive care, which may require intubation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-D immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization to the D antigen and has no role in acute lung injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antihistamines and epinephrine treat allergic reactions, which present with urticaria, itching, and wheezing that this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunosuppression is part of the supportive management of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which appears days later with fever, rash, and diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydration and diuresis are the treatment of an acute hemolytic reaction, which would show back pain and hemoglobinuria.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for a persistent nosebleed. He is adopted and his family history is unknown. On examination he has diffuse ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show a normal platelet count, a normal PT/INR, and a prolonged PTT that corrects when normal plasma is added to the sample. A specific factor assay returns a low factor VIII activity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemophilia C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: A prolonged PTT that corrects with mixing plus a low factor VIII assay identifies hemophilia A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia A results from a defect in factor VIII, part of the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade, so the PTT is prolonged while the PT is normal. Because the defect is a missing factor rather than an inhibitor, adding normal plasma restores the factor and corrects the PTT. A specific factor assay showing low factor VIII activity confirms hemophilia A and distinguishes it from hemophilia B.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia B is caused by a factor IX defect; the specific factor assay here showed low factor VIII, not factor IX.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia C is an extremely rare factor XI disorder; the low factor VIII assay points to hemophilia A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune thrombocytopenia would produce a low platelet count, but this patient's platelet count is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand disease impairs platelet plug formation and is associated with petechiae, which hemophilia patients characteristically lack.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade to understand the pathophysiology of hemophilia. In this pathway, activated factor VIII (VIIIa) exerts its primary hemostatic effect through which of the following actions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating the extrinsic pathway via tissue factor and factor VIIa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anchoring platelets to collagen at damaged blood vessel walls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converting prothrombin to thrombin independently of activated factor X

choices.label: D
choices.text: Directly cleaving fibrinogen into fibrin monomers in the clot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serving as a cofactor for activated factor IX to activate factor X

explanation.summary: Factor VIIIa is a cofactor for factor IXa, and together they activate factor X to start the common pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the intrinsic arm, activated factor VIII (VIIIa) serves as a cofactor for activated factor IX (IXa). They cooperate to activate factor X to Xa at the start of the common pathway, which eventually leads to fibrin formation that stabilizes the clot. A defect in factor VIII (or factor IX) therefore impairs fibrin formation and causes excessive bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The extrinsic pathway is initiated by tissue factor and factor VIIa and is unaffected in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anchoring platelets to damaged vessels is the role of von Willebrand factor, not factor VIIIa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by factor Xa (with factor Va) after factor X is activated, not directly by factor VIIIa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen is cleaved to fibrin by thrombin downstream in the common pathway, not by factor VIIIa.

questions.stem: A medical student is counseling a family about the genetics of hemophilia A and B. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of these two disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: Both hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both hemophilia A and hemophilia B are X-linked recessive disorders. Because males have only one X chromosome, they are affected far more often; females are usually protected by a second, normal X chromosome, though rare heterozygous females can be affected through unequal lyonization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant is the pattern of von Willebrand disease, not hemophilia A or B.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive describes hemophilia C (factor XI), not hemophilia A or B.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is unrelated to the factor VIII and IX genes involved in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked dominant does not describe hemophilia; the disease is recessive and predominantly affects males.

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia B is planning to have children and is worried about passing on his bleeding disorder. His wife has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. If the couple has a son, what is the chance the son will have hemophilia B?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cannot be determined

explanation.summary: A son inherits his father's Y chromosome and his mother's X, so an affected father cannot pass X-linked hemophilia to a son.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia B is X-linked recessive. A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X chromosome from his unaffected mother, so he has no chance of inheriting the disease from his affected father. (In contrast, all daughters would receive the father's affected X and their mother's normal X, making them carriers.)

whyWrongByChoice.B: 100% describes the carrier status of daughters, not the disease risk in sons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25% would apply to certain autosomal recessive crosses, not to a son of an affected father in an X-linked disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50% would be the risk if the mother were a carrier, but she has no family history of bleeding disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The risk can be determined precisely from the X-linked recessive inheritance pattern; it is 0% for a son.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with a suspected bleeding disorder undergoes coagulation testing. Which of the following combinations of results is most consistent with hemophilia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low platelet count with normal aPTT and PT

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal aPTT and normal PT

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal aPTT and prolonged PT

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolonged aPTT and normal PT

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged aPTT and prolonged PT

explanation.summary: Hemophilia impairs the intrinsic pathway, producing a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aPTT measures the intrinsic coagulation pathway, while the PT measures the extrinsic pathway. Because hemophilia causes a defect in the intrinsic arm, the aPTT is prolonged. The PT remains normal because the extrinsic arm is unaffected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemophilia does not lower the platelet count; a low platelet count suggests a platelet disorder instead.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal aPTT and PT would not explain the bleeding tendency of hemophilia, which prolongs the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A prolonged PT with a normal aPTT points to an extrinsic pathway defect, which is not the pattern in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prolonged PT and aPTT together suggest a common pathway or combined defect, not isolated hemophilia.

questions.stem: A patient presents complaining of easy bruising and bleeding that takes a long time to stop. On examination, which of the following findings would suggest that the patient has a bleeding disorder OTHER than hemophilia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Family history of bleeding disorders

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemarthrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal PT

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged PTT

explanation.summary: Petechiae reflect a platelet/vessel (primary hemostasis) problem and are characteristically absent in hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disorders that impair platelet plug formation, such as von Willebrand disease, can be confused with hemophilia, but hemophilia patients lack petechiae. Petechiae result from bleeding caused by minor damage in capillary blood vessels, pointing to a primary hemostasis disorder rather than hemophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A family history of bleeding disorders is consistent with inherited hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints) is more common in hemophilia, so it supports rather than argues against the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A normal PT is a typical finding in hemophilia because the extrinsic pathway is unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prolonged PTT is expected in hemophilia due to the intrinsic pathway defect.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with mild hemophilia A due to reduced factor VIII production sustains a minor bleeding episode after a small laceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prothrombin complex concentrates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant factor IX

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIIa

explanation.summary: Desmopressin raises factor VIII levels and is appropriate for mild hemophilia A with reduced factor production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Desmopressin can be used to treat some patients with mild hemophilia A because it stimulates the release of von Willebrand factor from platelets, increasing factor VIII stability and leading to increased factor VIII levels. It is effective specifically in patients with reduced factor VIII production, as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma is considered contraindicated for hemophilia A because it contains only very low concentrations of factor VIII and is not extensively treated to prevent infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prothrombin complex concentrates are used to bypass an inhibitor, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombinant factor IX is used to treat hemophilia B, not hemophilia A.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIIa is reserved for patients who have developed an inhibitor, not for a simple mild bleed.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia A has been treated with recombinant factor VIII infusions for several years. He now has worsening bleeding, and repeat testing shows a prolonged PTT that fails to correct when mixed with normal plasma. Which of the following best explains this new finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A newly acquired deficiency of factor IX

choices.label: B
choices.text: Development of an antibody against factor VIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: Development of von Willebrand disease later in life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newly acquired severe thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Newly developed vitamin K deficiency

explanation.summary: A prolonged PTT that no longer corrects with mixing indicates a factor VIII inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 15% of patients with severe hemophilia A develop antibodies to recombinant factor VIII because their bodies recognize it as a foreign protein; this antibody is called an inhibitor. In these patients the prolonged PTT is not corrected when mixed with normal plasma because the antibodies bind the free factor VIII, preventing its function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A new factor IX deficiency would still correct with a mixing study, since normal plasma supplies factor IX.
whyWrongByChoice.C: von Willebrand disease is inherited (autosomal dominant) and would not suddenly appear or cause failure of a mixing study in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombocytopenia is a low platelet count and would not cause a mixing study to fail to correct the PTT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency mainly affects the PT and the vitamin K–dependent factors and corrects with mixing.

questions.stem: A patient with hemophilia A and a high-titer inhibitor develops an acute joint bleed. The team selects an agent that controls bleeding by directly generating factor Xa and thrombin, bypassing the need for factor VIII. Which of the following was most likely used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recombinant factor IX

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIIa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIII

explanation.summary: Recombinant factor VIIa bypasses an inhibitor by directly forming factor Xa and thrombin.
explanation.whyCorrect: For moderate- or high-titer inhibitors, patients can be given recombinant factor VIIa for acute bleeding because it directly forms factor Xa and thrombin, bypassing the inhibited factor VIII. This makes it well suited to control acute bleeding when a high-titer inhibitor is present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate is considered contraindicated in hemophilia A and does not bypass an inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin only modestly raises factor VIII and is used for mild hemophilia A, not for a high-titer inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recombinant factor IX treats hemophilia B and does not bypass a factor VIII inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIII would be bound and neutralized by the high-titer inhibitor, so it would not control bleeding.

questions.stem: A newborn boy with a family history of hemophilia A is found on factor assay to have less than 1% of normal factor VIII activity. Based on this factor level, which of the following bleeding patterns is he most likely to experience?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding only from mucosal surfaces with petechiae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many bleeding episodes, often spontaneous

choices.label: C
choices.text: No bleeding tendency at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occasional trauma-induced bleeds that rarely cause crippling effects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rare bleeding episodes, usually only after major trauma or surgery

explanation.summary: Factor activity below 1% defines severe hemophilia with frequent spontaneous bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the clinical classification of hemophilia, severe disease corresponds to less than 1% factor activity and is characterized by many bleeding episodes that are usually spontaneous; such patients rarely reach adulthood without treatment. This newborn's factor VIII activity below 1% places him in the severe category.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucosal bleeding with petechiae is characteristic of platelet/vWF disorders; hemophilia patients lack petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Even mild hemophilia carries a bleeding risk; a level below 1% produces frequent, often spontaneous bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occasional trauma-induced bleeds without crippling effects describes moderate disease (1–5% activity).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rare bleeding only after major trauma or surgery describes mild disease (6–30% activity), not severe disease.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and no prior bleeding problems develops large spontaneous hematomas and muscle bleeds. Laboratory studies show a prolonged PTT that does not correct with a mixing study, and an antibody against factor VIII is identified. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired hemophilia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited hemophilia A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: A new factor VIII autoantibody in an older non-hemophiliac patient defines acquired hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acquired hemophilia arises when a non-hemophiliac patient develops an autoantibody against a specific coagulation factor, most commonly factor VIII. It tends to occur in older individuals with a female predominance and is associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease such as lupus, medications, or is idiopathic. Patients present with secondary hemostasis-type bleeding such as large hematomas and muscle bleeds, and the PTT does not correct with mixing because of the inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia C is a rare inherited factor XI deficiency, not an acquired factor VIII autoantibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inherited hemophilia A presents in childhood and has a lifelong bleeding history, not new-onset bleeding at age 72.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT and corrects with a mixing study; it does not produce a factor VIII antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand disease is inherited and associated with petechiae and impaired platelet function, and its PTT would correct with mixing.

questions.stem: A hematologist is explaining to trainees the most feared bleeding complication in patients with hemophilia. Which of the following is the most common cause of death from hemorrhage in these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cutaneous ecchymoses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gastrointestinal bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemarthrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hematuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intracranial bleeding

explanation.summary: Intracranial hemorrhage is the most common cause of death from hemorrhage in hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Additional sources of hemorrhage in hemophiliac patients include deep tissue bleeds and intracranial bleeds, and intracranial hemorrhage is identified as the most common cause of death from hemorrhage for patients with hemophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutaneous ecchymoses (easy bruising) is a common but superficial and non-fatal manifestation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastrointestinal bleeding causes blood in the stool but is not the leading cause of hemorrhagic death.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemarthrosis causes joint deformity and disability but is not the most common fatal hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hematuria reflects genitourinary bleeding and is not typically fatal.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent swelling of the right knee and prolonged bleeding after a fall. His platelet count and PT are normal, his PTT is prolonged and corrects with a mixing study, and factor VIII activity is 2%. No relative on either side of the family has ever had a bleeding problem. Which of the following best explains his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spontaneous mutation arising in the factor VIII gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: An acquired autoantibody directed against circulating factor VIII

choices.label: C
choices.text: An inherited deficiency of von Willebrand factor from his father

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inheritance of two mutated alleles from unaffected carrier parents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maternal transmission of a mutation in the factor IX gene

explanation.summary: About 30% of hemophilia A cases arise from spontaneous mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most hemophilia cases are inherited, but roughly 30% of hemophilia A cases arise from spontaneous mutations in the factor VIII gene. A boy with a low factor VIII activity, a prolonged PTT that corrects with mixing, and a normal PT therefore has hemophilia A even when no family member is affected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An autoantibody against factor VIII would prevent correction of the PTT on mixing, and this patient's PTT corrects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: von Willebrand disease is autosomal dominant and produces petechiae, which hemophilia patients lack.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive rather than autosomal recessive, so two mutated alleles inherited from carrier parents do not explain it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A factor IX mutation causes hemophilia B; this boy's factor VIII activity is the abnormal assay.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing how often hemophilia occurs and how the two main types compare in frequency. Which of the following best describes the epidemiology of hemophilia A and B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 in 5,000 live male births combined, with A about four times more common than B

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1 in 5,000 live male births combined, with B about four times more common than A

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1 in 50,000 live male births combined, with A about four times more common than B

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 1 in 500 live male births combined, with A and B occurring about equally often

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 1 in 500 live male births combined, with B about four times more common than A

explanation.summary: Both hemophilias are rare, with a combined frequency of about 1 in 5,000 live male births, and hemophilia A is about four times more common than B.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both types of hemophilia are rare, with only a combined frequency of about 1 in 5,000 live male births. Of the two types, hemophilia A is about four times more common than hemophilia B.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The combined frequency is correct here, but hemophilia A is the more common of the two types.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 in 50,000 understates the combined frequency, which is about 1 in 5,000 live male births.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The two types are not equally common, and 1 in 500 overstates the combined frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1 in 500 greatly overstates the frequency, and hemophilia A, not B, is the more common type.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with hemophilia B has had repeated episodes of painful joint swelling since he began walking. Which of the following groups of joints is most likely involved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hips, shoulders, and wrists

choices.label: B
choices.text: Knees, ankles, and elbows

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metacarpophalangeal joints and cervical spine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sacroiliac joints and lumbar spine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints

explanation.summary: Hemarthroses in hemophilia most often involve the knees, ankles, and elbows.
explanation.whyCorrect: Parts of the body subject to repeated mechanical stress, particularly the joints, experience "spontaneous" hemorrhages called hemarthroses. The most commonly affected joints are the knees, ankles, and elbows, and repeated bleeding into them can ultimately produce joint deformities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hips, shoulders, and wrists are not the joints identified as most commonly affected in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metacarpophalangeal joints and the cervical spine are not the characteristic hemarthrosis sites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sacroiliac joints and lumbar spine are not typical sites of hemarthrosis in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints are not the joints most commonly affected by hemarthrosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with severe hemophilia A has had repeated bleeding into both knees since childhood. He now has constant knee pain and markedly limited mobility, and his orthopedic surgeon is discussing joint replacement. Which of the following best explains his chronic symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune synovitis triggered by repeated recombinant factor infusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating inhibitor antibodies binding directly to joint cartilage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of crystals within the joint space over many years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Septic arthritis from hematogenous seeding of the joint space

choices.label: E
choices.text: Structural damage to muscle, nerve, and bone from recurrent bleeding

explanation.summary: Recurrent hemarthroses damage the surrounding muscles, nerves, and bone, producing chronic pain and impaired mobility that may require joint replacement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Due to recurrent joint bleeding, the surrounding muscles, nerves, and underlying bones all suffer structural damage. This leads to chronic pain and impaired mobility, and progressive worsening of the symptoms may eventually lead to joint replacement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recombinant factor infusions may provoke an inhibitor antibody, but they are not described as causing autoimmune synovitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibitors are antibodies against infused clotting factor, and they cause bleeding rather than binding cartilage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crystal deposition is not the mechanism of the joint destruction seen after recurrent hemarthroses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemophilic joint disease results from bleeding into the joint, not from infection seeding the joint space.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is referred after bleeding excessively during a dental extraction and again during an appendectomy. He has never had a spontaneous bleeding episode, and his bleeding disorder was not recognized until adulthood. A factor IX assay is abnormal. His factor IX activity is most likely in which of the following ranges?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1% to 5% of normal activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: 31% to 50% of normal activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6% to 30% of normal activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greater than 50% of normal activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Less than 1% of normal activity

explanation.summary: Mild hemophilia (6-30% activity) causes rare bleeding limited to major trauma or surgery and may not be discovered until adulthood.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the clinical classification of hemophilia, mild disease corresponds to 6-30% factor activity. These patients have rare bleeding episodes, usually only in the setting of major trauma or surgery, and the disorder may not be discovered until adulthood, exactly as in this man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activity of 1-5% is moderate disease, with occasional, usually trauma-induced bleeding beginning well before adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Activity of 31-50% is above the range at which symptomatic patients with decreased factor levels typically fall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Activity above 50% would not account for excessive surgical bleeding from a factor deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Activity below 1% is severe disease, with many bleeding episodes that are usually spontaneous.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with hemophilia B has occasional bleeding problems, nearly all of which follow identifiable trauma, and he has no crippling joint disease. His factor IX activity is 3% of normal. Which of the following best classifies his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mild disease, corresponding to 1-5% activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mild disease, corresponding to 6-30% activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moderate disease, corresponding to 1-5% activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe disease, corresponding to 6-30% activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe disease, corresponding to less than 1% activity

explanation.summary: Moderate hemophilia is defined by 1-5% factor activity with occasional, usually trauma-induced bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical classification of hemophilia defines moderate disease as 1-5% factor activity. Such patients have occasional bleeding problems that are usually trauma-induced and can reach adulthood without crippling effects, which matches this boy's 3% factor IX activity and clinical course.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The label is wrong for this range: 1-5% activity defines moderate, not mild, disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mild disease is correctly paired with 6-30% activity, but this boy's level of 3% is below that range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The label is wrong for this range: 6-30% activity defines mild, not severe, disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severe disease is correctly paired with activity below 1%, and this boy's activity is higher than that.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with known hemophilia B presents with a swollen, painful left knee after a soccer game. He has no history of an inhibitor. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prednisone plus rituximab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant factor IX infusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIII infusion

explanation.summary: Hemophilia B is treated by replacing the deficient factor with recombinant factor IX.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both hemophilia A and B are treated by replacing the deficient clotting factor with recombinant factor infusions. Because hemophilia B results from a defect in factor IX, acute bleeding such as a hemarthrosis is treated with recombinant factor IX.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmopressin raises factor VIII levels by releasing von Willebrand factor and is used in mild hemophilia A.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma contains only very low factor concentrations and is not extensively treated to prevent infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone and rituximab are immunosuppressants used to eliminate an inhibitor, which this boy does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIII replaces the factor deficient in hemophilia A, which is not this boy's defect.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a lifelong mild bleeding tendency is found to have a deficiency of factor XI. Her sister has the same deficiency, and neither of her parents has a bleeding disorder. Which of the following is the inheritance pattern of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: Hemophilia C, an inherited factor XI disorder, is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia C is an inherited disorder of factor XI and is extremely rare, accounting for about 1% of hemophilia cases in the United States. Unlike hemophilia A and B, it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, which fits an affected woman with an affected sister and unaffected parents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance describes von Willebrand disease, not a factor XI deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is unrelated to the clotting factor genes involved in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked dominant inheritance does not describe any of the hemophilias.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked recessive inheritance describes hemophilia A and B, which affect males far more often than females.

questions.stem: A woman whose brother has hemophilia A is shown to be a carrier of a factor VIII gene mutation. Her husband has no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder. Which of the following best describes the expected outcomes for their children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All sons affected; all daughters carriers

choices.label: B
choices.text: All sons unaffected; half of daughters affected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Half of sons affected; half of daughters carriers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Half of sons carriers; half of daughters affected

choices.label: E
choices.text: No sons affected; all daughters affected

explanation.summary: In an X-linked recessive cross of a carrier mother and unaffected father, half of sons are affected and half of daughters are carriers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive. A carrier mother passes either her mutated or her normal X chromosome to each child, while the unaffected father contributes a normal X to daughters and a Y to sons. The expected offspring are therefore an unaffected son, an affected son, an unaffected daughter, and a carrier daughter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All sons would be affected only if the mother carried the mutation on both X chromosomes, which a carrier does not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sons receive their single X from the carrier mother, so half of them are expected to be affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Males have only one X chromosome and cannot be silent carriers; daughters here receive a normal X from their father.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Daughters receive a normal X chromosome from their unaffected father, so they are carriers rather than affected.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman whose father has hemophilia A bleeds heavily after a dental extraction. Her PT is normal, her PTT is prolonged and corrects with a mixing study, and her factor VIII activity is 18% of normal. Which of the following best explains her bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A coexisting autosomal dominant deficiency of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: A spontaneous mutation arising in her factor IX gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: An autoantibody against factor VIII acquired in adulthood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous inheritance of factor VIII mutations from both parents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inactivation of the X chromosome carrying her normal factor VIII gene

explanation.summary: Unequal lyonization can silence the normal factor VIII allele in most cells, allowing a heterozygous female to manifest hemophilia A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia is uncommon in females because a normal second X chromosome usually compensates. However, hemophilia A can be seen in heterozygous females in the rare event that the X chromosome carrying the normal factor VIII gene is inactivated in most cells, a situation termed unequal lyonization. As the daughter of an affected father, this woman is an obligate carrier, and her reduced factor VIII activity with a correcting PTT fits this mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: von Willebrand disease is associated with petechiae and impaired platelet plug formation, which are not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A factor IX mutation would cause hemophilia B; the abnormal assay here is factor VIII.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An acquired antibody against factor VIII prevents the PTT from correcting on mixing, and this patient's PTT corrects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her father transmitted an affected X chromosome, but there is no indication her mother did as well; she is heterozygous.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with mild hemophilia A has a normal circulating factor VIII protein level but markedly reduced factor VIII activity. He is given desmopressin before a dental procedure and still bleeds excessively. Which of the following best explains the failure of therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin acts only on factor IX and is ineffective in hemophilia A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin depletes von Willebrand factor and lowers factor VIII stability

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desmopressin works only in patients whose factor activity is below 1%

choices.label: D
choices.text: He has hemophilia C, in which desmopressin has no therapeutic effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: His mutation yields dysfunctional factor VIII rather than reduced factor VIII production

explanation.summary: Desmopressin raises the amount of factor VIII, so it fails when the mutation produces a dysfunctional factor at normal levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many different mutations can lead to hemophilia: some cause decreased levels of clotting factors, while others cause defective factor function with normal levels. Desmopressin works by stimulating release of von Willebrand factor, which increases factor VIII stability and raises factor VIII levels. It is therefore effective in patients with reduced factor VIII production but not in those with reduced factor VIII function and normal levels, as in this man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmopressin raises factor VIII levels and is used in mild hemophilia A, not in factor IX deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin stimulates release of von Willebrand factor from platelets rather than depleting it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desmopressin is used in mild disease, not in patients with severe deficiency below 1% activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemophilia C is a factor XI disorder; this patient's abnormality is in factor VIII function.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a severe form of von Willebrand disease is found to have a low factor VIII activity level in addition to her platelet-type bleeding, closely resembling hemophilia A. Which of the following properties of von Willebrand factor best explains her low factor VIII?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cleaves circulating factor VIII into its activated form

choices.label: B
choices.text: It converts factor X to factor Xa at the start of the common pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is required for hepatic synthesis of the factor VIII protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: It protects circulating factor VIII from degradation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It serves as the cofactor for activated factor IX in the intrinsic arm

explanation.summary: von Willebrand factor protects circulating factor VIII from degradation, so severe vWF deficiency lowers factor VIII and mimics hemophilia A.
explanation.whyCorrect: von Willebrand factor anchors platelets to damaged blood vessels and protects circulating factor VIII from degradation. Severe forms of von Willebrand disease can strongly resemble hemophilia A because the lack of vWF decreases the stability of circulating factor VIII, lowering its measured activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: von Willebrand factor does not cleave or activate factor VIII; it protects it from degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor X is activated by the factor IXa and VIIIa complex, not by von Willebrand factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: von Willebrand factor stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation rather than being needed for its synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Activated factor VIII, not von Willebrand factor, serves as the cofactor for activated factor IX.

questions.stem: Two unrelated boys are evaluated for bleeding. One is later proven to have hemophilia A and the other hemophilia B, yet both have an identical pattern on routine coagulation testing: a prolonged PTT that corrects with mixing and a normal PT. Which of the following best explains why routine coagulation testing cannot distinguish the two disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both factors are consumed during the prothrombin time reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both factors are stabilized by von Willebrand factor in the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both factors are vitamin K dependent and reported by the PT

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor IX cooperates with factor VIII to activate factor X in the intrinsic arm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The PTT reagent measures fibrinogen rather than individual factors

explanation.summary: Because factors VIII and IX work together in the intrinsic arm, either deficiency prolongs the PTT while leaving the PT normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia B is clinically indistinguishable from hemophilia A on routine coagulation testing because factor IX cooperates with factor VIII in the activation of factor X. Deficiencies of either factor impair the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade, so both forms show a prolonged PTT and a normal PT, and specific assays for factors VIII and IX are needed to tell them apart.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The PT tests the extrinsic pathway and is normal in hemophilia; factors VIII and IX are not what it reports.
whyWrongByChoice.B: von Willebrand factor protects factor VIII, but it is not what makes the two hemophilias look alike on testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PT measures the extrinsic arm, which is unaffected in hemophilia, so neither factor is reported by it here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The PTT measures the intrinsic coagulation pathway rather than fibrinogen concentration.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A continues to bleed despite recombinant factor VIII infusions, and laboratory testing quantifies his inhibitor in Bethesda units. A higher Bethesda unit value in this patient indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A greater degree of joint damage from prior hemarthroses

choices.label: B
choices.text: A higher inhibitor titer that is more difficult to treat

choices.label: C
choices.text: A higher residual factor VIII activity in his plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: A larger dose of recombinant factor VIII already administered

choices.label: E
choices.text: A lower inhibitor titer that is easier to treat

explanation.summary: Bethesda units quantify inhibitor titer: the higher the number, the higher the titer and the harder the patient is to treat.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhibitor levels are measured in Bethesda units. The higher the number, the higher the titer of the inhibitor and the more difficult the patient is to treat. Titer also determines management: low-titer inhibitors can be overwhelmed with more factor VIII, while moderate- and high-titer inhibitors require bypassing agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bethesda units are a laboratory measure of inhibitor titer and say nothing about joint damage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bethesda units measure the strength of the inhibitor antibody, not residual factor VIII activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bethesda units quantify the antibody present, not the cumulative dose of factor already given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The relationship is the reverse: a higher Bethesda value means a higher, not lower, titer.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A has developed an inhibitor that is quantified as low titer. He presents with bleeding after a fall. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this episode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated prothrombin complex concentrates to bypass the inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Emicizumab started at the time of the bleed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher doses of factor VIII to overwhelm the inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prednisone with cyclophosphamide to suppress the antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIIa infusion

explanation.summary: Low-titer inhibitors can be overcome by giving higher doses of factor VIII.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of an inhibitor depends on its titer in Bethesda units. For low-titer inhibitors, patients are typically given higher doses of factor VIII to overwhelm the inhibitor. Bypassing strategies are reserved for patients whose inhibitor titer is moderate or high.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activated prothrombin complex concentrates bypass the inhibitor and are reserved for moderate- or high-titer inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emicizumab is among the options for patients with moderate- or high-titer inhibitors, not low-titer inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunosuppression to eliminate an inhibitor is the approach used in acquired hemophilia, not in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIIa is used for acute bleeding in patients with moderate- or high-titer inhibitors.

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia A and a high-titer inhibitor is started on emicizumab. Which of the following best describes how this drug works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A concentrate of prothrombin complex factors that bypasses the inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody directed against factor IXa and factor X

choices.label: C
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody that depletes the B cells making the inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recombinant factor that directly forms factor Xa and thrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: An agent that releases von Willebrand factor and raises factor VIII levels

explanation.summary: Emicizumab is a monoclonal antibody against factor IXa and factor X used in hemophilia A patients with inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: For patients with moderate- or high-titer inhibitors, treatment options include recombinant factor VIIa, activated prothrombin complex concentrates, and emicizumab, which is a monoclonal antibody against factor IXa and factor X. Acting on these factors allows hemostasis to proceed despite the antibody that neutralizes factor VIII.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bypassing the inhibitor with a factor concentrate describes activated prothrombin complex concentrates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Depleting antibody-producing B cells describes rituximab, which is used as immunosuppression in acquired hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Directly forming factor Xa and thrombin describes recombinant factor VIIa, a different bypassing agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Releasing von Willebrand factor to raise factor VIII levels describes desmopressin, used in mild hemophilia A.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and no prior bleeding history develops large hematomas and muscle bleeds. A factor VIII autoantibody is identified. She is given recombinant factor VIIa for the acute bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional therapy to eliminate the inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin given before each procedure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lifelong prophylactic recombinant factor VIII infusions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prednisone with or without cyclophosphamide or rituximab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serial cryoprecipitate transfusions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy to remove the site of antibody production

explanation.summary: Acquired hemophilia is treated with a bypassing agent for acute bleeding plus immunosuppression to eliminate the autoantibody.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acquired hemophilia is fundamentally an autoimmune disease in which a non-hemophiliac patient develops an antibody against a coagulation factor, most often factor VIII. Treatment includes recombinant factor VIIa or prothrombin complex concentrates for acute bleeding, plus immunosuppression to eliminate the inhibitor with prednisone with or without cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmopressin raises factor VIII levels in mild hemophilia A and does not eliminate an autoantibody.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infused factor VIII would be bound by the autoantibody and does nothing to remove the inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cryoprecipitate is not used in this setting and carries an infection risk because it is not extensively treated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not among the therapies described for eliminating an acquired factor VIII inhibitor.

questions.stem: A hematologist is counseling a 74-year-old woman newly diagnosed with acquired hemophilia. A workup for malignancy, autoimmune disease, and culprit medications is unrevealing, and she asks how often a cause is never found. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Approximately 1% of cases have no known precipitating cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: Approximately half of cases have no known precipitating cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nearly all cases follow an occult malignancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearly all cases occur in the post-partum period

choices.label: E
choices.text: The great majority of cases are caused by medications

explanation.summary: About half of acquired hemophilia cases are idiopathic, with no identified precipitating cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acquired hemophilia is rare, occurs predominantly in older individuals with a female predominance, and can occur with malignancy, autoimmune diseases such as lupus, in response to medications, or rarely post-partum. Approximately half of cases are idiopathic, meaning no precipitating cause is identified, so an unrevealing workup is common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Idiopathic cases are far more than 1%; roughly half of all cases have no identified cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignancy is one recognized association, but it accounts for only a minority of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The post-partum period is described as a rare setting for acquired hemophilia, not the usual one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Medications are one recognized trigger but do not account for the great majority of cases.

questions.stem: A resident proposes giving cryoprecipitate to a patient with hemophilia A who is bleeding, noting that cryoprecipitate contains factor VIII. The attending explains that this product is considered contraindicated for hemophilia A. Which of the following best supports that recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains factor IX rather than any appreciable factor VIII activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is effective only in patients whose factor VIII protein is dysfunctional

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not extensively treated to prevent infection, so it carries an infection risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: It must be given in prohibitively large volumes to reach a therapeutic factor VIII level

choices.label: E
choices.text: It provokes an inhibitor antibody against factor VIII in most recipients

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate contains factor VIII but is not extensively treated to prevent infection, so it is contraindicated in hemophilia A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma are both considered contraindicated for treatment of hemophilia A. Cryoprecipitate does contain factor VIII, but it is not extensively treated to prevent infection, so there is an infection risk. Recombinant factor infusions avoid this problem and are the standard replacement therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate does contain factor VIII; its problem is the infection risk, not the absence of the factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Replacement products supply factor VIII protein and are not selectively effective in patients with dysfunctional factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Needing large volumes because of a very low factor VIII concentration is the specific drawback of fresh frozen plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibitors develop in about 15% of patients with severe hemophilia A treated with recombinant factor VIII, not in most cryoprecipitate recipients.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with moderate hemophilia B is scheduled for a dental extraction. He has had no recent bleeding episodes and feels well. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to his procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consult a hematologist and ensure clotting factor is available

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defer all dental care indefinitely because of his bleeding risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give high-dose aspirin beforehand for periprocedural pain control

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proceed without special preparation because dental extractions are minor procedures

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse platelets immediately before the extraction

explanation.summary: Patients with hemophilia undergoing surgical or major dental procedures need planning, hematology input, and clotting factor on hand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with bleeding disorders such as hemophilia should be monitored carefully for bleeding when they have surgical or major dental procedures, such as dental extractions. This might include extra testing, consulting a hematologist, and ensuring that clotting factors are available should problems arise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dental care is not deferred indefinitely; it is performed with appropriate planning and factor availability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aspirin would further impair hemostasis rather than protect a patient with a bleeding disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dental extractions are specifically identified as procedures that require careful monitoring in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemophilia is a clotting factor defect with a normal platelet count, so platelet transfusion does not address the problem.

questions.stem: A student studying hemostasis asks about the role of fibrinolysis. Which of the following best describes this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of factor X to factor Xa by the factor IXa and VIIIa complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adhesion of circulating platelets to a damaged vessel wall by von Willebrand factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin by factor Xa in the common pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cross-linking of fibrinogen into fibrin by thrombin at the end of the common pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Destruction of the blood clot, triggered by the activation of plasminogen

explanation.summary: Fibrinolysis is the plasminogen-triggered destruction of a clot that occurs after the clot is no longer needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrinolysis is the process of destroying the blood clot and is triggered by the activation of blood plasminogen. It occurs later, after the clot has outlived its usefulness, and is therefore distinct from the clot-forming steps of the coagulation cascade that are impaired in hemophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation of factor X by factors IXa and VIIIa is the step of the intrinsic arm impaired in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet adhesion to a damaged vessel is a function of von Willebrand factor in primary hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin is a clot-forming step of the common pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Converting fibrinogen to fibrin builds the clot; fibrinolysis dismantles it.

questions.stem: A researcher tracing the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade notes that factor XI is converted to its activated form, XIa, before factor IX is activated. Which of the following mediates the conversion of factor XI to factor XIa?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor Va

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor VIIIa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasminogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor

explanation.summary: Thrombin activates factor XI to XIa at the top of the intrinsic arm, upstream of factor IX.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade, thrombin converts factor XI to factor XIa, which then activates factor IX to IXa. Factor IXa, with factor VIIIa as its cofactor, activates factor X at the start of the common pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor Va is a cofactor in the common pathway for the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor VIIIa serves as the cofactor for factor IXa downstream of factor XI activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasminogen is activated during fibrinolysis, which destroys the clot rather than building it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic pathway together with factor VIIa and does not act on factor XI.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with hemophilia A lacerates his forearm. Bleeding slows initially, but several hours later the wound bleeds heavily again. His platelet count and PT are normal and his PTT is prolonged. Which of the following best explains the delayed rebleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capillary fragility produces petechial bleeding around the wound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess plasmin activity dissolves the platelet plug prematurely

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelets fail to adhere to the damaged vessel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prothrombin is not synthesized because of vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: The clot does not stabilize because fibrin cannot be formed

explanation.summary: In hemophilia, an initial platelet plug forms but the clot is not stabilized because fibrin cannot be generated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mutations in factor VIII or IX decrease the activity of their clotting factors, which impairs activation of factor X and leads to a defect in fibrin formation. Because of the inability to form fibrin, the clot does not stabilize with the fibrin "glue," and excessive bleeding occurs, especially after trauma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Petechiae arise from minor capillary damage and are characteristically absent in hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess plasmin activity describes accelerated fibrinolysis, not the factor deficiency that produces this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet adhesion depends on von Willebrand factor and is intact in hemophilia, which has a normal platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency would prolong the PT, which is normal in this patient.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with severe hemophilia A develops worsening right flank and back pain over two days with a falling hematocrit. He has no external bleeding, no headache or neurologic findings, no joint swelling, a negative stool guaiac test, and a urinalysis with no blood. Which of the following is the most likely source of his hemorrhage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gastrointestinal luminal bleeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemarthrosis of the right hip and knee

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intracranial subdural hemorrhage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retroperitoneal deep tissue bleeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper genitourinary tract bleeding

explanation.summary: Deep tissue bleeds, including retroperitoneal hemorrhage, are a recognized source of major blood loss in hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Additional sources of hemorrhage in hemophiliac patients include deep tissue bleeds, specifically deep muscle and retroperitoneal bleeding, as well as intracranial bleeds. Flank and back pain with a falling hematocrit and no external or luminal bleeding localizes the hemorrhage to the retroperitoneum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrointestinal bleeding in hemophilia produces blood in the stool, and his stool guaiac test is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemarthrosis produces a painful, swollen joint, and his joints are not swollen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intracranial hemorrhage is the most common fatal bleed in hemophilia, but he has no headache or neurologic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genitourinary bleeding causes persistent hematuria, and his urinalysis shows no blood.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with von Willebrand disease has severely reduced levels of von Willebrand factor (vWF). As a direct consequence of this deficiency, which of the following is most likely to undergo increased degradation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor IX

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VII

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets

explanation.summary: One of vWF's two major functions is to bind and stabilize circulating factor VIII.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factor VIII rapidly degrades unless it is bound to vWF, which acts as its protector in the circulation. When vWF is severely deficient, factor VIII is left unprotected and its levels fall; in a small number of cases the decrease is pronounced enough to mimic hemophilia A.

whyWrongByChoice.A: vWF anchors platelets to the subendothelium; its loss does not cause degradation of endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor IX does not interact with vWF; its deficiency causes hemophilia B, an unrelated disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor VII is not bound or stabilized by vWF, so its degradation is unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are not degraded by loss of vWF; rather, they fail to adhere to the vessel wall.

questions.stem: A woman diagnosed with von Willebrand disease is found to be heterozygous for the gene defect. She is having a child with a man who has no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder. Assuming the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, what is the chance that their child will also have the disease?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cannot be determined

explanation.summary: Most vWD is autosomal dominant, with affected people typically heterozygous for the defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The father, having no signs of disease, is assumed homozygous for normal vWF, while the mother is heterozygous for the defective allele. In an autosomal dominant cross of a heterozygote with an unaffected homozygote, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the defective allele and the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A heterozygous affected parent does transmit the dominant allele to half of offspring, so risk is not zero.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 100% would require the affected parent to be homozygous, which is rare in dominant vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25% describes an autosomal recessive cross of two carriers, not this dominant scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The inheritance pattern and parental genotypes are known, so the risk can be determined.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with von Willebrand disease has major bleeding, and recombinant vWF concentrate is not available at the facility. The team decides to give a blood product that provides a concentrated, bioactive source of von Willebrand factor. Which of the following treatments contains bioactive vWF?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminocaproic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desmopressin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tranexamic acid

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated source of clotting factors, including vWF, used when vWF concentrates are unavailable.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated solution of clotting factors obtained by freezing and thawing fresh frozen plasma; it contains von Willebrand factor and serves as an alternative source when vWF concentrates are not available for major bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminocaproic acid is an antifibrinolytic that prevents clot dissolution and contains no vWF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desmopressin releases the patient's own stored vWF from endothelial cells but is not itself a source of vWF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet transfusion supplies platelets to correct thrombocytopenia or aggregation defects, not vWF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that prevents clot breakdown and contains no vWF.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male is referred to the emergency department for refractory bleeding that began immediately after a wisdom tooth extraction and that the dentist was unable to stop. He reports lifelong weekly nosebleeds that take up to two hours to stop, and his father and sister have frequent nosebleeds. PT and PTT are normal. A CBC is normal, including a normal platelet count and normal platelet appearance on blood smear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemophilia B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Mucocutaneous bleeding with a positive family history and normal platelet count and coagulation times points to vWD.
explanation.whyCorrect: The picture of mucosal bleeding (nosebleeds, post-extraction bleeding), a family history suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance, and normal PT/PTT with a normal platelet count and smear is classic for von Willebrand disease. The diagnosis would be confirmed with vWF antigen and activity testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome, caused by a glycoprotein Ib mutation, presents with thrombocytopenia and abnormally large platelets, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is X-linked, typically affects males with deep tissue and joint bleeding and a prolonged PTT, not a normal PTT with only mucosal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia B is also X-linked with deep tissue and joint bleeding and a prolonged PTT, inconsistent with the normal PTT here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura involves platelet consumption with thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, not a normal platelet count with isolated mucosal bleeding.

questions.stem: When a blood vessel is injured, subendothelial collagen is exposed and von Willebrand factor acts as the glue that adheres platelets to this collagen. Binding of vWF to which of the following platelet receptors mediates this initial platelet adhesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor VIII (antihemophilic factor)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen (factor I)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib (GpIb)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GpIIb/IIIa)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombin receptor (PAR-1)

explanation.summary: vWF adheres platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen through platelet glycoprotein Ib.
explanation.whyCorrect: In damaged vessels, vWF bridges platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen via platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb). This adhesion is the first step in building the platelet plug that prevents blood loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIII is a coagulation factor stabilized by vWF, not a platelet adhesion receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen bridges platelets through GpIIb/IIIa during aggregation; it is not the receptor for vWF adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen to mediate platelet-to-platelet aggregation, not vWF-mediated adhesion to collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thrombin receptor participates in platelet activation but is not the site of vWF-mediated adhesion to subendothelium.

questions.stem: A newborn of consanguineous parents has severe bleeding involving both mucosal surfaces and a joint. Laboratory testing shows a virtually complete absence of von Willebrand factor along with markedly decreased factor VIII. Which type of von Willebrand disease does this child most likely have?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 2N (Normandy)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3

explanation.summary: Type 3 is the most severe form: complete absence of vWF, autosomal recessive, with decreased factor VIII.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 3 vWD is the most severe form, characterized by complete absence of von Willebrand factor and inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion (fitting consanguinity). Because these patients also have decreased factor VIII, they experience both primary and secondary hemostasis bleeding, explaining the combined mucosal and joint bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The recessive inheritance, consanguinity, and neonatal onset indicate an inherited absence rather than an acquired syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 1 is the mildest form with only a partial quantitative deficiency and intact function, not complete absence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type 2 is a qualitative defect in which vWF is present but functionally abnormal, not absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 subtypes are qualitative abnormalities beyond the brick's scope and do not feature complete absence of vWF.

questions.stem: During the workup of a patient with suspected von Willebrand disease, the laboratory adds the antibiotic ristocetin to the patient's blood in a test tube. In this assay, ristocetin is used to measure which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of factor VIII in the blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concentration of fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: The function of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The integrity of the intrinsic coagulation cascade

choices.label: E
choices.text: The total quantity of von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: The ristocetin cofactor assay measures vWF function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ristocetin activates von Willebrand factor so that it binds platelets, causing agglutination in the test tube. The degree of agglutination reflects how well the vWF functions, making this a test of vWF activity rather than quantity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIII amount is measured by a factor VIII clotting activity assay, which is unrelated to ristocetin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen concentration is not measured by the ristocetin cofactor test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The intrinsic coagulation cascade is assessed by the partial thromboplastin time, not the ristocetin assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The quantity of vWF is measured by a separate vWF antigen assay, not by ristocetin.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is evaluated for easy bruising and heavy menses and is found to have a partial reduction in von Willebrand factor with normal vWF function; her family history suggests autosomal dominant inheritance. Which type of von Willebrand disease is she most likely to have, and how common is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type 1, the most common form

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type 2, the most common form

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2, the most severe form

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 3, the mildest form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3, the most common form

explanation.summary: Type 1 is a partial quantitative deficiency with intact function, autosomal dominant, and the most common form.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 1 vWD is the mildest and most common form, featuring a partial (quantitative) absence of vWF while function remains intact, and it is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, matching this presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 2 is a qualitative abnormality (functionally abnormal vWF), not a partial quantitative deficiency with intact function, and is not described as the most common.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type 2 is defined by qualitative dysfunction and is not the most severe form.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 is the most severe, not the mildest, form of vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 is the most severe form with complete absence of vWF, not the most common or mildest.

questions.stem: A brick describes a clotting disorder that is, in a sense, the 'opposite' of von Willebrand disease. In this disorder there is impaired cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers, leading initially to widespread platelet aggregation and clot formation and eventually to depletion of circulating platelets. Which disorder is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb defect)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe type 3 von Willebrand disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

explanation.summary: TTP is the thrombotic 'opposite' of vWD, driven by impaired cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers.
