explanation.whyCorrect: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, ultra-large vWF multimers are not cleaved properly, producing excess vWF and widespread platelet aggregation (causing thrombosis), which eventually depletes circulating platelets and can then cause bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a platelet receptor (GpIb) defect causing bleeding, not multimer-driven thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is a factor VIII deficiency causing bleeding, not a thrombotic disorder from excess vWF multimers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune thrombocytopenia is platelet destruction by antibodies and does not involve impaired vWF multimer cleavage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 vWD is the complete absence of vWF causing severe bleeding, the opposite of excess vWF multimers.

questions.stem: A patient with mild von Willebrand disease and residual endothelial stores of vWF has minor bleeding. The physician chooses desmopressin (DDAVP). By what mechanism does desmopressin help control bleeding in vWD?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly supplies recombinant vWF to the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It prevents dissolution of already-formed clots

choices.label: D
choices.text: It releases vWF from cellular storage compartments

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replaces deficient platelets

explanation.summary: Desmopressin releases the patient's own stored vWF from endothelial compartments.
explanation.whyCorrect: Desmopressin (DDAVP) works by releasing vWF from cellular compartments, making it useful in patients who have residual endothelial storage of vWF. Because not all patients have such stores, it does not work for everyone and is most often used in less severe bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cleaving ultra-large vWF multimers is the normal process impaired in TTP, unrelated to desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Direct supplementation describes vWF replacement therapy, not desmopressin's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preventing clot dissolution is the mechanism of antifibrinolytics such as aminocaproic and tranexamic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Replacing platelets describes platelet transfusion, not desmopressin.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with blood type O is found on routine testing to have a low vWF level that falls within the range seen in type 1 von Willebrand disease. He has no history of abnormal bleeding, easy bruising, or heavy bleeding after surgery, and no family history of a bleeding disorder. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He should be diagnosed with type 1 von Willebrand disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: He should be diagnosed with type 3 von Willebrand disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: He should be started on prophylactic desmopressin

choices.label: D
choices.text: He should immediately begin vWF replacement therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: He should not be diagnosed with von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: People with blood type O naturally have lower vWF; without bleeding symptoms they should not be diagnosed with vWD.
explanation.whyCorrect: People with blood type O generally have lower levels of vWF even without any vWD gene mutation. A person with type O and low vWF but no bleeding symptoms should not be diagnosed with von Willebrand disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A diagnosis of type 1 vWD is not appropriate when the low vWF is explained by blood type O and there are no bleeding symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 3 vWD is a severe disorder with complete absence of vWF and severe bleeding, not this asymptomatic mild reduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desmopressin is a treatment for bleeding in diagnosed vWD, not indicated in an asymptomatic person who should not be diagnosed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: vWF replacement is reserved for bleeding or surgical prophylaxis in diagnosed disease, not an asymptomatic type O individual.

questions.stem: A patient has von Willebrand disease in which the measured quantity of von Willebrand factor is roughly normal, but the vWF that is present does not work properly. Based on this, how is this patient's disease best classified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type 1, a qualitative abnormality

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type 1, a quantitative abnormality

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 2, a qualitative abnormality

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 3, a qualitative abnormality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3, a quantitative abnormality

explanation.summary: Type 2 is a qualitative abnormality: vWF amount may be normal but it is functionally abnormal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 2 vWD is a qualitative abnormality in which the amount of vWF may be normal or decreased, but the vWF is functionally abnormal. In contrast, types 1 and 3 are quantitative abnormalities (partial or complete loss with normal function).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 is quantitative, not qualitative; this mislabels the abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 1 is a quantitative abnormality with reduced amount but normal function, not a functional defect with normal quantity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 3 is quantitative (complete absence), not a qualitative abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 is a quantitative abnormality with complete absence of vWF, not normal quantity with abnormal function.

questions.stem: A hematologist counsels a family of European descent about heritable causes of abnormal bleeding and notes that one disorder is far more likely than the others in this population. Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemophilia B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and is most prevalent in people of European descent.
explanation.whyCorrect: vWD, caused by a deficiency or defect in von Willebrand factor, is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and it is most prevalent in people of European descent. Its high prevalence is part of why an evaluation for unexplained mucocutaneous bleeding usually starts here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an uncommon inherited platelet disorder caused by a mutation in glycoprotein Ib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII and is less common than vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia B is an X-linked bleeding disorder that is rarer still than hemophilia A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a thrombotic disorder of impaired vWF multimer cleavage, not the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: The severity of von Willebrand disease varies widely, and many affected people have no clinically significant symptoms for decades. Patients in this group most often first come to medical attention after which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A febrile upper respiratory tract infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: A major hemostatic challenge such as surgery or trauma

choices.label: C
choices.text: A routine course of oral iron for mild anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Routine whole blood donation at a community blood drive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained aerobic exercise such as distance running

explanation.summary: Mild or absent symptoms mean many vWD patients are not diagnosed until a major hemostatic challenge occurs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many patients with vWD go undiagnosed because they have no clinically significant symptoms, and diagnosis is often made only when they are subjected to a significant hemostatic challenge such as surgery, dental extraction, or major trauma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A febrile respiratory infection does not stress hemostasis and does not unmask the disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral iron treats anemia and does not provoke the bleeding that reveals vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Routine blood donation is not described as a trigger that reveals otherwise silent vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Strenuous exercise is not one of the hemostatic challenges that unmasks the disease.

questions.stem: A clinic's records show that von Willebrand disease is diagnosed considerably more often among its female patients than its male patients, even though the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating vWF is degraded more rapidly in women than in men

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen blocks the binding of vWF to platelet glycoprotein Ib

choices.label: C
choices.text: Men with the gene defect are usually homozygous and asymptomatic

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vWF gene defect is carried on the X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Women more often notice prolonged menstrual and childbirth bleeding

explanation.summary: vWD is diagnosed more often in women because menstruation and childbirth make abnormal bleeding easier to notice.
explanation.whyCorrect: The disease affects both sexes because it is autosomal, but women are more likely to notice prolonged bleeding during menstruation or childbirth. Menorrhagia is one of the characteristic symptoms, so women more often present for evaluation and are diagnosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no sex difference in the rate of vWF degradation; vWF is degraded no faster in women.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen is not described as interfering with vWF binding to glycoprotein Ib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygous deficiency is very rare and produces more severe, not absent, symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: vWD is autosomal, not X-linked; X-linked inheritance describes hemophilia A and B.

questions.stem: von Willebrand factor is a multimeric glycoprotein, meaning it is built from multiple monomers whose subunits carry binding sites for platelet glycoprotein receptors and for collagen. The individual monomers within a vWF multimer are held to one another by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium bridges from activated platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Covalent peptide bonds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrin strands formed by thrombin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib receptors on adjacent platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Noncovalent bonds

explanation.summary: vWF multimers are assemblies of monomers joined by noncovalent bonds.
explanation.whyCorrect: vWF is multimeric: it is built from multiple molecules (monomers) held together with noncovalent bonds, and its subunits contain the binding sites for both platelet glycoprotein receptors and collagen. Multimer size is one of the features used to classify the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium bridges from platelets are not what holds vWF monomers together.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The monomers are not joined by covalent peptide bonds; the linkage is noncovalent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin is generated later in coagulation as clotting factors are activated; it does not assemble vWF multimers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycoprotein Ib is the platelet receptor that vWF binds during adhesion, not the link between vWF monomers.

questions.stem: von Willebrand disease has three main types along with a number of subtypes. This classification is based on which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ABO blood group and the sex of the patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: The age of symptom onset and the sites of bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: The amount of vWF, multimer size, and multimer function

choices.label: D
choices.text: The platelet count, platelet size, and smear appearance

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prothrombin time, thrombin time, and fibrinogen level

explanation.summary: vWD types and subtypes are defined by vWF quantity, multimer size, and multimer functionality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Classification of vWD is based on the amount of vWF, the size of the multimers, and multimer functionality. These three features are what separate a partial quantitative loss (type 1), a functional abnormality (type 2), and complete absence (type 3).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood type O lowers vWF levels but is not used to assign a vWD type, and the disease is autosomal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Age of onset and bleeding site influence treatment decisions but are not the basis of the classification scheme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet count and size are normal in vWD and instead point toward disorders such as Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These coagulation studies do not distinguish the vWD types; classification rests on vWF quantity, multimer size, and function.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has recurrent nosebleeds and easy bruising, and laboratory testing establishes a diagnosis of von Willebrand disease. Neither parent, nor any sibling or grandparent, has ever had abnormal bleeding. Which of the following best accounts for his disease despite this negative family history?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inheritance of blood type O from both parents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal mitochondrial inheritance of the vWF gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vWF gene defect arose as an acquired random mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive transmission through unaffected female carriers

explanation.summary: Although most vWD is inherited, some cases occur via acquired random mutations, so family history may be negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are several genetic defects that cause vWD, and most are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. However, some cases occur via acquired random mutations, which explains disease in a patient whose relatives are all unaffected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Impaired cleavage of ultra-large multimers produces thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, not vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood type O lowers vWF levels, but a person with type O and no bleeding symptoms should not be diagnosed with vWD, and it does not explain his established disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vWF gene is nuclear and is not transmitted through mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: vWD is autosomal rather than X-linked; X-linked transmission characterizes hemophilia A and B.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with type 3 von Willebrand disease is admitted with bleeding into the knee joint in addition to his usual nosebleeds and gum bleeding. Which of the following best explains the deep tissue and joint bleeding in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating platelets are abnormally large and dysfunctional

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased factor VIII impairs secondary hemostasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess fibrinolysis dissolves clots after they have formed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrinogen is consumed by widespread microvascular thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultra-large vWF multimers accumulate and are not cleaved

explanation.summary: Type 3 patients also have decreased factor VIII, so they bleed from failures of both primary and secondary hemostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 3 vWD features complete absence of vWF, and because vWF normally protects factor VIII from degradation, these patients also have decreased factor VIII. The loss of platelet adhesion causes primary hemostasis bleeding (mucosal), while the factor VIII deficit causes secondary hemostasis bleeding such as hemarthrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abnormally large, dysfunctional platelets characterize Bernard-Soulier syndrome; platelet size is normal in vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excess fibrinolysis is the process that antifibrinolytic drugs oppose; it is not the mechanism of type 3 bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Consumption by widespread thrombosis is a feature of the TTP mechanism, not of type 3 vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure to cleave ultra-large multimers describes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, the thrombotic opposite of vWD.

questions.stem: After platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen at a site of vessel injury, they are linked to one another through the GpIIb/IIIa complex as the platelet plug is built. Which of the following molecules bridges adjacent platelets at this complex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor VIII

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ristocetin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subendothelial collagen

explanation.summary: Fibrinogen links platelets to one another at the GpIIb/IIIa complex during platelet plug formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adhesion tethers platelets to the vessel wall through vWF and GpIb, and the growing plug is then held together by fibrinogen bridging adjacent platelets at their GpIIb/IIIa complexes, as shown in the brick's diagram of the damaged vessel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIII is a coagulation factor carried and stabilized by vWF, not a platelet-to-platelet bridge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycoprotein Ib is the platelet receptor for vWF during adhesion, not the molecule bridging platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ristocetin is an antibiotic used in the laboratory to activate vWF and is not present in vivo.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Collagen is the subendothelial target for adhesion; it does not bridge one platelet to another.

questions.stem: In most cases of von Willebrand disease, the genetic abnormality in vWF causes bleeding chiefly through which of the following direct mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated fibrinolysis of an otherwise normal clot

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of circulating platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumption of platelets by widespread thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the liver to synthesize clotting factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired platelet adhesion and reduced plug formation

explanation.summary: The primary mechanism of bleeding in vWD is impaired platelet adhesion and reduced platelet plug formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In most cases of vWD, genetic abnormalities in vWF directly cause impaired platelet adhesion and reduced platelet plug formation. Inadequate protection of factor VIII is an additional, secondary mechanism that lowers factor VIII levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accelerated clot dissolution is what antifibrinolytic drugs prevent; it is not the primary defect in vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody-mediated platelet destruction is not the mechanism of vWD; the platelet count is typically normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet consumption by thrombosis describes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, not vWD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: vWD is a defect of a single clotting protein, not a failure of hepatic clotting factor synthesis.

questions.stem: A patient with von Willebrand disease has a reduction in factor VIII pronounced enough that the disease mimics hemophilia A. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A markedly reduced platelet count

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prolonged partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prolonged prothrombin time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Abnormally large platelets on the peripheral smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: An elevated serum fibrinogen level

explanation.summary: The PTT assesses the intrinsic arm of the cascade and is prolonged when factor VIII is decreased.
explanation.whyCorrect: Partial thromboplastin time is used to assess the intrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade, and if factor VIII is decreased the PTT will be prolonged. Because vWF protects factor VIII from degradation, severe vWF deficiency lowers factor VIII enough to lengthen the PTT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The platelet count is characteristically normal in vWD; low counts suggest another disorder entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The prothrombin time does not evaluate the intrinsic arm and is not the study prolonged by a low factor VIII.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abnormally large platelets point to Bernard-Soulier syndrome, in which glycoprotein Ib is mutated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrinogen levels are not the test used to detect a decrease in factor VIII.

questions.stem: As part of the evaluation of a patient with suspected von Willebrand disease, a factor VIII clotting activity assay is ordered. This test is performed primarily for which of the following reasons?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To assess the extrinsic arm of the coagulation cascade, where factor VIII acts

choices.label: B
choices.text: To determine how well the patient's platelets aggregate

choices.label: C
choices.text: To exclude factor VIII deficiency as a diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: To measure the size of circulating vWF multimers

choices.label: E
choices.text: To quantify the amount of vWF antigen in the blood

explanation.summary: Factor VIII clotting activity is measured to exclude factor VIII deficiency, an alternative diagnosis to vWD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factor VIII clotting activity measures the amount of factor VIII in the blood in order to rule out factor VIII deficiency, an alternative diagnosis for von Willebrand disease. It is one of the less specific tests used alongside the vWF antigen and activity assays.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIII sits in the intrinsic arm, which is assessed by the partial thromboplastin time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet function is examined with platelet aggregation studies, a different, less specific test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multimer size is assessed as part of vWF testing, not by a factor VIII clotting activity assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The quantity of vWF is measured by the vWF antigen assay rather than by a factor VIII assay.

questions.stem: Ristocetin is added to a tube containing a patient's blood, and the platelets clump together. Ristocetin produces this agglutination through which of the following actions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates vWF so that vWF binds platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: It anchors factor VIII to the platelet surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers into smaller units

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cross-links fibrinogen between adjacent platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: It exposes subendothelial collagen within the sample

explanation.summary: Ristocetin activates vWF, which then binds platelets and causes agglutination in the test tube.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the ristocetin cofactor and vWF activity tests, the antibiotic ristocetin activates vWF, which then binds platelets and causes agglutination in the test tube. Because the reaction depends on working vWF, the degree of agglutination reports vWF function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: vWF binds and stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation; ristocetin does not anchor factor VIII to platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage of ultra-large multimers is the process that is impaired in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen cross-linking at GpIIb/IIIa occurs during platelet aggregation in vivo, not through ristocetin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No subendothelial collagen is present in a test tube; ristocetin acts directly on vWF.

questions.stem: During the physical examination of a patient being evaluated for a possible bleeding disorder, tiny dots of bleeding are noted within the skin and on the mucosal surfaces of the mouth. These findings are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep tissue hematomas

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemarthroses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heme-positive stools

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Telangiectasias

explanation.summary: Petechiae are tiny dots of bleeding within the skin and mucosal surfaces.
explanation.whyCorrect: The physical examination in suspected vWD includes a search for bruises or signs of bleeding, especially in the gums and mouth, and petechiae, tiny dots of bleeding within the skin and mucosal surfaces, may be seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deep tissue hematomas are large collections of blood typical of factor deficiency, not pinpoint mucocutaneous dots.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemarthroses are bleeds into joints and reflect failure of secondary hemostasis rather than pinpoint skin bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heme-positive stools are an occasional finding in these patients but are a laboratory result, not a skin finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telangiectasias are dilated small vessels, not the pinpoint hemorrhages sought on this examination.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent nosebleeds, and von Willebrand disease is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in her evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin an empiric trial of desmopressin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a factor VIII clotting activity level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order platelet aggregation studies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take a personal and family bleeding history

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse cryoprecipitate

explanation.summary: Evaluation for vWD begins with the personal and family history, then laboratory studies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Evaluation focuses first on the patient's personal and family history, including a family history looking for bleeding disorders, followed by laboratory studies to rule out more common causes of bleeding and then tests to confirm vWD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmopressin is a treatment for bleeding and does not belong before a diagnosis has been pursued.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A factor VIII clotting activity level is a later, less specific laboratory test used to exclude factor VIII deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet aggregation studies are among the additional, less specific tests ordered after the history directs the workup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cryoprecipitate is an alternative source of vWF for major bleeding, not a diagnostic maneuver.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has lifelong nosebleeds and easy bruising. Her platelet count is low and the peripheral smear shows abnormally large platelets. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 1 von Willebrand disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3 von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a glycoprotein Ib mutation with thrombocytopenia and abnormally large platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an inherited platelet disorder caused by a mutation in glycoprotein Ib, the vWF receptor, and it presents with decreased platelets that are abnormally large in appearance. That combination separates it from vWD, in which the platelet count and smear are normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency with deep tissue and joint bleeding and a prolonged PTT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura involves impaired cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers with thrombosis, not a receptor mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 1 vWD is a partial quantitative deficiency of vWF with a normal platelet count and normal platelet appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 vWD is the complete absence of vWF itself rather than a mutation in its platelet receptor.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has repeated bleeding into his knees and ankles and a large thigh hematoma after minor trauma. His platelet count and smear are normal, the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged, and vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity are both normal. Factor VIII clotting activity is markedly decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 2 von Willebrand disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3 von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Deep tissue and joint bleeding with a prolonged PTT, low factor VIII, and normal vWF studies indicates hemophilia A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemophilia A is a hereditary disease in which factor VIII is decreased or absent; it presents with deeper tissue bleeding such as muscle bleeds and bleeding into joints, along with an elevated PTT. Normal vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity exclude von Willebrand disease as the source of the low factor VIII.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome causes thrombocytopenia with abnormally large platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding, not this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura produces platelet aggregation and thrombosis with falling platelet counts, not isolated factor VIII deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 vWD is a qualitative defect, so the ristocetin cofactor activity would be abnormal despite a normal antigen level.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 vWD shows complete absence of vWF, which is incompatible with the normal vWF antigen reported here.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with von Willebrand disease is taken for urgent surgery for a bleeding duodenal ulcer and needs rapid correction of his hemostatic defect. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminocaproic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local pressure and observation alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: vWF replacement therapy

explanation.summary: Direct vWF replacement is the treatment for major bleeding or before surgery in vWD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most patients respond to vWF replacement, and direct supplementation to raise circulating vWF is especially valuable in patients who require rapid correction of major bleeding or who are going to surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminocaproic acid prevents dissolution of formed clots and is used in moderate bleeding, not for rapid correction of major bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma is a last-choice alternative used only when vWF concentrates are unavailable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Observation is inadequate when major bleeding requires rapid hemostatic correction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet transfusion corrects thrombocytopenia or platelet aggregation defects, which are not the problem here.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with von Willebrand disease requires vWF supplementation before a tonsillectomy. Both recombinant vWF and plasma-derived vWF concentrate are stocked by the hospital pharmacy. Which of the following is the most appropriate product for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma-derived vWF concentrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet concentrate transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant vWF concentrate

explanation.summary: Recombinant vWF is approved only for adults; children are treated with plasma-derived concentrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The recombinant version of vWF is approved for use only in adults. Children may be treated with plasma-derived concentrates, which also contain factor VIII, making the plasma-derived product the appropriate choice for surgical prophylaxis in this 7-year-old.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate is likewise an alternative source used only when vWF concentrates cannot be obtained.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma is a last-choice alternative reserved for major bleeding when concentrates are unavailable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet transfusion addresses thrombocytopenia or platelet aggregation defects rather than supplying vWF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The recombinant product is approved for adults only and is therefore not appropriate for a child.

questions.stem: A hospital that stocks no vWF concentrate must treat major bleeding in a patient with von Willebrand disease, and the team considers fresh frozen plasma. Which of the following is the principal limitation of using fresh frozen plasma for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be given to patients with blood type O

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contains little vWF, so large volumes are required

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contains no factor VIII whatsoever

choices.label: D
choices.text: It dissolves clots that have already formed

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works only in patients with residual endothelial vWF stores

explanation.summary: FFP holds little vWF, so large volumes would be needed for any effect, making it a last-choice option.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate are last-choice alternative sources of vWF for major bleeding. FFP does not contain much vWF, so large volumes would be required for any effect, and these alternatives are also not intensively treated to prevent infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood type O is associated with lower native vWF levels but is not a contraindication to plasma transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma products are not devoid of factor VIII; the plasma-derived concentrates given to children contain factor VIII.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dissolution of formed clots is the process that antifibrinolytic drugs prevent; plasma does not cause it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dependence on residual endothelial stores is the limitation of desmopressin, not of fresh frozen plasma.

questions.stem: A patient with mild von Willebrand disease is scheduled for a dental procedure, and the team wishes to prevent mucosal bleeding during it. Which of the following agents accomplishes this by preventing dissolution of clots once they have formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant vWF concentrate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tranexamic acid

explanation.summary: Antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid prevent formed clots from dissolving and are used for mucosal bleeding during dental procedures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid work by preventing dissolution of the formed clots. They are useful alongside desmopressin in moderate bleeding, and for preventing mucosal bleeding during surgical procedures such as dental procedures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate supplies clotting factors including vWF rather than preventing clot breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin releases vWF from cellular compartments; it does not act on clot dissolution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet transfusion corrects thrombocytopenia or platelet aggregation defects, not fibrinolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombinant vWF directly supplements circulating vWF and has no antifibrinolytic action.

questions.stem: In certain patients with von Willebrand disease, platelet transfusion is included in the treatment plan. Which of the following is the indication for platelet transfusion in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To correct thrombocytopenia or aggregation defects

choices.label: B
choices.text: To prevent the dissolution of formed clots

choices.label: C
choices.text: To release stored vWF from endothelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: To replace factor VIII in hemophilia-like disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: To supply bioactive vWF to the circulation

explanation.summary: Platelets are transfused in vWD to correct thrombocytopenia or platelet aggregation defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: In certain types of vWD, platelets are used to correct thrombocytopenia or platelet aggregation defects in patients with acquired or inherited platelet disorders. The transfusion addresses the platelet problem itself rather than the vWF deficit.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Preventing clot dissolution is the action of aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Releasing vWF from cellular compartments is the mechanism of desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor VIII is supplied by plasma-derived vWF concentrates, which also contain factor VIII, not by platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bioactive vWF comes from vWF concentrates or cryoprecipitate, not from transfused platelets.

questions.stem: Depending on the severity of the bleed and the patient's baseline vWF level, treatment of a bleeding episode in von Willebrand disease may need to be continued for up to which of the following durations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: 14 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 24 hours

explanation.summary: Therapy for a bleeding episode in vWD may be required for up to 14 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Depending on the severity of the bleed and baseline vWF levels, patients might need therapy for up to 14 days. Specific treatment otherwise depends on the severity and site of the bleed and the type of vWD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Three days falls short of the maximum duration described for treatment of a bleeding episode.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six months describes chronic maintenance, not the treatment course for a bleeding episode.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Six weeks exceeds the stated maximum duration of therapy for a bleeding episode.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single day of therapy understates the duration that severe bleeds may require.

questions.stem: In a disorder in which ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers fail to be cleaved properly, which of the following is the initial consequence of the resulting excess of von Willebrand factor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of circulating platelets with mucosal bleeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of platelets to adhere to subendothelial collagen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolongation of the prothrombin time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid degradation of circulating factor VIII

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widespread platelet aggregation causing thrombosis

explanation.summary: Excess uncleaved vWF multimers first drive widespread platelet aggregation and thrombosis, and only later deplete platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: When cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers is impaired, the excess vWF causes widespread platelet aggregation, which produces thrombosis. Only eventually does this consume and deplete the circulating platelets, at which point bleeding appears.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelet depletion and bleeding are the eventual, not the initial, result of the excess multimers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of platelet adhesion is the defect in von Willebrand disease, the opposite situation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The prothrombin time is not the study altered by impaired multimer cleavage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor VIII degrades when vWF is deficient; an excess of vWF would if anything protect it.

questions.stem: A patient with von Willebrand disease receives desmopressin for a moderate nosebleed but has no meaningful response. Which of the following best explains the failure of this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin acts only on clots that have already formed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin is approved for use only in adults

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desmopressin requires at least 14 days of therapy to act

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient lacks residual endothelial stores of vWF

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's blood type O prevents any response

explanation.summary: Desmopressin works only when the patient has residual endothelial stores of vWF to release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Desmopressin releases vWF from cellular compartments and is useful in patients with residual endothelial storage of vWF. Not all vWD patients have such stores, so the drug does not work in all patients and is most often used in less severe bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acting on already-formed clots describes the antifibrinolytic drugs aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The adults-only restriction applies to recombinant vWF, not to desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Up to 14 days describes how long therapy for a bleeding episode may be needed, not a delay before desmopressin acts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood type O is associated with lower baseline vWF levels but does not block the response to desmopressin.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. Over the past 2 days he had fever, a severe headache, and neck stiffness; he is now unresponsive. Temperature is 39.7°C (103.4°F), heart rate 126/min, and blood pressure 80/60 mm Hg. He has diffuse petechiae, and blood continues to ooze from the IV puncture site. Laboratory studies show a very low platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, and schistocytes on the peripheral smear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 1 von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Sepsis with simultaneous bleeding and clotting, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, and prolonged PT/aPTT is classic for DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: DIC is a secondary thrombo-hemorrhagic disorder triggered by a severe underlying illness such as gram-negative sepsis. Rampant clotting consumes platelets and coagulation factors (causing prolonged PT and aPTT and bleeding), while fibrin strands shear red cells to produce schistocytes. The combination of petechiae, oozing lines, low platelets, prolonged coagulation times, and schistocytes in a septic patient is the signature of DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TTP also causes schistocytes and thrombocytopenia, but its coagulation studies (PT/aPTT) are characteristically normal, unlike the prolonged times seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT/aPTT and no schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency that prolongs the aPTT alone, with a normal platelet count and PT and no schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand disease produces mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal platelet count and normal PT, not this consumptive picture.

questions.stem: After a complicated, full-term delivery of her first child, a 23-year-old woman has a large postpartum hemorrhage that has been difficult to control over the past 24 hours. Which set of laboratory findings would be most indicative of disseminated intravascular coagulation in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Platelets decreased, fibrinogen decreased, PT decreased, aPTT prolonged

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelets decreased, fibrinogen decreased, PT prolonged, aPTT prolonged

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelets decreased, fibrinogen increased, PT prolonged, aPTT decreased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets increased, fibrinogen increased, PT decreased, aPTT decreased

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets increased, fibrinogen increased, PT prolonged, aPTT prolonged

explanation.summary: DIC consumes platelets and coagulation factors, giving low platelets, low fibrinogen, and prolonged PT and aPTT.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC, rampant clotting depletes platelets and clotting factors. This produces a decreased platelet count, decreased fibrinogen (fibrinogen is a coagulation factor converted into fibrin), and prolonged PT and aPTT. Obstetric complications are a classic trigger by dumping procoagulants into the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A decreased (shortened) PT is inconsistent with DIC, where factor depletion prolongs the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In DIC fibrinogen is decreased and the aPTT is prolonged, not increased fibrinogen with a shortened aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased platelets and fibrinogen with shortened coagulation times is the opposite of the consumptive coagulopathy of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets and fibrinogen are consumed and therefore decreased in DIC, not increased.

questions.stem: A critically ill patient in the intensive care unit is suspected of having disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following peripheral blood smear findings would most strongly support this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased platelets alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased white blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large red blood cells with a purplish cast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells with pointed contours

explanation.summary: Schistocytes, fragmented red cells with sharp angular contours, are the hallmark smear finding of the microangiopathy in DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistocytes are red cell fragments produced when red cells are sliced by sharp fibrin strands as they squeeze through microvascular clots. They are smaller than normal red cells and angular rather than round, lacking central pallor, and are never seen in normal blood, so their presence points to a microangiopathic process such as DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blast cells suggest leukemia or a myeloproliferative disorder, not DIC itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although platelets are decreased in DIC, thrombocytopenia has many more common causes and is nonspecific without schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated white blood cell count reflects infection and is not itself indicative of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Large red cells with a purplish cast are reticulocytes, seen in small numbers normally and increased in hemolysis generally, not specific for DIC.

questions.stem: In a patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation, how do fibrin degradation products directly contribute to the abnormal bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They create new endothelial injury, exposing subendothelial collagen

choices.label: B
choices.text: They inhibit new clot formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit protein C formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They initiate widespread microvascular thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate platelet aggregation

explanation.summary: Fibrin degradation products are not inert; they actively inhibit new clot formation and worsen bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the body lyses the widespread clots of DIC, fibrin is broken down into fibrin degradation products. These fragments actively prevent the formation of new blood clots, aggravating the bleeding that is already occurring from consumption of platelets and coagulation factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Creating new endothelial injury would promote clotting, not the anticoagulant, bleeding-promoting effect of FDPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FDPs do not act by inhibiting protein C; they directly interfere with clot formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Initiating widespread thrombosis would increase clotting, the opposite of how FDPs aggravate bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating platelet aggregation would favor clotting rather than the bleeding caused by FDPs.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with sepsis and develops disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to bacterial meningitis. Which of the following is the single most important treatment to manage the DIC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: Because DIC is always secondary, the first and most important step is to treat the underlying condition, here with antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: DIC is not a primary disorder; it is driven by an underlying severe illness. The first goal of management is to treat that trigger. For DIC secondary to bacterial meningitis and sepsis, antibiotics are the fundamental treatment. Blood-product transfusions are individualized and reserved for significant bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryoprecipitate is used to replace fibrinogen and factor VIII when the patient is bleeding with low fibrinogen, not as the primary therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fresh frozen plasma corrects a prolonged PT and aPTT in a bleeding patient but does not address the underlying infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin is reserved for thrombosis-predominant DIC with large thrombi or tissue necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion is used for significant bleeding with thrombocytopenia, not to cure the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A patient has schistocytes and thrombocytopenia on evaluation, raising concern for a thrombotic microangiopathy. Which laboratory feature best distinguishes disseminated intravascular coagulation from the other thrombotic microangiopathies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decreased platelet count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated D-dimer level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated indirect bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presence of schistocytes on the smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged PT and aPTT

explanation.summary: Prolongation of the coagulation times (PT and aPTT) sets DIC apart from other thrombotic microangiopathies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC, rampant fibrin production depletes coagulation factors, so the PT, INR, aPTT, and thrombin time are all prolonged. This distinguishes DIC from other forms of thrombotic microangiopathy, in which the coagulation times are typically normal because factors are not consumed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low platelet count is common to all thrombotic microangiopathies and is nonspecific.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D-dimer is elevated whenever clots break down and is sensitive but nonspecific, so it does not separate DIC from other microangiopathies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated indirect bilirubin reflects hemolysis, which occurs in any microangiopathic process, not just DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes appear in any thrombotic microangiopathy, so they do not distinguish DIC.

questions.stem: A patient with gram-negative sepsis develops disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following best describes the mechanism that inappropriately activates the coagulation cascade in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A congenital deficiency of protein C removes an anticoagulant brake

choices.label: B
choices.text: A deficiency of ADAMTS13 allows large von Willebrand multimers to accumulate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoantibodies inhibit factor VIII activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Circulating antibodies destroy platelets in the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vessel wall injury releases tumor necrosis factor

explanation.summary: Endothelial injury releases TNF, which drives endothelial cells to release tissue factor and activate the extrinsic pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC, vessel wall injury releases tumor necrosis factor, which causes endothelial cells to release tissue factor. Tissue factor is the stimulus that activates the extrinsic coagulation pathway, and the cascade becomes supercharged, generating excessive fibrin in vessels throughout the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congenital protein C deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia, not the acquired tissue-factor-driven activation seen in DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ADAMTS13 deficiency with large von Willebrand multimers is the mechanism of TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoantibodies against factor VIII describe acquired hemophilia, not DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic antibody-mediated platelet destruction describes immune thrombocytopenia, not the tissue-factor mechanism of DIC.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation is found to be anemic, and the smear shows numerous fragmented red cells. Which of the following best explains the origin of these red cell fragments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of red cells by the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired erythropoietin production reducing red cell survival

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic swelling and rupture of red cells in hypotonic plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin forming Heinz bodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red cells being sliced by fibrin strands

explanation.summary: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia in DIC results from red cells being sheared by intravascular fibrin strands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red cells are pliable but cannot easily flex around the sharp fibrin strands of forming microvascular clots. Some are destroyed completely, and others are sliced into fragments that reseal as schistocytes. This mechanical shearing produces microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated splenic destruction describes autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which produces spherocytes, not shear fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced erythropoietin lowers production but does not fragment circulating red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic rupture in hypotonic plasma is not the mechanism; hemolysis in DIC is mechanical.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heinz bodies from oxidative injury are characteristic of G6PD deficiency, not microangiopathy.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation is actively bleeding, and laboratory studies show a markedly low fibrinogen level. Which of the following blood-derived products is most appropriate to replace the fibrinogen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparin infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet concentrate

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen (and factor VIII) in a bleeding DIC patient with a low fibrinogen level.
explanation.whyCorrect: When bleeding in DIC is being corrected with transfusions, cryoprecipitate is given specifically to replace fibrinogen and factor VIII. It is the product of choice for correcting the hypofibrinogenemia caused by consumption of fibrinogen during widespread clotting.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Heparin is an anticoagulant used for thrombosis-predominant DIC and would worsen bleeding, not replace fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous immunoglobulin has no role in replacing clotting factors in DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity in anemia but do not replace fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet concentrate replaces consumed platelets, not fibrinogen.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation develops progressive ischemia and early gangrene of several fingers and toes from large occlusive thrombi. Bleeding is minimal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this thrombosis-predominant presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: When thrombosis predominates with large thrombi or tissue necrosis, anticoagulation with heparin is used.
explanation.whyCorrect: If thrombosis is the predominant feature of DIC, treatment must weigh the risk of bleeding against the risk of further clot formation. For large thrombi or tissue necrosis, such as digital gangrene, anticoagulation with heparin is used to limit ongoing clotting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen for bleeding, not thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma replaces coagulation factors for bleeding and would not address the thrombotic complication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells treat anemia and have no effect on the occlusive thrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion is for bleeding with thrombocytopenia and could add fuel to thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with newly diagnosed pancreatic adenocarcinoma is found to have laboratory evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following best describes how this malignancy triggers DIC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It causes an inherited deficiency of antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly damages the vascular endothelium with bacterial toxins

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inflames blood vessel walls as a vasculitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces autoantibodies against platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: It releases procoagulant substances into the circulation

explanation.summary: Mucinous adenocarcinomas trigger DIC as 'dumpers' by releasing procoagulant substances into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The causes of DIC can be divided into dumpers (things that dump procoagulants into the blood) and rippers (things that damage the endothelium). Adenocarcinomas, especially very mucinous ones like pancreatic adenocarcinoma, are classic dumpers that release procoagulant material into the circulation and set off the coagulation cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inherited antithrombin deficiency is a congenital thrombophilia, not how adenocarcinoma triggers DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxin-mediated endothelial damage describes a ripper such as gram-negative sepsis, not a mucinous tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vasculitis (e.g., in systemic lupus erythematosus) is a ripper that damages endothelium, not the procoagulant-dumping mechanism of adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antiplatelet autoantibodies describe immune thrombocytopenia, not the mechanism of malignancy-associated DIC.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation and a very low platelet count is examined. Which of the following is the most common skin manifestation of DIC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythema nodosum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Malar rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: Palpable purpura from immune-complex vasculitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urticaria

explanation.summary: Petechiae are the most common skin manifestation of DIC, reflecting microvascular hemorrhage from thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The skin in DIC commonly shows petechiae, the pinpoint microvascular hemorrhages typical of any patient with a low platelet count. Because DIC consumes platelets, petechiae are the most common cutaneous finding, and patients may also bleed from intravenous and other line sites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis associated with infections and sarcoidosis, unrelated to DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A malar rash is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus, not a manifestation of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Palpable purpura from immune-complex deposition characterizes a primary small-vessel vasculitis, not the platelet-poor microhemorrhages of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urticaria is an allergic or histamine-mediated reaction, not a consequence of consumptive thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: Most cases of disseminated intravascular coagulation arise from a limited group of underlying illnesses. Which of the following groups accounts for most cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia, myelofibrosis, radiation injury, and hypersplenism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, vitamin K deficiency, and liver failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and obesity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency, thalassemia, lead poisoning, and anemia of chronic disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Malignancy, obstetric complications, sepsis, and trauma

explanation.summary: Most cases of DIC are associated with MOST: malignancy, obstetric complications, sepsis, and trauma.
explanation.whyCorrect: DIC is always secondary to another severe illness, and four categories account for the majority of cases: malignancy, obstetric complications, sepsis, and trauma. The mnemonic MOST captures this group. Recognizing these four settings tells you when to be actively looking for DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These marrow and splenic disorders lower blood counts but are not the typical precipitants of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are primary bleeding and factor-deficiency disorders; they are not the usual triggers that set off widespread intravascular clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These endocrine and metabolic conditions are not among the common underlying illnesses that precipitate DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are causes of anemia and do not inappropriately activate the coagulation cascade.

questions.stem: The causes of disseminated intravascular coagulation can be grouped by whether they dump procoagulant substances into the blood or damage the endothelium. Which of the following triggers DIC principally by damaging the endothelium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amniotic fluid embolism during delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Envenomation from a venomous snake bite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Newly diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe gram-negative bacterial infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widely metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma

explanation.summary: Severe gram-negative sepsis is a classic 'ripper' that damages endothelium, in contrast to the 'dumpers' that release procoagulants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Causes of DIC divide into dumpers, which dump procoagulants into the blood, and rippers, which damage the endothelium or tissue. Severe gram-negative, toxin-producing bacterial infections are listed among the endothelium-damaging causes, along with trauma or thermal burns and vasculitis such as that of systemic lupus erythematosus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic fluid embolism is an obstetric complication that dumps procoagulant substances into the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Venomous snake bites introduce procoagulant substances into the blood and are therefore dumpers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is a dumper; it releases procoagulant material into the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Very mucinous adenocarcinomas such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma act as dumpers of procoagulant material.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man in the intensive care unit after severe polytrauma develops disseminated intravascular coagulation. His coagulation cascade has been inappropriately activated and is producing excessive amounts of fibrin. Which of the following events most directly produces the widespread microvascular thrombi?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiplatelet antibodies opsonize platelets within the microvasculature

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess fibrin lodges in small vessels and combines with platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrin degradation products cross-link circulating platelets into aggregates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate and tether platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell fragments aggregate and occlude the capillary beds

explanation.summary: In DIC the excess fibrin generated by the supercharged cascade lodges in small vessels and combines with platelets to form thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once the cascade is activated when it should not be, it becomes supercharged and makes excessive unnecessary fibrin throughout the body. That fibrin lodges in small vessels and combines with platelets to form thrombi, which is why DIC is considered a secondary form of thrombotic microangiopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody opsonization of platelets describes immune-mediated platelet destruction, which does not generate microvascular thrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin degradation products inhibit new clot formation rather than building thrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Accumulation of large von Willebrand multimers is the mechanism of a different thrombotic microangiopathy, not the fibrin-driven process of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell fragments are a consequence of the thrombi, not the material that forms them.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman in the intensive care unit with disseminated intravascular coagulation becomes oliguric, and her serum creatinine rises steadily over 24 hours. Which of the following best explains her renal failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumed coagulation factors have allowed bleeding into the renal pelvis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrin degradation products are directly toxic to the renal tubules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free hemoglobin from lysed red cells has obstructed the collecting ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli has produced a nephritic syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombi are occluding renal vessels and reducing regional blood flow

explanation.summary: Occlusive microthrombi reduce regional blood flow, producing tissue ischemia and organ failure such as oliguria and acute renal failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombi in DIC occlude vessels and reduce regional blood flow, causing tissue ischemia and sometimes necrosis. DIC is often a multi-organ disease, and the renal system is one of the systems affected, with oliguria and acute renal failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleeding can occur in DIC, but oliguria with a rising creatinine reflects ischemic injury, not hemorrhage into the renal pelvis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin degradation products aggravate bleeding by inhibiting clot formation; direct tubular toxicity is not their described action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal injury in DIC comes from vascular occlusion and ischemia rather than obstruction by free hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex glomerulonephritis is a distinct renal disease and not the mechanism of renal failure in DIC.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with mucinous gastric adenocarcinoma has had a mildly low platelet count and slightly prolonged coagulation times documented at several outpatient visits over 2 months. He bruises easily but has never been acutely ill. Which of the following best characterizes disseminated intravascular coagulation in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It begins abruptly and is invariably accompanied by shock

choices.label: B
choices.text: It develops only after the primary tumor has been surgically resected

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has an insidious onset, unlike the acute onset typical of sepsis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces only bleeding manifestations and never causes thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It represents a primary clotting disorder unmasked by the malignancy

explanation.summary: The onset of DIC varies with its cause: acute in sepsis, more insidious in cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because DIC has many different causes, the clinical presentation varies widely. The onset may be acute, as in sepsis, or more insidious, as in cancer. A cancer patient may therefore show smoldering laboratory abnormalities and mild bleeding over weeks rather than the explosive presentation of septic DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abrupt onset with shock characterizes septic DIC, not the insidious cancer-associated presentation described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The malignancy itself triggers DIC by releasing procoagulant material; resection is not a prerequisite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Some cases of DIC are dominated by bleeding, but others present with extensive clotting such as gangrene or organ infarcts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DIC is never a primary disorder; it is always secondary to an underlying severe medical disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has schistocytes and a reduced platelet count reported on her peripheral blood smear. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these two findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are a common normal variant and require no further evaluation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are diagnostic of DIC, so no further laboratory testing is required

choices.label: C
choices.text: They indicate marrow failure and should prompt an immediate bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: They occur in any thrombotic microangiopathy and do not by themselves establish DIC

choices.label: E
choices.text: They point to an underlying leukemia and should prompt flow cytometry

explanation.summary: Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia are the smear picture of any thrombotic microangiopathy, not of DIC specifically.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a peripheral blood smear in DIC you may see schistocytes and reduced platelets, but these findings are seen in any form of thrombotic microangiopathy, not just DIC. Additional testing, particularly coagulation times, is needed because prolonged PT, INR, aPTT, and thrombin time are what distinguish DIC from the other microangiopathies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Schistocytes are never seen in normal blood, so their presence always requires explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The smear findings are shared by all thrombotic microangiopathies, so they cannot confirm DIC on their own.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow failure lowers counts but does not fragment circulating red cells into schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blast cells rather than schistocytes are the smear finding that suggests leukemia.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation has a platelet count of 28,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains this low platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies are destroying circulating platelets within the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelets are being sequestered within a markedly enlarged spleen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelets are consumed in the clotting process and drop out of circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bone marrow has stopped producing megakaryocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfused intravenous fluids have diluted the circulating platelet pool

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia in DIC is consumptive: platelets are used up making the widespread thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, DIC is characterized by a decreased platelet count. As platelets are consumed in the clotting process, they drop out of circulation. On a normal smear several platelets would be visible, whereas in DIC they are conspicuously reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated splenic destruction is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenia, not of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenic sequestration is a separate cause of thrombocytopenia and is not the mechanism described in DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow production is not the problem in DIC; platelets are being used up in the periphery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dilution does not account for the profound thrombocytopenia that accompanies widespread clotting.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation has a serum fibrinogen level well below the reference range. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrinogen is being lost into the urine through damaged renal glomeruli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen is being neutralized by circulating antifibrinogen antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrinogen is being sequestered within a markedly enlarged spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrinogen is consumed as it is converted to fibrin during rampant clotting

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver has abruptly stopped synthesizing fibrinogen because of shock

explanation.summary: Fibrinogen is a coagulation factor that is consumed as it is turned into fibrin, so it is typically decreased in DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main problem in DIC is rampant, uncontrolled fibrin production and clot formation. Coagulation factors are depleted in the process, and fibrinogen, the precursor converted into fibrin, is typically decreased. This is why a bleeding patient with a low fibrinogen level is given cryoprecipitate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urinary loss of fibrinogen is not a described mechanism in DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antifibrinogen antibodies are not part of the pathophysiology of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic sequestration applies to cells, not to circulating fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Depletion in DIC results from consumption of the circulating factor rather than from a synthetic failure.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation is noted to have an elevated serum indirect bilirubin. Which of the following best accounts for this laboratory finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cholestasis caused by microthrombi obstructing the bile ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of coagulation factors within the hepatic sinusoids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired hepatic conjugation caused by tumor necrosis factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ongoing hemolysis of red blood cells in the microvasculature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma to correct the coagulopathy

explanation.summary: The indirect bilirubin rises in DIC because red cells are continuously being destroyed in the microcirculation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typically the serum indirect bilirubin is elevated in DIC due to the ongoing hemolysis. Red cells are destroyed or fragmented as they pass the sharp fibrin strands of forming microvascular clots, and the released heme is processed into unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary obstruction raises the conjugated fraction and is not a described feature of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor consumption prolongs the coagulation times; it has no effect on bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tumor necrosis factor in DIC acts by causing endothelial cells to release tissue factor, not by impairing bilirubin conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fresh frozen plasma is given to correct PT and aPTT and does not itself raise the indirect bilirubin.

questions.stem: A critically ill patient being evaluated for suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation has a markedly elevated D-dimer level. Which of the following best describes the limitation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can be interpreted only after heparin has been withheld for 24 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is frequently falsely low in DIC, so it misses many affected patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reflects platelet consumption rather than the breakdown of fibrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It rises only after several days of clotting, so it is too slow to be useful

choices.label: E
choices.text: It rises with even minor clot formation, so it cannot prove pathologic clotting

explanation.summary: FDPs and D-dimers are super-sensitive and rise even with minor clot formation, so an elevated level is not specific for DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrin degradation products and D-dimers form any time a clot starts to break down. Because these tests are super-sensitive, they are elevated even in conditions of minor clot formation. They are therefore not specific and are not very helpful in proving that a patient has pathologic clotting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Withholding heparin is not a described requirement for interpreting the test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The tests are sensitive with few false negatives; falsely low results are not the limitation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D-dimers and FDPs are products of fibrin breakdown, not markers of platelet consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These products form as soon as a clot begins to break down, so a delayed rise is not the issue.

questions.stem: A critically ill patient is being evaluated for pathologic clot formation, and the fibrin degradation product level comes back low. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A major clot is unlikely to be lurking anywhere in the patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient has a thrombotic microangiopathy other than DIC

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patient's platelet count is also within the normal range

choices.label: D
choices.text: The result cannot be interpreted without a simultaneous thrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: The result confirms that a large thrombus is present somewhere

explanation.summary: Because FDP testing is highly sensitive with few false negatives, a low level is most useful for ruling pathologic clotting out.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although not specific, FDPs are sensitive for diagnosing DIC, with few false negatives, and are therefore great at ruling out pathologic clotting. If the FDP level is low, you can be reasonably confident that a major clot is not lurking somewhere.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A low FDP argues against significant clot breakdown altogether rather than pointing to an alternative microangiopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The FDP level says nothing about the platelet count, which is measured separately.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rule-out value of a low FDP level stands on its own and does not require a thrombin time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A low level argues against, not for, the presence of a major thrombus.

questions.stem: A patient with established disseminated intravascular coagulation is being treated in the intensive care unit. Which of the following is the most useful application of serial fibrin degradation product levels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculating the dose of heparin required for therapeutic anticoagulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deciding whether the patient needs a diagnostic bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Determining which blood-derived product should be transfused next

choices.label: D
choices.text: Establishing that the patient has DIC rather than another microangiopathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Following the levels over time to see whether the condition is improving

explanation.summary: Once DIC is diagnosed, trending FDP levels shows whether the condition is responding to treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: FDP testing is sensitive but not specific, so its value after diagnosis is in monitoring. Once the diagnosis of DIC is made, monitoring FDP levels over time indicates whether the condition is improving with treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The FDP level is not used to dose anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bone marrow biopsy has no role in evaluating or monitoring DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Product selection is driven by what the bleeding patient is deficient in, such as fibrinogen or coagulation factors, not by the FDP level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FDPs are nonspecific and cannot separate DIC from other thrombotic microangiopathies; prolonged coagulation times do that.
