questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit with gram-negative sepsis has a platelet count of 60,000/mm3 with prolonged PT and aPTT. He has no bleeding, and no medical or surgical procedures are planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of his coagulopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin a heparin infusion to interrupt the ongoing consumption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue treating the underlying infection without transfusing blood products

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfuse cryoprecipitate until the coagulation studies normalize

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma until the PT and aPTT normalize

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse platelets until the platelet count normalizes

explanation.summary: Transfusion in DIC is individualized and reserved for significant bleeding or an upcoming procedure, not for abnormal numbers alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first goal of managing DIC is to treat the underlying condition. Correcting the coagulopathy more directly is reserved for patients with significant bleeding or those who will undergo a medical or surgical procedure. Transfusions should be individualized and used to correct significant bleeding, not to correct abnormal coagulation studies alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heparin is reserved for DIC in which thrombosis predominates with large thrombi or tissue necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cryoprecipitate is given to a bleeding patient with a low fibrinogen level, not to normalize studies in a patient who is not bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fresh frozen plasma is used for a bleeding patient with depleted coagulation factors, not to chase laboratory values.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion is indicated when a patient is bleeding with significant thrombocytopenia, which this patient is not.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation is bleeding significantly and has a prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. Which blood-derived product is given specifically to correct these prolonged coagulation times?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet concentrate

explanation.summary: Fresh frozen plasma is the product used to correct a prolonged PT and aPTT in a bleeding patient with DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment for significant bleeding in DIC may include transfusion of platelets, red blood cells, cryoprecipitate, and fresh frozen plasma. Of these, fresh frozen plasma is the product given to correct the PT and aPTT, because it supplies the coagulation factors that rampant clotting has depleted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryoprecipitate is used to replace fibrinogen and factor VIII rather than to correct the PT and aPTT broadly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous immunoglobulin supplies antibodies, not coagulation factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity in the anemic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet concentrate replaces consumed platelets and does not correct prolonged coagulation times.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate is transfused to a bleeding patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following components does this product replace?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrinogen and factor VIII

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immunoglobulin and albumin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelets and red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein C and antithrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate is given in DIC to replace fibrinogen and factor VIII.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the blood-derived products used for significant bleeding in DIC, cryoprecipitate is specifically described as replacing fibrinogen and factor VIII. That makes it the right choice for a bleeding patient whose fibrinogen has been consumed by widespread fibrin formation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin and albumin are unrelated to the coagulopathy of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelets and red blood cells are transfused as separate products in DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cryoprecipitate is not used as a source of natural anticoagulants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Replacing the full set of coagulation factors is accomplished with fresh frozen plasma, which corrects the PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to metastatic adenocarcinoma is not bleeding but is scheduled for an urgent surgical procedure tomorrow. Which of the following best describes the role of correcting his coagulopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Correction is contraindicated because it will worsen microvascular thrombosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Correction is indicated before the procedure even though he is not bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Correction is unnecessary because surgery does not affect the coagulopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Correction should be accomplished with heparin rather than blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: Correction should be deferred until bleeding actually occurs during surgery

explanation.summary: Besides significant bleeding, an upcoming medical or surgical procedure is the other indication to correct the coagulopathy of DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: After treating the underlying condition, some patients need their coagulopathy corrected more directly, especially if they have significant bleeding or will undergo a medical or surgical procedure. A patient facing urgent surgery falls squarely into that second group even without active bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Replacing consumed platelets and factors is a standard part of DIC management, not a contraindicated maneuver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A procedure in a patient with depleted platelets and factors carries a real bleeding risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin is reserved for thrombosis-predominant DIC with large thrombi or tissue necrosis and would worsen procedural bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting for intraoperative hemorrhage forfeits the opportunity to correct a known coagulopathy beforehand.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit is suspected of having disseminated intravascular coagulation. Beyond ordering laboratory studies, which of the following best describes the role of a careful history and physical examination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To decide whether the patient will require a diagnostic bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: To determine whether the peripheral blood smear can safely be omitted

choices.label: C
choices.text: To estimate the platelet count from the extent of the petechial rash

choices.label: D
choices.text: To predict which patients will respond best to fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: To search for other causes of thrombotic microangiopathy such as drugs

explanation.summary: The history and physical in suspected DIC are aimed at the differential diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy and at the underlying trigger.
explanation.whyCorrect: To make a diagnosis of DIC, perform a careful history and physical exam, looking for other causes of thrombotic microangiopathy such as drugs, infections, and malignancy. Because DIC is always secondary, this search also identifies the underlying illness that must be treated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow biopsy is not part of the described diagnostic approach to DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The blood smear is a characteristic part of the evaluation and is not omitted on the basis of the exam.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Petechiae indicate a low platelet count but cannot be used to estimate its numerical value.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Response to plasma transfusion is not predicted by examination findings.

questions.stem: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is described as a secondary form of thrombotic microangiopathy. Which of the following best defines a thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A condition in which inflamed vessel walls rupture and hemorrhage

choices.label: B
choices.text: A disease in which small thrombi occlude multiple small blood vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: A disease in which the marrow overproduces platelets and white cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: A disorder in which antibodies destroy circulating platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: A disorder in which large veins of the legs and pelvis become occluded

explanation.summary: A thrombotic microangiopathy is a disease due to small thrombi occluding multiple small blood vessels, and DIC is a secondary form of it.
explanation.whyCorrect: DIC is considered a secondary form of thrombotic microangiopathy, a disease due to small thrombi occluding multiple small blood vessels. In DIC the excess fibrin generated by the supercharged cascade lodges in small vessels with platelets, producing exactly that pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inflammation of vessel walls describes vasculitis, which is listed as a trigger of DIC rather than its definition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow overproduction of cells describes a myeloproliferative disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibody-mediated platelet destruction describes immune thrombocytopenia, which does not occlude microvessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Occlusion of large deep veins is macrovascular thrombosis, not a microangiopathy.

questions.stem: In the term disseminated intravascular coagulation, which of the following does the word disseminated convey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: That the clotting is confined to a single organ

choices.label: B
choices.text: That the clotting occurs only after an operation

choices.label: C
choices.text: That the clotting takes place outside the blood vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: That the process is inherited and lifelong

choices.label: E
choices.text: That the process is systemic and widespread

explanation.summary: Disseminated means the condition is systemic or widespread; intravascular means within the vessels; coagulation means clotting is involved.
explanation.whyCorrect: Examining the name explains the disease. Disseminated means that the condition is systemic or widespread, intravascular refers to the process occurring within blood vessels, and coagulation indicates that blood clotting is involved. DIC is a thrombo-hemorrhagic disorder that involves the entire body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Involvement of a single organ would be the opposite of a disseminated, whole-body process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Surgery is only one of many settings; the term refers to the extent of the process, not its trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The word intravascular, not disseminated, locates the process within blood vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DIC is an acquired disorder secondary to another severe illness, not an inherited one.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation presents with a picture dominated by clotting rather than bleeding. Which of the following findings would be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuous oozing from an intravenous catheter site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diffuse petechiae over the trunk and extremities

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gangrene of the fingers and infarcts in internal organs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large ecchymoses at sites of minor pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistent gum bleeding after brushing the teeth

explanation.summary: DIC is thrombo-hemorrhagic: some cases are dominated by bleeding, others by extensive clotting with gangrene and organ infarcts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because DIC has so many causes, its presentation varies widely. Some cases are dominated by bleeding, and others present with extensive clotting, producing gangrene of fingers, toes, or skin and infarcts in internal organs. These ischemic findings are the hallmark of the thrombosis-predominant form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oozing from intravenous lines reflects the consumptive coagulopathy and bleeding tendency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Petechiae are the most common skin manifestation of the bleeding side of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ecchymoses at pressure sites likewise reflect bleeding rather than vascular occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gum bleeding is a hemorrhagic manifestation rather than evidence of thrombosis.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation becomes cyanotic and develops respiratory failure. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrin degradation products have produced severe bronchospasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis has abolished the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin has caused diffuse alveolar hemorrhage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microvascular thrombi have involved the pulmonary vasculature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfused platelets have triggered an allergic airway reaction

explanation.summary: DIC is often a multi-organ disease, and pulmonary involvement produces cyanosis and respiratory failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: DIC is often a multi-organ system disease with the potential to affect the lungs, causing cyanosis and respiratory failure, as well as the nervous system, renal system, and cardiovascular system. The widespread fibrin thrombi that lodge in small vessels throughout the body include those of the pulmonary circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin degradation products inhibit new clot formation; bronchospasm is not among their effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis contributes to anemia but does not abolish oxygen carriage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heparin is used only in thrombosis-predominant DIC and is not the described cause of pulmonary failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An allergic transfusion reaction is a separate event and does not explain DIC-related organ failure.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation is forming clots throughout the microvasculature yet is bleeding from several sites. Apart from the effect of fibrin degradation products, which of the following best explains the bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies against factor VIII have developed during the illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial cells have released an excess of plasminogen activator

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrin strands have mechanically ruptured the walls of the capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rampant clotting has consumed the platelets and coagulation factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: The intestine has failed to absorb vitamin K during critical illness

explanation.summary: Bleeding in DIC is consumptive: the widespread clotting uses up the platelets and coagulation factors needed for hemostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: All the rampant clotting in DIC consumes most of the available platelets and coagulation factors, which can lead to hemorrhage. Adding to this, as the body lyses the clots, fibrin is broken into fibrin degradation products that themselves inhibit clotting. That is how DIC manifests with systemic microthrombi and hemorrhage at the same time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired inhibitors of factor VIII are a separate bleeding disorder and are not part of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the anticoagulant effect to fibrin degradation products rather than to excess plasminogen activator release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin strands shear red cells into schistocytes; they do not rupture vessel walls to cause the bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K malabsorption causes a distinct factor deficiency unrelated to the consumptive process.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are damaged as they pass through the microvascular thrombi of disseminated intravascular coagulation, producing anemia. Which of the following terms describes this anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic inflammatory disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aplastic anemia from marrow failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Megaloblastic macrocytic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Anemia from red cell destruction within microvascular thrombi is called microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA).
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombi damage passing red blood cells, leading to anemia from hemolysis, termed microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). MAHA is characterized by abnormal schistocytes on the peripheral smear and is one of the two defining hematologic features of DIC along with thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia of chronic disease is a hypoproliferative anemia without hemolysis or schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplastic anemia results from marrow failure, not from destruction of circulating red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis and produces large rather than fragmented red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is antibody mediated rather than caused by mechanical damage in the microvasculature.

questions.stem: A patient with disseminated intravascular coagulation has extensive thrombosis, and the team is weighing anticoagulation. Which of the following best describes the principal risk of that decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It may worsen bleeding in a patient already depleted of platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will accelerate the consumption of circulating fibrinogen stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will interfere with the interpretation of the peripheral blood smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will prevent the normal clearance of fibrin degradation products

choices.label: E
choices.text: It will reverse the underlying condition far too abruptly

explanation.summary: Anticoagulating a patient with DIC means balancing the risk of bleeding against the risk of forming more thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: If thrombosis is the predominant feature of a patient's DIC, treatment decisions must weigh the risk of bleeding against the risk of forming more thrombi. The patient's platelets and coagulation factors have already been consumed by rampant clotting, so heparin is reserved for large thrombi or tissue necrosis, where the thrombotic risk outweighs the bleeding risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticoagulation limits further fibrin formation and would not accelerate fibrinogen consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anticoagulation does not change the appearance of schistocytes or platelets on the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin does not block clearance of fibrin degradation products.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation does not treat the underlying condition at all; treating the trigger is a separate goal.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome after presenting with a deep vein thrombosis and two prior miscarriages. She has no personal or family history of a hereditary clotting disorder. Which of the following underlying conditions is she most likely to also have?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterozygous factor V Leiden

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A carrier state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smoldering multiple myeloma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inherited protein C deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus

explanation.summary: Systemic lupus erythematosus is the systemic disease most commonly associated with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: APS is associated with other autoimmune diseases, most commonly systemic lupus erythematosus, which is present about 50% of the time. Roughly 20% to 40% of patients with SLE demonstrate antiphospholipid antibodies, and this is the most common cause of secondary APS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor V Leiden is a hereditary thrombotic disorder, not an autoimmune disease linked to APS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder, the opposite of the prothrombotic state seen in APS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple myeloma is a neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells producing monoclonal antibodies and is not associated with APS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein C deficiency is another inherited thrombophilia, unrelated to the autoimmune basis of APS.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis and two spontaneous miscarriages, who is otherwise healthy, presents to the clinic for evaluation. Which of the following laboratory findings would be most consistent with a diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Markedly elevated international normalized ratio

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytosis with a raised platelet count

explanation.summary: APS characteristically produces a paradoxically prolonged aPTT despite the hypercoagulable in vivo state.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibodies bind and inhibit the thromboplastin reagent used in coagulation studies, prolonging the aPTT in vitro even though the antibodies act as procoagulants in vivo. A prolonged aPTT is therefore a supportive laboratory finding in APS.

whyWrongByChoice.B: APS is not associated with an elevated INR; the characteristic in vitro abnormality is a prolonged aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocytosis is not a feature of APS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The aPTT is characteristically prolonged in APS, not normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APS is associated with thrombocytopenia from platelet consumption in clots, not thrombocytosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is examined in the clinic. Which of the following skin findings is most likely to be present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epistaxis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gum bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Livedo reticularis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Palmar erythema

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spider angiomas

explanation.summary: Livedo reticularis, a mottled net-like skin discoloration, is the characteristic cutaneous finding in APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Livedo reticularis is a clinical finding of APS caused by obstruction of superficial capillaries by small blood clots. It reflects the prothrombotic nature of the disease at the level of the skin microvasculature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epistaxis is associated with bleeding disorders such as clotting factor deficiencies, not the prothrombotic state of APS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gum bleeding likewise reflects a bleeding tendency rather than the thrombosis seen in APS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palmar erythema is associated with liver disease, not APS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spider angiomas are also associated with liver disease rather than APS.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the pathophysiology of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Which of the following statements is most accurate about the "two-hit" theory of APS?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiphospholipid antibodies are the only component of APS pathophysiology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Risk factors such as smoking and surgery prevent the full manifestation of APS.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presence of antiphospholipid antibodies alone does not lead to APS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two incidents of blunt-force trauma can lead to the development of APS.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two or more thrombosis risk factors are required to diagnose APS.

explanation.summary: The two-hit theory holds that antiphospholipid antibodies plus an additional hypercoagulable insult are needed for clinical APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because antiphospholipid antibodies alone do not lead to APS, researchers proposed a two-hit theory: the first hit is the presence of the antibodies, and the second hit is an additional risk factor for hypercoagulability. The antibodies alone do not produce the full manifestation of disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The theory specifically states the antibodies are not the only component; a second hit is required.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factors such as smoking and surgery deliver the second hit that unmasks APS; they do not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The two hits refer to antibodies plus a hypercoagulable risk factor, not blunt-force trauma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The theory does not specify a required number of additional conventional risk factors for the full development of APS.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome presents to the hospital with a deep venous thrombosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticoagulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor replacement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: APS-associated thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation, then long-term warfarin therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with APS and thrombi are treated with anticoagulants, just like any patient with a thrombus, and are kept on long-term anticoagulation because of the risk of re-thrombosis. Most physicians use warfarin for ongoing prophylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin is used for bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease and hemophilia, not for thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor replacement is used for bleeding disorders from factor deficiency, the opposite of the APS prothrombotic state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors for bleeding and would not treat an APS thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion treats disorders of platelet number or function causing bleeding, not APS thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with an unexplained deep vein thrombosis has a positive lupus anticoagulant on initial testing. Her physician wants to confirm a diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding laboratory confirmation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diagnose APS immediately based on the single positive result

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order genetic testing for Factor V Leiden

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the antibody testing after 48 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the antibody testing at least 12 weeks later

explanation.summary: APS lab abnormalities must be confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart.
explanation.whyCorrect: A positive antiphospholipid antibody must be confirmed on 2 occasions at least 12 weeks apart. This interval excludes transient, insignificant antibodies, such as those following a viral infection, which represent the majority of positive results and would not indicate true APS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single positive test may reflect a transient antibody; diagnosis requires confirmation on two occasions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bone marrow biopsy is not part of the diagnostic workup for APS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor V Leiden is a separate hereditary thrombophilia and does not confirm APS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retesting after 48 hours is far too soon; the confirmatory interval is at least 12 weeks.

questions.stem: A patient with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is noted to have a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time, even though the patient is clinically in a hypercoagulable state with recurrent thrombosis. Which of the following best explains this paradoxical laboratory result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibodies activate the fibrinolytic system in vivo

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antibodies bind and inhibit the phospholipid in the assay reagent

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibodies cause a true deficiency of factor VIII

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibodies deplete circulating fibrinogen in the patient

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antibodies destroy platelets, prolonging the clotting time

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid antibodies inhibit the thromboplastin reagent in vitro, prolonging the aPTT even though they are procoagulant in vivo.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prolonged aPTT occurs because antiphospholipid antibodies bind to and inhibit the reagent (thromboplastin) used in the coagulation studies. This means the antibodies inhibit coagulation in vitro, whereas they act as procoagulants in vivo, producing the apparent paradox.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The abnormality is an in vitro artifact of reagent inhibition, not fibrinolytic activation in vivo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no true factor VIII deficiency; the antibodies interfere with the test, not with factor synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prolonged aPTT reflects interference with the assay reagent, not fibrinogen depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although thrombocytopenia can occur in APS, platelet destruction does not explain the prolonged aPTT.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and prior pregnancy loss becomes pregnant again and is referred to a high-risk pregnancy specialist. Which of the following regimens is most appropriate to reduce her risk of recurrent pregnancy loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-dose corticosteroids alone throughout pregnancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP) at the onset of labor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term warfarin therapy throughout the pregnancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin plus low-dose aspirin

choices.label: E
choices.text: No pharmacologic therapy is indicated during pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnant APS patients are managed with low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin.
explanation.whyCorrect: For women with APS who become pregnant, anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin is often recommended to try to avoid recurrent loss of the pregnancy. This differs from the long-term warfarin used outside of pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids alone are not the recommended regimen for preventing recurrent APS-related pregnancy loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin is used for bleeding disorders and has no role in preventing APS pregnancy loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pregnant APS patients are not usually treated with long-term warfarin; warfarin is used for non-pregnant thrombosis prophylaxis and is generally avoided in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treatment is recommended; low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin reduce the risk of recurrent loss.

questions.stem: A physician is deciding which laboratory studies to order to confirm antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Which of the following antibodies is one of the accepted criteria for the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibody

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anti-mitochondrial antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anti-smooth muscle antibody

explanation.summary: Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I is one of the three antibodies whose presence supports a diagnosis of APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Labs indicating APS include the presence in serum of lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies. Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I is one of these three confirmatory criterion antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody is associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-double-stranded DNA is specific for SLE, not a diagnostic criterion for APS itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-mitochondrial antibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-smooth muscle antibody is associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is found to have circulating antiphospholipid antibodies but has never had a thrombosis or pregnancy loss. According to the two-hit theory, which of the following additional factors would most likely serve as a second hit that could precipitate the full manifestation of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beginning a low-sodium diet

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing aerobic exercise

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing caffeine intake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Starting an oral contraceptive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Taking a daily multivitamin

explanation.summary: A second hit is an additional hypercoagulable risk factor such as oral contraceptive use.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the two-hit theory, the first hit is the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies and the second hit is any additional risk factor for hypercoagulability, such as smoking, surgery, diabetes, pregnancy, oral contraceptive intake, or malignancy. Starting an oral contraceptive is an example of such a second hit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low-sodium diet is not a recognized hypercoagulable risk factor for the APS second hit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aerobic exercise is not among the listed prothrombotic second-hit risk factors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing caffeine intake does not increase clotting risk and is not a second hit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A daily multivitamin does not promote hypercoagulability and is not a second hit.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a myocardial infarction and has no family history of heart disease and no traditional cardiac risk factors. Workup reveals antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Which of the following best describes the epidemiologic significance of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a benign condition that never causes organ damage

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is most common in men over the age of 60

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is primarily a disorder of impaired platelet production

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the most common acquired disorder of thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the most common inherited disorder of thrombosis

explanation.summary: APS is the most common acquired disorder of thrombosis and can strike young patients without other risk factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: APS is an autoimmune disorder characterized by prothrombotic circulating autoantibodies and is the most common acquired disorder of thrombosis. Some patients present in their 20s with myocardial infarction or stroke in the absence of any family history of heart disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APS can cause serious thrombotic complications including DVT, PE, stroke, myocardial infarction, and fetal loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: APS often affects young adults, including women of reproductive age, rather than being a disorder of older men.
whyWrongByChoice.C: APS is a prothrombotic disorder; any thrombocytopenia results from platelet consumption, not impaired production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APS is acquired and autoimmune, not an inherited thrombophilia like Factor V Leiden.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had three spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks of gestation with no identifiable cause. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin empiric warfarin therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order a peripheral blood smear only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform a splenectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassure her that testing is not warranted

choices.label: E
choices.text: Test for antiphospholipid antibodies

explanation.summary: Recurrent unexplained pregnancy loss is an indication to test for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testing for APS is indicated in patients with one or more unexplained episodes of pregnancy loss beyond 10 weeks, or three or more spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks. This patient's history of three early losses meets that threshold and warrants antiphospholipid antibody testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Empiric warfarin before establishing a diagnosis is inappropriate and is not the management of APS in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A peripheral smear alone would not detect antiphospholipid antibodies or establish the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenectomy has no role in the evaluation of recurrent pregnancy loss due to suspected APS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her history of three unexplained early losses is exactly the scenario in which APS testing is recommended.

questions.stem: A hematologist is teaching residents how frequently antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is encountered in the general population. The estimated prevalence of this disorder is closest to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 per 1,000,000 population

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 per 1,000,000 population

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 per 100 population

choices.label: D
choices.text: 50 per 100,000 population

choices.label: E
choices.text: 500 per 10,000 population

explanation.summary: The estimated prevalence of APS is 50 per 100,000 population.
explanation.whyCorrect: APS has an estimated prevalence of 50 per 100,000 population, with an annual incidence of about 2.1 per 100,000. It is uncommon in absolute terms yet still the most common acquired disorder of thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This figure is far below the stated prevalence of 50 per 100,000.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A rate of roughly 2 per million confuses the order of magnitude of the annual incidence, which is 2.1 per 100,000.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5 per 100 corresponds to the proportion of healthy people who carry circulating antiphospholipid antibodies, not the prevalence of the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 500 per 10,000 equals 5%, which vastly overstates how common APS is.

questions.stem: An obstetrician is reviewing contributors to pregnancy loss in her practice. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is estimated to be present in approximately what proportion of patients with pregnancy losses?

explanation.summary: APS is seen in an estimated 10% of patients with pregnancy losses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although APS is uncommon overall, it is seen in an estimated 10% of patients with pregnancy losses. This is why recurrent or unexplained fetal loss is one of the main triggers for antiphospholipid antibody testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% understates the estimated contribution of APS to pregnancy losses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25% is higher than the estimated figure for APS among patients with pregnancy losses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50% is the frequency with which APS is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, not the share of pregnancy losses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 80% would make APS the dominant cause of pregnancy loss, which it is not.

questions.stem: A researcher screens healthy volunteers with no history of thrombosis or pregnancy loss for antiphospholipid antibodies. Circulating antiphospholipid antibodies are estimated to be present in up to what percentage of healthy individuals?

explanation.summary: Up to 5% of healthy individuals have circulating antiphospholipid antibodies without disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Not everyone with antiphospholipid antibodies develops blood clots; up to 5% of healthy individuals are estimated to have circulating antiphospholipid antibodies. The antibodies alone do not always cause significant harm, which is why clinical events are required before APS is suspected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.1% is far lower than the estimated carriage rate in healthy people.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1% understates how often these antibodies are found in healthy individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 2% is closer but still below the stated figure of up to 5%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 20% is the lower end of the range seen in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, not in healthy individuals.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is found to have anticardiolipin antibodies during testing performed for an unrelated research study. She has never had a thrombotic event, a pregnancy loss, or an autoimmune diagnosis. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about her situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her antibodies establish an underlying diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her antibodies indicate an inherited thrombophilia that requires family testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: She does not have APS, because the antibodies alone do not cause disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: She has APS and should begin lifelong warfarin prophylaxis now

choices.label: E
choices.text: She will have APS as soon as a second antibody test returns positive

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid antibodies without clinical events do not constitute antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibodies do not always cause significant harm, and their presence alone does not usually cause disease. APS should be suspected only once a person with these antibodies develops symptoms such as recurrent thrombosis or fetal loss; diagnosis rests on both clinical and laboratory findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiphospholipid antibodies may be idiopathic in about half of cases and do not by themselves establish lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are acquired autoantibodies, unlike hereditary thrombophilias such as Factor V Leiden.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticoagulation is directed at patients with thrombosis or pregnancy loss, not at an asymptomatic antibody carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeat positivity satisfies only the laboratory half of the diagnosis; a clinical event is still required.

questions.stem: A student is reviewing the immunology of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. The antibodies responsible for this disorder are directed against which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citrullinated peptides within synovial joints

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double-stranded DNA within cell nuclei

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzymes of the inner mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycoprotein receptors on the platelet surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phospholipids and phospholipid-related proteins

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid antibodies target phospholipids and phospholipid-related proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibodies are a group of antibodies that attack phospholipids, including those in cell membranes, as well as phospholipid-related proteins. The phospholipid bilayer is the universal component of cell membranes, which explains the breadth of targets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies to citrullinated peptides are associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies to double-stranded DNA are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus rather than of APS itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: APS is not defined by antibodies against platelet surface receptors, even though thrombocytopenia can occur.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome has had thrombi involving her leg veins, her lungs, and her cerebral circulation. Which of the following best explains why this disorder can affect essentially any organ?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clots form only where prior inflammation has damaged the endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement is deposited only in the endothelium of large arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phospholipids are a universal component of cell membranes throughout the body

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibodies are synthesized locally within each affected organ

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antibodies are trapped and concentrated exclusively in the spleen

explanation.summary: APS can involve any organ because its antibody targets, phospholipids, are present everywhere.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phospholipid bilayer is the universal component of cell membranes, so antiphospholipid antibodies have targets throughout the body. Consequently APS can affect any organ, producing deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, stroke, myocardial infarction, and skin findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombosis in APS is not confined to previously inflamed vascular beds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement consumption in APS reflects immune complex formation and is not restricted to large arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The autoantibodies circulate in serum rather than being produced within each involved organ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic trapping does not explain multiorgan thrombosis in APS.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man tests positive for antiphospholipid antibodies two weeks after an influenza-like viral illness. He has never had a thrombotic event and has no autoimmune disease. Which of the following best characterizes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It confirms APS and warrants immediate long-term anticoagulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It indicates an underlying hereditary disorder of thrombosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is almost certainly a laboratory error requiring a new specimen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It most likely represents a transient antibody with no clinical consequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: It predicts the future development of a plasma cell malignancy

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid antibodies that follow a viral infection are usually transient and clinically insignificant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibodies can arise from drugs, infections, or idiopathic autoimmune disease. Those due to infections are usually related to a viral infection and are transient, with no clinical consequence, which is precisely why confirmatory testing is separated by at least 12 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single positive result in an asymptomatic patient does not establish APS or justify anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The antibodies are acquired, not a marker of an inherited thrombophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The result is a genuine transient antibody rather than an analytic error.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antiphospholipid antibodies are not a precursor marker for multiple myeloma.

questions.stem: A rheumatologist is reviewing why patients form antiphospholipid antibodies. In approximately what proportion of patients is the formation of these antibodies idiopathic?

explanation.summary: In half of patients, antiphospholipid antibody formation has no identifiable cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: In 50% of patients the formation of antiphospholipid antibodies is idiopathic. In the remainder, systemic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, as well as drugs and infections, account for antibody development.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5% refers to the share of healthy individuals carrying circulating antiphospholipid antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 10% corresponds to the proportion of patients with pregnancy losses who have APS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25% underestimates the idiopathic fraction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 90% would leave almost no role for the recognized secondary causes such as lupus, drugs, and infections.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus asks how likely she is to have antiphospholipid antibodies. Approximately what proportion of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus demonstrate these antibodies?

explanation.summary: Roughly 20% to 40% of patients with lupus have antiphospholipid antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Systemic lupus erythematosus is the systemic disease that most commonly predisposes to antiphospholipid antibody development, and approximately 20% to 40% of patients with lupus have these antibodies. This association is the origin of the name lupus anticoagulant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% to 5% approximates the carriage rate in healthy individuals rather than in lupus patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5% to 10% is below the observed frequency in lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50% is the frequency with which APS is associated with lupus, not the share of lupus patients with the antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nearly universal positivity is not seen in lupus.

questions.stem: One of the antibodies detected in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is called the lupus anticoagulant, even though affected patients clot excessively. This confusing name originates from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It delays coagulation when measured in the laboratory

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is detected only in patients who carry a diagnosis of lupus

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is secreted by anticoagulant-producing lymphocytes in the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces clinically significant bleeding in most patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: It protects patients from thrombosis while they take warfarin

explanation.summary: The lupus anticoagulant is named for its in vitro anticoagulant effect, not for any in vivo bleeding tendency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The name originates from the laboratory observation that this antibody delays coagulation in vitro. It is called lupus because 20% to 40% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus have antiphospholipid antibodies, even though the patient's actual problem is too much coagulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The lupus anticoagulant also occurs in patients without lupus, including idiopathic cases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibody is an autoantibody against phospholipids, not a splenic anticoagulant product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patients characteristically thrombose rather than bleed despite the abnormal clotting assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The antibody does not confer protection from clotting; patients remain hypercoagulable in vivo.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and a recent deep vein thrombosis has a platelet count of 95,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains her low platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated suppression of megakaryocytes in the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of platelets within the clots that are forming

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilution of platelets by aggressive intravenous fluid therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired platelet production from a nutritional deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of platelets within a markedly enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia in APS results from platelet consumption in thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: A low platelet count is one of the other blood abnormalities seen in APS, and it results from platelet consumption in the clots. It reflects ongoing thrombosis rather than a production defect, and it accompanies findings such as low serum complement and a prolonged aPTT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APS lowers platelets through peripheral consumption, not marrow suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dilution does not account for the thrombocytopenia associated with this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nutritional deficiency is unrelated to the platelet consumption seen in APS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenomegaly with sequestration is not a described feature of APS.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is noted to have a low serum complement level. Which of the following best accounts for this laboratory finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited deficiency of the terminal complement pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of complement to the thromboplastin assay reagent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumption of complement during immune complex formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased hepatic synthesis of complement proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary loss of complement proteins through damaged glomeruli

explanation.summary: Low serum complement in APS reflects complement consumption as part of the autoimmune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low serum complement is one of the other blood abnormalities in APS and results from complement consumption in immune complex formation as part of the autoimmune response. It sits alongside the low platelet count and the prolonged aPTT as supportive laboratory abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The complement deficiency here is acquired and consumptive, not inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is the antiphospholipid antibodies, not complement, that bind and inhibit the thromboplastin reagent and prolong the aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The complement level falls from consumption rather than from reduced hepatic production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal protein loss is not the described mechanism for hypocomplementemia in APS.

questions.stem: Five patients each present with a first episode of deep vein thrombosis. In which of the following patients is testing for antiphospholipid antibodies most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 24-year-old man with no identifiable risk factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 31-year-old woman in the third trimester of pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 45-year-old woman one day after a 14-hour airline flight

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 68-year-old man five days after total hip replacement

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 72-year-old woman with newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer

explanation.summary: Test for antiphospholipid antibodies in patients with thrombi who are young or lack other risk factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: In general, testing is directed at patients who have thrombi and who are young or lack other risk factors. A 24-year-old with an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis fits that description, whereas a clot explained by a conventional provoking factor does not prompt testing first.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pregnancy is itself a hypercoagulable risk factor that accounts for the clot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Long air travel is a recognized provoking factor for deep vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recent surgery is a conventional risk factor that explains the thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cancer is one of the listed alternative explanations for thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had an unexplained fetal loss at 16 weeks' gestation. How many such unexplained losses beyond 10 weeks of gestation prompt consideration of antiphospholipid antibody testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four

choices.label: B
choices.text: One

choices.label: C
choices.text: Six

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two

explanation.summary: A single unexplained pregnancy loss beyond 10 weeks is enough to consider testing for APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testing should be considered in patients with one or more unexplained episodes of pregnancy loss beyond 10 weeks. The higher threshold of three or more losses applies only to spontaneous abortions occurring before 10 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Four losses far exceeds any stated threshold for testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Six losses is well beyond the point at which evaluation is recommended.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Three losses is the threshold for spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks, not after.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting for a second late loss delays testing beyond the stated threshold.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome has had two fetal deaths in the second trimester and one premature birth. Which of the following best explains the pregnancy outcomes in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomal aneuploidy induced in the developing fetus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of neural tube closure caused by the antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal iron deficiency that limits fetal growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placental insufficiency caused by thrombosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplacental antibody-mediated hemolysis of fetal red cells

explanation.summary: Fetal loss in APS follows from thrombosis producing placental insufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: A characteristic feature of APS is frequent fetal loss during pregnancy from premature birth, placental insufficiency, and fetal death. The clinical findings in APS, including these obstetric events, are all caused by thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibodies do not induce chromosomal abnormalities in the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neural tube defects are unrelated to antiphospholipid antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency is not the mechanism of pregnancy loss described in APS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APS antibodies target phospholipids and promote clotting rather than causing fetal hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is admitted with an ischemic stroke. She has had two miscarriages, has a mottled net-like purplish discoloration over both thighs, and her activated partial thromboplastin time is above the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newly diagnosed multiple myeloma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 1 von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Arterial thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, livedo reticularis, and a prolonged aPTT together point to APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: APS produces arterial and venous thrombi such as stroke, recurrent fetal loss, and livedo reticularis, and it characteristically prolongs the aPTT because the antibodies inhibit the thromboplastin reagent in vitro. This combination in a young woman is the classic presentation of the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder and does not cause stroke or miscarriage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency anemia would not explain thrombosis, livedo reticularis, or a prolonged aPTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells producing monoclonal antibodies, not this thrombotic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding rather than thrombosis and fetal loss.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome has completed initial anticoagulant treatment for a pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue long-term warfarin for prophylaxis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give desmopressin during any future acute illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Provide clotting factor replacement as needed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schedule periodic prophylactic platelet transfusions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop anticoagulation once the clot has fully resolved

explanation.summary: After a thrombotic event, APS patients stay on long-term anticoagulation, usually warfarin.
explanation.whyCorrect: After treatment, patients with APS and thrombi should be kept on long-term anticoagulation because of the risk of re-thrombosis, and most physicians use warfarin for prophylaxis. Stopping therapy once the acute clot resolves leaves the patient exposed to recurrence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmopressin is a treatment for bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease and hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor replacement is used for bleeding disorders caused by factor deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet transfusion treats disorders involving platelets and has no prophylactic role here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Discontinuing anticoagulation ignores the ongoing risk of re-thrombosis in APS.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome has a mottled, net-like purplish discoloration of the skin over both thighs. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of immune complexes along the dermal-epidermal junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilation of superficial dermal venules from estrogen excess

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extravasation of red cells through fragile capillary walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of superficial capillaries by small blood clots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactive proliferation of dermal arterioles and venules

explanation.summary: Livedo reticularis in APS is produced by small clots obstructing superficial capillaries.
explanation.whyCorrect: Livedo reticularis, a mottled pattern of skin discoloration, is caused by obstruction of superficial capillaries by small blood clots. It is one of the skin manifestations of the thrombosis that underlies all of the clinical findings in APS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune complex deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction does not account for this mottled pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen-related vascular dilation produces findings such as spider angiomas associated with liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell extravasation implies a bleeding tendency, which is not the problem in APS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular proliferation describes lesions such as spider angiomas rather than livedo reticularis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has a second unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. His father and his brother each had a deep vein thrombosis before age 40. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies are negative on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his thrombophilia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor V Leiden

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemophilia A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple myeloma

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: A familial pattern of young-onset thrombosis with negative antibody testing suggests a hereditary thrombophilia such as Factor V Leiden.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factor V Leiden is a hereditary thrombotic disorder, which fits a patient whose father and brother also clotted at a young age. APS is an acquired disorder requiring antiphospholipid antibodies confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, and his testing is persistently negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APS cannot be diagnosed when the criterion antibodies are absent on confirmatory testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder, the opposite of a prothrombotic state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a neoplastic plasma cell proliferation producing monoclonal antibodies, not a familial thrombophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand disease causes bleeding rather than recurrent thrombosis.

questions.stem: A patient with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome asks why she was not given desmopressin (DDAVP) when she was treated for her clot. Desmopressin is typically used in the treatment of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep venous thrombosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Livedo reticularis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary embolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recurrent fetal loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand disease

explanation.summary: Desmopressin treats bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease, not thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Desmopressin is a treatment typically used for bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease and hemophilia. Patients with APS and thrombi instead receive anticoagulation, followed by long-term warfarin prophylaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deep venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Livedo reticularis reflects microvascular thrombosis and is not treated with desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary embolism likewise requires anticoagulation rather than desmopressin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrent fetal loss in APS is managed with low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman had an ischemic stroke at age 35 with no conventional risk factors. Lupus anticoagulant and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies are negative, but anticardiolipin antibodies are positive on two occasions 14 weeks apart. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Testing must be repeated because all three antibodies must be positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: The diagnosis is excluded because the lupus anticoagulant is negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings support a diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: The positive result most likely reflects a transient post-viral antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: The results remain inconclusive until a third specimen is drawn

explanation.summary: One persistently positive criterion antibody plus a clinical event establishes APS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Labs indicating APS include the presence in serum of one or more of lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, confirmed on 2 occasions at least 12 weeks apart. She has a persistently positive anticardiolipin antibody together with an unexplained thrombotic event in a young patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only one or more of the three criterion antibodies must be present, not all three.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A negative lupus anticoagulant does not exclude APS when another criterion antibody is persistently positive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transient post-infectious antibodies disappear and would not still be present 14 weeks later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two positive results separated by at least 12 weeks already satisfy the confirmatory requirement.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome who previously had a deep vein thrombosis now presents with acute right-sided weakness and is found to have an ischemic stroke. Which of the following best explains the occurrence of both events in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: APS produces both venous and arterial thrombi

choices.label: B
choices.text: APS produces venous thrombi only, so the stroke is unrelated

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stroke indicates a superimposed inherited bleeding disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stroke represents bleeding caused by her prolonged aPTT

choices.label: E
choices.text: The stroke resulted from platelet clumps embolizing from marrow

explanation.summary: APS causes thrombosis in both the venous and arterial circulations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical findings in APS are caused by venous and arterial thrombi, producing deep vein thrombosis in the legs, pulmonary emboli, stroke, myocardial infarction, and skin disorders. A prior deep vein thrombosis and a later stroke are both expressions of the same prothrombotic process.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Arterial events such as stroke and myocardial infarction are part of the APS spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A bleeding disorder would not explain an ischemic stroke in a hypercoagulable patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prolonged aPTT is an in vitro artifact; patients clot rather than bleed in vivo.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow-derived platelet emboli are not a described mechanism in APS.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has had three miscarriages and has just been diagnosed with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. She is not currently pregnant but hopes to conceive again and asks what can be done. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise her that future pregnancy is contraindicated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plan platelet transfusion at the time of conception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassure her that no treatment alters her risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refer her to a high-risk pregnancy specialist

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start warfarin now to protect a future pregnancy

explanation.summary: A woman with APS and prior pregnancy loss should be referred for high-risk pregnancy care, since treatment lowers miscarriage risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: APS causes blood clots to form and increases the chance of recurrent miscarriage, so a patient who wishes to conceive again should be referred to a high-risk pregnancy specialist. Treatment options such as anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin decrease the risk of miscarriage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pregnancy is not prohibited; it is managed with specialist care and anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusion treats disorders involving platelets and has no role in preventing fetal loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anticoagulation during pregnancy does reduce the risk of recurrent loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pregnant patients with APS are not usually treated with long-term warfarin anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is scheduled for an elective cholecystectomy. Preoperative testing shows an activated partial thromboplastin time above the normal range, and the surgeon is concerned about intraoperative bleeding. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of her hemostatic risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desmopressin should be given to correct the prolonged aPTT

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her prolonged aPTT reflects true clotting factor consumption

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is at increased risk for thrombosis rather than for bleeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: She requires factor VIII replacement before the operation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The operation must be cancelled because of bleeding risk

explanation.summary: In APS the prolonged aPTT is an in vitro phenomenon; the patient's real risk is thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibodies bind and inhibit the thromboplastin reagent used in coagulation studies, so they inhibit coagulation in vitro while acting as procoagulants in vivo. The prolonged aPTT therefore does not signal a bleeding tendency, and surgery is itself an additional hypercoagulable risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmopressin is used for bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease and hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The abnormal result comes from reagent inhibition, not from consumption of clotting factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no true factor deficiency to replace; the assay is being interfered with by antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The laboratory abnormality alone does not indicate a bleeding risk that would preclude surgery.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a second unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. Genetic testing reveals a factor V Leiden mutation. Which of the following best explains why this mutation predisposes her to thrombosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mutant factor V cannot interact with factor X

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutant factor V is immediately cleaved to its inactive form

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mutant factor V is present at markedly reduced levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutant factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutant factor V shows increased reactivity to prothrombin

explanation.summary: Factor V Leiden is an abnormal factor V that cannot be cleaved and inactivated by protein C, so clotting is not turned off normally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The factor V Leiden gene carries a single-point mutation causing an arginine-to-glutamine substitution at the exact site where protein C normally cleaves and inactivates factor V. The abnormal factor V participates in coagulation like normal factor V, but when it is time to stop making fibrin, protein C cannot inactivate it, so thrombosis increases abnormally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor V Leiden interacts with the cascade just like normal factor V; its interaction with other factors is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The opposite is true: the whole problem is that factor V Leiden cannot be cleaved to its inactive form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factor V Leiden is present at normal levels; the defect is functional resistance to protein C, not deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor V Leiden shows no change in reactivity to prothrombin.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with his third episode of unilateral lower-extremity swelling and pain. He is diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis, and thrombophilia workup is positive for a mutation in the gene encoding factor II. Which of the following best explains how this mutation leads to hypercoagulability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased amount of antithrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased activation of existing prothrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased intrinsic activity of thrombin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased production of prothrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance of thrombin to antithrombin

explanation.summary: The prothrombin G20210A mutation causes overproduction of factor II, providing more substrate for thrombin generation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The factor II (prothrombin G20210A) mutation is a point mutation substituting guanine for adenine at position 20210 of the prothrombin gene, leading to overproduction of factor II. More prothrombin means more thrombin, which converts more fibrinogen to fibrin and increases the tendency to clot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased antithrombin describes antithrombin deficiency, a separate disorder, not the factor II mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mutation raises the quantity of prothrombin produced, not the efficiency of activating existing prothrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombin activity itself is not intrinsically altered; there is simply more of it because there is more prothrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance of clotting factors to antithrombin is not the mechanism of the factor II mutation.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with several prior episodes of deep vein thrombosis is found to have a deficiency in protein C. Which of the following mechanisms most directly accounts for her recurrent thrombosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor Va resistance to deactivation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased activity of factors Va and VIIIa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased production of prothrombin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased venous blood stasis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of antithrombin cofactor activity

explanation.summary: Protein C normally inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; with deficiency, these factors remain active and clotting continues unchecked.
explanation.whyCorrect: Activated protein C terminates coagulation by directly inactivating factors Va and VIIIa. When protein C is deficient, factors Va and VIIIa retain increased activity, so the coagulation cascade is not turned off and thrombosis increases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A factor Va that is resistant to deactivation describes factor V Leiden; protein C deficiency instead leaves normal Va and VIIIa unopposed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased prothrombin production is the mechanism of the factor II gene mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased blood stasis is an acquired, provoked cause of DVT (e.g., prolonged immobility), not the mechanism of protein C deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of cofactor activity describes protein S deficiency (protein S is the cofactor for protein C).

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left lower-leg swelling and pain and reports multiple prior similar episodes. He has no established risk factors for thrombosis. Which of the following underlying disorders is most likely responsible for his recurrent symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiphospholipid syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factor V Leiden

choices.label: C
choices.text: Malignancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein C deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prothrombin gene mutation

explanation.summary: Factor V Leiden is the most common hereditary thrombotic disorder and is the most likely cause of unexplained recurrent DVT.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent unprovoked venous thrombi in a young patient without classic risk factors suggest an inherited thrombophilia. Factor V Leiden is the most common hereditary thrombotic disorder, accounting for 40-50% of unexplained thrombosis, making it the single best answer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiphospholipid syndrome can cause DVT but is an acquired disorder classically associated with recurrent miscarriage/stillbirth and is less likely than factor V Leiden here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignancy causes a hypercoagulable state, but nothing suggests cancer in this young, otherwise healthy patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein C deficiency causes thrombosis but is considerably less common than factor V Leiden.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The prothrombin gene mutation also causes hypercoagulability but is less common than factor V Leiden.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with sudden redness and swelling of his right leg; compression Doppler ultrasound confirms a femoral vein DVT, and testing shows he is heterozygous for the factor V Leiden mutation. His family history includes a father with a pulmonary embolism and a sister with a pregnancy-associated clot. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for his DVT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin, leg elevation, and warm soaks to the calf

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate inferior vena cava filter placement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin alone for 6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin bridging to warfarin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral warfarin alone without a heparin bridge

explanation.summary: A femoral DVT is treated with anticoagulation; heparin bridges to warfarin, and the inherited thrombophilia does not change this initial treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Standard treatment uses low-molecular-weight heparin together with warfarin, with heparin acting as a bridge until warfarin becomes therapeutic (about 2 days). The presence of an inherited thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden does not change the initial treatment of the DVT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin, elevation, and warm soaks are not adequate therapy for a femoral vein DVT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An IVC filter is not first-line treatment for an uncomplicated DVT that can be anticoagulated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heparin alone is incomplete because heparin is parenteral; since months of anticoagulation are needed, an oral agent such as warfarin is preferred for long-term therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin alone is inappropriate initially because it takes several days to become therapeutic and starting it without a bridge can transiently worsen thrombosis or cause skin necrosis.
