questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on warfarin has severe gastrointestinal bleeding and receives prothrombin complex concentrate. Vitamin K is administered at the same time. Giving vitamin K in this setting accomplishes which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds circulating warfarin and inactivates it directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediately restores circulating factors II, VII, IX, and X

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevents recurrent hemorrhage over the next several days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverses the transient hypercoagulability seen at initiation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shortens the half-life of warfarin already absorbed

explanation.summary: Vitamin K does not reverse severe bleeding acutely; it repletes vitamin K and prevents further bleeding over the following days.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that giving vitamin K will not reverse severe bleeding, but it will replete vitamin K and prevent further bleeding in the coming days because of the long half-life of warfarin. That is why it is often given together with prothrombin complex concentrate, which addresses the acute bleed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No agent described in the brick binds and inactivates warfarin; protamine sulfate binds heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immediate replacement of the depleted factors is what prothrombin complex concentrate accomplishes, not vitamin K.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transient hypercoagulability occurs at warfarin initiation from falling proteins C and S and is not the issue in an actively bleeding patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K does not change warfarin's long half-life, which is exactly why continued bleeding risk must be covered.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin develops excessive bleeding at a hospital where prothrombin complex concentrate is not available. Which of the following is the most appropriate alternative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antithrombin concentrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Idarucizumab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protamine sulfate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tranexamic acid

explanation.summary: Fresh frozen plasma can reverse warfarin-related bleeding but is less effective than PCC and is reserved for when PCC is unavailable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that fresh frozen plasma can also be used to reverse excessive bleeding caused by warfarin; however, it is less effective than prothrombin complex concentrate and should only be used when PCC is not available, exactly the situation described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antithrombin is an endogenous anticoagulant; giving it would worsen rather than reverse bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Idarucizumab specifically neutralizes dabigatran and does not replace warfarin-depleted factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protamine sulfate is the antidote for heparin products and has no role in warfarin-related bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tranexamic acid is an antidote for thrombolytic drugs, not for warfarin.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman who started warfarin several days ago develops sharply demarcated areas of dying skin on both thighs. In addition to stopping warfarin, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Idarucizumab and a pooled platelet transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous protamine sulfate infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tranexamic acid and fresh frozen plasma alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

explanation.summary: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is treated by stopping warfarin and giving vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that if skin necrosis occurs it should be treated by stopping warfarin and giving vitamin K and PCC. These measures counteract the transient hypercoagulable state created when warfarin lowers the short-lived anticoagulant proteins C and S.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Idarucizumab is specific for dabigatran and has no role in a warfarin complication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protamine sulfate reverses heparin, which is not the drug responsible for this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adding another anticoagulant and an antiplatelet agent is not the treatment the brick describes for this complication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tranexamic acid reverses thrombolytic drugs, and fresh frozen plasma is only a second-line substitute when PCC is unavailable.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a previous deep vein thrombosis learns she is 6 weeks pregnant. Warfarin should be avoided in this patient for which of the following reasons?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only be administered intravenously

choices.label: B
choices.text: It causes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a potent teratogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is inactivated by vitamin K-containing prenatal supplements

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its effect cannot be reversed if bleeding occurs

explanation.summary: Warfarin is a potent teratogen and should be avoided during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists warfarin's contraindications and states plainly that warfarin is a potent teratogen, so the drug should be avoided during pregnancy. Other contraindications include active bleeding or a tendency to bleed, recent or potential eye or CNS surgery, and unsupervised patients likely to be noncompliant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Warfarin is an oral agent, and route of administration is not the reason it is avoided in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HITT is an autoimmune reaction to heparin, not an effect of warfarin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K intake affects the INR and requires consistency, but that is a monitoring issue rather than the reason to avoid warfarin in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin bleeding can be addressed with prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K, so irreversibility is not the concern.

questions.stem: Warfarin is being considered for several patients on the medicine service. In which of the following patients is warfarin contraindicated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 34-year-old woman with factor V Leiden and recurrent thromboses

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 45-year-old woman with a first deep vein thrombosis and controlled hypertension

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 58-year-old man who is scheduled for CNS surgery next week

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 60-year-old man who eats spinach and broccoli several times each week

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 70-year-old man with a mechanical prosthetic heart valve

explanation.summary: Recent or potential surgery of the eye or CNS is a contraindication to warfarin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists contraindications to warfarin as active bleeding or a tendency to bleed, recent or potential surgery of the eye or CNS, and unsupervised patients with a high potential for noncompliance, in addition to pregnancy because warfarin is a potent teratogen. Planned CNS surgery falls squarely in that list.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recurrent thromboses from a thrombotic disorder are precisely what warfarin therapy is used to treat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deep vein thrombosis is a standard indication for anticoagulant therapy, and controlled hypertension is not listed as a contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patients on warfarin need not avoid vitamin K-rich foods; they need only keep their intake consistent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A mechanical prosthetic valve is an indication for warfarin, with a slightly higher INR goal of 2.5 to 3.5.

questions.stem: A patient whose INR has been stable on warfarin begins a new diet with large daily servings of spinach, broccoli, and kiwi. Two weeks later, her laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prolonged PTT with a normal PT and INR

choices.label: B
choices.text: A subtherapeutic INR with an increased risk of clots

choices.label: C
choices.text: A supratherapeutic INR with an increased risk of bleeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: An INR that changes only if a CYP 2C9 inhibitor is added

choices.label: E
choices.text: No change, because dietary intake does not influence warfarin

explanation.summary: A large increase in vitamin K-rich foods decreases warfarin's effectiveness, producing a subtherapeutic INR and clotting risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that many foods are abundant in vitamin K, including green leafy vegetables such as spinach, broccoli, and kiwi. Too much vitamin K intake could decrease the effectiveness of warfarin and cause a decreased or subtherapeutic INR, increasing the risk for clots. Patients need not avoid these foods but must be consistent in their intake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Warfarin affects both the PT/INR and the PTT, and the PT/INR is the earlier and primary monitoring test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A supratherapeutic INR results from things that increase warfarin effect, such as starting a CYP 2C9 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drug interactions through CYP 2C9 are important, but dietary vitamin K also changes the INR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is notorious for interactions with foods as well as drugs, and those interactions show up on the INR.

questions.stem: Unfractionated heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin both work through antithrombin. Compared with unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin is best characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It inhibits factors II, IX, X, XI, and XII to an equivalent degree

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits thrombin directly rather than working through antithrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a larger molecule and must therefore be given intravenously

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is reversed by idarucizumab rather than by protamine sulfate

choices.label: E
choices.text: It more selectively augments antithrombin inhibition of factor X

explanation.summary: LMWHs are smaller, fractionated fragments that are more selective than UFH, chiefly boosting antithrombin's inhibition of factor X.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes LMWHs such as enoxaparin, dalteparin, and fondaparinux as smaller molecules than UFH and active, fractionated fragments of the larger heparin molecule. It states that LMWH is more selective than UFH, principally augmenting antithrombin inhibition of factor X.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Broad inhibition of factors II, IX, X, XI, and XII describes unfractionated heparin acting through antithrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acting directly on thrombin without a cofactor describes the direct thrombin inhibitors, not any heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LMWHs are smaller than unfractionated heparin and are given subcutaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Idarucizumab is specific for dabigatran; heparin products are reversed with protamine sulfate.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with acute venous thromboembolism requires intravenous anticoagulation. Which of the following agents can be given by the intravenous route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dalteparin sodium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enoxaparin sodium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fondaparinux sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unfractionated heparin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist)

explanation.summary: Unfractionated heparin is the heparin product given intravenously; the low-molecular-weight heparins are given subcutaneously.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that high-molecular-weight heparin, more commonly called unfractionated heparin, is given intravenously or subcutaneously (subcutaneous dosing for prophylaxis only), while the low-molecular-weight heparins are given subcutaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dalteparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin given by the subcutaneous route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin and is given subcutaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fondaparinux is grouped with the low-molecular-weight heparins and is given subcutaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is an oral vitamin K antagonist with a delayed onset and is not used for immediate intravenous anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A patient receiving unfractionated heparin is also taking aspirin and an antibiotic, and the team is concerned that the activated PTT may give inaccurate results. Which of the following tests is more specific for this drug's activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-Xa level

choices.label: B
choices.text: International normalized ratio

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prothrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum heparin drug level

explanation.summary: Many institutions monitor heparin with the anti-Xa level because it is more specific to heparin activity than the activated PTT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that heparin was traditionally monitored with the activated PTT, but many institutions have changed to the anti-Xa level because the activated PTT is more susceptible to inaccurate results from other medications such as aspirin, antihistamines, and some antibiotics, whereas anti-Xa is more specific to heparin activity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The INR is the clinical equivalent of the PT and is used to follow warfarin, not heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The platelet count is relevant to detecting HITT but does not measure anticoagulant activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prothrombin time mainly monitors the extrinsic and common pathways and is the warfarin monitoring test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monitoring uses a coagulation or activity assay rather than a drug level, since the concern is how well clotting is inhibited.

questions.stem: A patient with a deep vein thrombosis is discharged on subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin without routine laboratory monitoring. Which of the following best explains why less-intensive monitoring is acceptable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its absorption and anticoagulant effect are highly predictable

choices.label: B
choices.text: No available laboratory assay can detect this drug's activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: This drug acts directly on thrombin and requires no cofactor

choices.label: D
choices.text: This drug carries essentially no risk of bleeding complications

choices.label: E
choices.text: This drug is followed with the INR instead of the activated PTT

explanation.summary: LMWH needs less-intensive monitoring because subcutaneous administration makes absorption and anticoagulant effect more predictable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that less-intensive monitoring is required for LMWH because, with subcutaneous administration, the absorption and anticoagulant effects are more predictable. Monitoring with anti-Xa and/or aPTT is still recommended for high-risk patients or those at extremes of body weight.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-Xa levels and the aPTT can both be used for LMWH when monitoring is indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct thrombin inhibition without a cofactor describes the direct thrombin inhibitors; LMWH works through antithrombin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bleeding is a common adverse effect of all the heparins, and protamine sulfate is available as the antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The INR is used to follow warfarin; heparin products are followed with anti-Xa levels or the activated PTT.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to heparin therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A history of HITT after a prior heparin exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: An age of older than 70 years at presentation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Concurrent use of a CYP 2C9 inhibitor such as fluconazole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pregnancy in the first trimester, because heparin crosses the placenta

choices.label: E
choices.text: The presence of a mechanical prosthetic heart valve

explanation.summary: Contraindications to heparin are active bleeding, heparin allergy, and a history of HITT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists contraindications to heparin as active bleeding, heparin allergy, and a history of HITT. A patient who has had HITT needs an alternative anticoagulant, and the direct thrombin inhibitors are used for exactly this indication.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Advanced age is not among the contraindications the brick lists for heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP 2C9 inhibitors matter for warfarin, which is metabolized hepatically by that enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin does not cross the placenta; pregnancy is the contraindication emphasized for warfarin, which is a potent teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A mechanical valve is an anticoagulation indication, not a reason to withhold heparin.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis needs a direct thrombin inhibitor that can be taken by mouth. Which of the following agents is appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Argatroban

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bivalirudin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dabigatran

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enoxaparin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fondaparinux

explanation.summary: Of the direct thrombin inhibitors, dabigatran is the orally administered agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the direct thrombin inhibitors include dabigatran, argatroban, and bivalirudin, and that dabigatran is given orally while argatroban and bivalirudin are only given intravenously. Their primary indication is as alternative anticoagulants for patients with a history of HITT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor, but it is only given intravenously.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bivalirudin is also restricted to intravenous administration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin and is contraindicated by a history of HITT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fondaparinux is grouped with the heparin products and is not a direct thrombin inhibitor.

questions.stem: A patient taking dabigatran develops life-threatening hemorrhage and is given idarucizumab, which neutralizes the anticoagulant effect within minutes. Which of the following best describes how this agent works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates antithrombin, which clears the drug from the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a positively charged molecule that binds the negatively charged drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an antibody fragment that binds the drug far more avidly than thrombin does

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the clotting factors that the drug has depleted

choices.label: E
choices.text: It restores gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors

explanation.summary: Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with far higher affinity than thrombin has for it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes idarucizumab as a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) that binds specifically to dabigatran and its acylglucuronide metabolites with an affinity for dabigatran about 350 times greater than that of thrombin, neutralizing the anticoagulant effect within minutes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activating antithrombin is the mechanism of heparin itself and would worsen, not reverse, anticoagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A positively charged molecule binding a negatively charged drug describes protamine sulfate binding heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor replacement describes prothrombin complex concentrate, which is used for warfarin and for argatroban or bivalirudin bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restoring gamma-carboxylation describes repletion of vitamin K after warfarin, not dabigatran reversal.

questions.stem: A patient receiving intravenous argatroban for anticoagulation develops severe bleeding. Which of the following is used to reverse the effect of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated PCC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Idarucizumab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protamine sulfate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tranexamic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K

explanation.summary: Activated PCC is used in severe bleeding to reverse argatroban and bivalirudin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that bleeding is the most common adverse effect of the direct thrombin inhibitors and that activated PCC is used in severe bleeding cases to reverse the effects of argatroban and bivalirudin. Dabigatran, in contrast, has a specific reversal agent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran specifically and is not used for argatroban.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protamine sulfate binds and inactivates heparin and has no effect on a direct thrombin inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tranexamic acid is the antidote for thrombolytic drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K addresses warfarin's inhibition of vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis, not direct thrombin inhibition.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis and a history of HITT requires anticoagulation with a direct thrombin inhibitor. Caution is advised in this patient because these drugs are primarily eliminated by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary excretion of unchanged drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to and clearance with antithrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glomerular filtration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatic metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrolysis by plasma esterases

explanation.summary: Direct thrombin inhibitors are metabolized primarily by the liver, so they must be used cautiously in liver disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that contraindications to the direct thrombin inhibitors include hypersensitivity and active, heavy bleeding, and that these agents should be used with caution in patients with liver disease because the liver is their primary route of metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary excretion of unchanged drug is not described as the primary route of elimination for these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Direct thrombin inhibitors act without a cofactor such as antithrombin, and antithrombin is not their route of elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal filtration is not the elimination route the brick identifies as the reason for caution with these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma esterase hydrolysis is not the mechanism the brick gives for clearance of direct thrombin inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for lifelong easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, and heavy menstrual periods. Physical exam shows scattered petechiae. A complete blood count reveals a low platelet count, and the peripheral smear shows strikingly large (giant) platelets. Platelet aggregation studies are normal in response to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine but show no response to ristocetin. Which of the following is the most likely defective protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-granule contents

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delta (dense) granules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycoprotein Ib

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

choices.label: E
choices.text: von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Giant platelets with thrombocytopenia and an absent ristocetin response indicate Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a defect in glycoprotein Ib.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by a defect in the glycoprotein Ib (GPIb) receptor, which normally binds von Willebrand factor to anchor platelets to the exposed subendothelium. Because ristocetin tests GPIb-mediated adhesion, the aggregation curve to ristocetin is absent, while responses to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine are preserved. The platelets are characteristically giant and the platelet count is often low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of alpha granules produces gray platelet syndrome, whose platelets appear empty/gray rather than simply giant, and ristocetin response is not the defining abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delta-granule deficiency shows histologically normal platelets on smear, not giant platelets, and requires electron microscopy to detect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A defect in GPIIb/IIIa causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, in which the platelet count and platelet appearance are normal and ristocetin aggregation is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The problem is the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor, not von Willebrand factor itself; vWF levels are not the primary defect in this inherited platelet disorder.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man has a history of severe mucocutaneous bleeding since childhood. His platelet count and platelet morphology on peripheral smear are normal. Aggregation studies show no aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, or arachidonic acid, but the response to high-dose ristocetin is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delta-granule deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gray platelet syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemophilia A

explanation.summary: Absent aggregation to all agonists except a preserved ristocetin response, with normal platelet count and appearance, is characteristic of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a defect of the GPIIb/IIIa receptor, which binds fibrinogen to bridge platelets during aggregation. As a result there is no aggregation to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, or arachidonic acid, while ristocetin (which depends on the intact GPIb-vWF pathway) remains normal. Platelet count and morphology are normal because this is an aggregation problem, not an adhesion or granule problem.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome shows the opposite aggregation pattern (absent ristocetin) plus giant platelets and a low platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delta-granule deficiency involves impaired dense-granule secretion and is diagnosed by electron microscopy, not this classic loss of all agonist responses with preserved ristocetin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gray platelet syndrome shows large, gray, empty platelets from absent alpha granules and often thrombocytopenia, not this aggregation pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemophilia A is a clotting-factor deficiency causing deep tissue and joint bleeding with a prolonged PTT, not a platelet aggregation defect.

questions.stem: During normal platelet plug formation, dense (delta) granules release small molecules that are essential for platelet activation. Which of the following pairs of substances is released primarily by delta granules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium and serotonin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collagen and thrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Factor VIII and factor IX

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heparin and histamine

explanation.summary: Delta (dense) granules release calcium and serotonin, small molecules essential for platelet activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that delta granules release small molecules such as calcium and serotonin, which are essential for platelet activation, whereas alpha granules release larger proteins. Loss of these granules underlies delta-granule deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Collagen is a subendothelial protein and thrombin is generated in the coagulation cascade; neither is a delta-granule content.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factors VIII and IX are plasma coagulation factors, not substances stored in platelet dense granules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor are released from alpha granules, not delta granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heparin and histamine are associated with mast cells and basophils, not platelet dense granules.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has easy bruising and mild thrombocytopenia. Her peripheral smear shows large platelets that appear pale, empty, and gray compared with normally pigmented platelets. Additional evaluation reveals myelofibrosis, splenomegaly, and an elevated serum vitamin B12 level. Which of the following best explains the abnormal platelet appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of dense (delta) granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective glycoprotein Ib receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defective glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deficiency of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction or absence of alpha granules

explanation.summary: Large, empty, gray platelets with thrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis, and elevated B12 describe gray platelet syndrome, caused by loss of alpha granules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gray platelet syndrome is defined by a reduction or complete absence of alpha granules. Without granule contents, the giant platelets look empty or gray on the smear. Other features described in the brick include progressive thrombocytopenia, myelofibrosis, splenomegaly, and elevated serum B12.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dense (delta) granule deficiency produces histologically normal-appearing platelets requiring electron microscopy, not gray empty platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A GPIb defect causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, whose giant platelets are not described as empty/gray and which lacks the myelofibrosis and elevated B12 picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A GPIIb/IIIa defect causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, with normal platelet count and appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: von Willebrand factor deficiency is von Willebrand disease, which does not produce empty gray platelets on the smear.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl has a history of easy bruising and recurrent bacterial infections; a maternal uncle had a bleeding disorder. Her complete blood count shows a low platelet count, and the platelets appear normal on the peripheral smear. PT and PTT are normal, but the PFA-100 is abnormal. A combined bleeding and immune deficiency such as Chediak-Higashi syndrome is suspected. Which of the following studies is most likely to confirm the platelet abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow karyotype analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electron microscopy of the platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prothrombin time and INR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat routine peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum ferritin and iron studies

explanation.summary: Delta-granule deficiency has normal light-microscopy platelets, so electron microscopy is needed to detect the abnormal granules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delta-granule deficiency is frequently found together with disorders such as Chediak-Higashi or Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, producing combined bleeding and immunodeficiency. Because the platelets look normal on routine smear, the brick states that electron microscopy is used to detect the abnormal dense granules.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Karyotype analysis does not visualize platelet granules and is not the test used to confirm delta-granule deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PT/INR reflects the coagulation cascade, which is normal in platelet disorders and does not identify a granule defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A routine light-microscopy smear appears normal in delta-granule deficiency, so repeating it will not reveal the defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron studies address iron deficiency, a supportive management issue, not the diagnosis of a granule abnormality.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with suspected hereditary platelet dysfunction undergoes laboratory testing. Which of the following sets of results would be most consistent with an inherited platelet disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, abnormal platelet function test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet function test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolonged PT, normal PTT, normal platelet function test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, abnormal platelet function test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolonged PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet function test

explanation.summary: In platelet disorders the coagulation cascade is intact, so PT and PTT are normal while the platelet function test is abnormal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because hereditary platelet disorders affect the platelets and not the coagulation cascade, the PT and PTT are normal. The platelet function analyzer (PFA-100), which has largely replaced the bleeding time, is abnormal, reflecting impaired platelet function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A prolonged PTT alone suggests an intrinsic-pathway factor deficiency such as hemophilia, not a platelet disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A prolonged PT alone suggests a factor deficiency in the extrinsic pathway, not impaired platelet function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet disorders do not prolong PT or PTT, so a picture with both prolonged is inconsistent with an isolated platelet defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prolonged PT and PTT with a normal platelet function test points to a coagulation-factor problem, not a platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A physician is teaching students about how hereditary platelet disorders present clinically. Which of the following bleeding patterns is LEAST consistent with an inherited platelet disorder and should instead raise concern for a clotting-factor deficiency such as hemophilia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding into joints and deep muscles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gum bleeding after a routine dental cleaning

choices.label: C
choices.text: Petechiae on the skin and oral mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purpura and ecchymoses on the extremities

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent nosebleeds and mucosal oozing

explanation.summary: Platelet disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding; deep tissue and joint bleeding instead suggests a clotting-factor deficiency like hemophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that bleeding involving deep tissues (muscles) or joints is not commonly associated with platelet disorders and is more typical of clotting-factor deficiencies such as hemophilia. Hereditary platelet disorders instead cause mucocutaneous bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gum bleeding on mucosal surfaces is typical mucocutaneous bleeding seen in platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Petechiae are small pinpoint capillary breaks seen on the skin and are a classic mucocutaneous sign of platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Purpura and ecchymoses are cutaneous bleeding lesions characteristic of platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nosebleeds (epistaxis) are a common mucocutaneous manifestation of platelet dysfunction.

questions.stem: A man with Glanzmann thrombasthenia and his wife, whose genetic background is unknown, ask about the chance their child will be affected. Both Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome follow which of the following inheritance patterns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are both autosomal recessive disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explicitly states that both Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are autosomal recessive. Two copies of the affected gene are required to produce disease, so an affected father must pass his gene and the mother must also be a carrier for the child to be affected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These receptor disorders are recessive, not dominant; a single copy of the gene does not produce the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These disorders result from nuclear gene defects in platelet glycoproteins, not mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inheritance is recessive and autosomal, not X-linked dominant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They are autosomal, not X-linked recessive. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an example of an X-linked disorder, but it is a different condition.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with Bernard-Soulier syndrome has recurrent bleeding episodes that are difficult to control. In addition to supportive measures, which of the following targeted therapies is most appropriate for this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A thrombopoietin agonist such as eltrombopag

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corticosteroids for immune-mediated platelet destruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily aspirin therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lifelong warfarin anticoagulation

explanation.summary: Bernard-Soulier syndrome can be treated with recombinant factor VIIa or a thrombopoietin agonist such as eltrombopag.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists recombinant factor VIIa or a thrombopoietin agonist (eltrombopag) as specific treatments for Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Thrombopoietin agonists can raise the platelet count and help control bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids treat immune-mediated platelet destruction, but Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an inherited structural receptor defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aspirin impairs platelet function and is avoided (like NSAIDs) in these patients, not used as therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IVIG is used for immune thrombocytopenia, not for the inherited receptor defect of Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is an anticoagulant that would worsen bleeding in a patient with a hereditary platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A patient with a hereditary platelet disorder has received numerous platelet transfusions over several years to control bleeding, but recent transfusions have become progressively less effective. Which of the following best explains this loss of effectiveness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of the disorder to acute leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of the patient's own clotting factors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Development of antiplatelet and HLA alloantibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development of iron overload in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Repeated platelet transfusions can induce antiplatelet and HLA antibodies that limit the effectiveness of subsequent transfusions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that repeated transfusions may lead to formation of antiplatelet antibodies (especially against platelet glycoproteins) and HLA antibodies. These alloantibodies limit the usefulness of later transfusions by targeting the transfused platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin K deficiency affects clotting factors and PT, not the effectiveness of platelet transfusions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary platelet disorders do not transform into acute leukemia as a result of transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clotting-factor depletion is not the mechanism; platelet disorders leave the coagulation cascade intact and transfusions supply platelets, not factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron overload is a concern with chronic red-cell transfusion but does not explain refractoriness to platelet transfusion.

questions.stem: A hematologist wants to order the single best laboratory test for assessing overall platelet function in a patient with suspected hereditary platelet dysfunction. Which of the following tests has largely replaced the bleeding time for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelet function analyzer (PFA-100)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prothrombin time (PT) with the INR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quantitative plasma D-dimer assay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quantitative plasma fibrinogen level

explanation.summary: The PFA-100 (platelet function analyzer) has largely replaced the bleeding time as the best test of platelet function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients with hereditary platelet disorders will have an abnormal platelet function test, such as the PFA-100, which has largely replaced the bleeding time as the best test for platelet function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PTT measures the intrinsic coagulation pathway and is normal in platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PT measures the extrinsic coagulation pathway, not platelet function, and is normal in platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: D-dimer reflects fibrin degradation and is used to evaluate thrombosis, not primary platelet function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrinogen level measures a clotting protein, not the functional capacity of platelets.

questions.stem: A newborn with Glanzmann thrombasthenia is noted to have leukocytosis, delayed separation of the umbilical cord, and a severe bacterial infection. These additional findings are best explained by co-occurrence of which of the following conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency of the newborn

explanation.summary: In infants, Glanzmann thrombasthenia can co-occur with leukocyte adhesion deficiency, explaining leukocytosis, delayed cord separation, and severe infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that Glanzmann thrombasthenia in infants often presents at birth with leukocytosis, delayed umbilical cord separation, or severe bacterial infections because the disorder often co-occurs with a leukocyte adhesion deficiency, a type of immunodeficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy with bleeding and clotting, not the inherited leukocyte defect described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary spherocytosis is a red-cell membrane disorder causing hemolytic anemia, unrelated to these leukocyte and infection findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency anemia causes fatigue and microcytic anemia, not leukocytosis with delayed cord separation and severe infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding from low clotting factors but does not cause leukocytosis or delayed umbilical cord separation.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl with a lifelong bleeding tendency is examined. Her shins are covered with numerous flat, nonblanching red lesions roughly 1 mm in diameter that represent small pinpoint breaks in capillaries at the skin surface. Which of the following terms best describes these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ecchymosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epistaxis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemarthrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purpura

explanation.summary: Petechiae are small, pinpoint breaks in capillaries seen at the skin surface.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines petechiae as small, pinpoint breaks in capillaries seen on the skin surface, one of the mucocutaneous findings shared by all the inherited platelet disorders. Purpura and ecchymosis are the larger lesions in the same family of findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ecchymoses are purple bruises, which are larger and discolored rather than pinpoint.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epistaxis refers to nosebleeds, a mucosal bleeding symptom rather than a skin lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemarthrosis is bleeding into a joint, a deep-tissue pattern more typical of clotting factor deficiency than of platelet disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Purpura are larger red/purple lesions, not the pinpoint capillary breaks described here.

questions.stem: A blood vessel is injured and its subendothelium is exposed. Which of the following events constitutes the initial adhesion step of normal platelet plug formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mesh network of platelets and fibrin is assembled over the injury

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha granules release fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor into the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delta granules release calcium and serotonin into the local environment

choices.label: D
choices.text: GpIb receptors attach to the complex of von Willebrand factor and collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: GpIIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen to bridge adjacent platelets

explanation.summary: Adhesion begins when platelet GpIb receptors attach to the vWF-collagen complex on exposed subendothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes plug formation as requiring initial adhesion of platelets to the subendothelium exposed after vessel injury, with platelet activation leading to attachment of GpIb receptors to the complex of von Willebrand factor and collagen. Only after this adhesion step do the later aggregation and granule-release events occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The platelet-fibrin mesh is the final product of the process, described as the ultimate step in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-granule release of fibrinogen and vWF further helps form the clot but is not the initial adhesion event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delta-granule release of calcium and serotonin supports platelet activation after platelets have already engaged the vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GpIIb/IIIa-fibrinogen bridging is the aggregation step, which follows adhesion rather than initiating it.

questions.stem: A patient's platelets are found to lack alpha granules almost entirely, so the substances normally stored in them cannot be released during clot formation. Which of the following pairs of substances is released by alpha granules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticoagulant protein C and protein S

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin sulfate and free histamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ionized calcium and serotonin (5-HT)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue factor (factor III) and thrombin

explanation.summary: Alpha granules release fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, which further help form the clot.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's account of normal plug formation, fibrinogen and vWF are released from alpha granules after GpIIb/IIIa-mediated aggregation begins and further help to form a clot. Loss of these granules is what defines gray platelet syndrome and stunts or stops plug formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein C and protein S are anticoagulant plasma proteins, not platelet granule contents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heparin and histamine are associated with mast cells and basophils rather than platelet granules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium and serotonin are the small molecules released by delta granules, not alpha granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue factor and thrombin belong to the coagulation cascade and are not stored in platelet alpha granules.

questions.stem: A family with gray platelet syndrome across three generations asks how the condition is passed on. Which of the following best describes the inheritance of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitochondrial, so the disorder is transmitted only by the mother

choices.label: B
choices.text: Strictly autosomal dominant with complete penetrance in carriers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strictly autosomal recessive, as in Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Variable: autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, or X-linked

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive in essentially all affected families

explanation.summary: Gray platelet syndrome has variable inheritance because several different alpha-granule genes can be involved.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cause of gray platelet syndrome is poorly understood, but multiple genes involved in alpha granule production have been implicated. The brick states that inheritance may be autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, or even X-linked, depending on which gene is involved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial inheritance is not among the patterns described for this alpha-granule disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal dominant transmission is only one of the possible patterns, not the rule for this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autosomal recessive inheritance is the fixed pattern of Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia, not of gray platelet syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked inheritance occurs with some implicated genes but does not describe most affected families.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with gray platelet syndrome undergoes a bone marrow biopsy, which is reported as showing myelofibrosis. Which of the following does this finding indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of iron-laden macrophages throughout the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete loss of megakaryocytes with preserved marrow fat

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expansion of the marrow by immature leukemic blasts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infiltration of the marrow by metastatic carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replacement of the bone marrow with connective tissue

explanation.summary: Myelofibrosis means the bone marrow has been replaced by connective tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines myelofibrosis as bone marrow replacement with connective tissue and lists it, along with progressive thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and elevated serum B12, among the other features that can accompany gray platelet syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron-laden macrophages reflect iron overload rather than connective tissue replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of megakaryocytes alone does not define myelofibrosis, which refers to the fibrous tissue itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Expansion by leukemic blasts describes acute leukemia, a different marrow pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow infiltration by carcinoma is a metastatic process, not the fibrous replacement meant by myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with Glanzmann thrombasthenia is bleeding after a dental extraction. His platelets adhere normally to the damaged vessel wall, and plug formation begins, yet no effective plug is produced. Which of the following best explains this failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha granules are absent, so fibrinogen and vWF are never released from platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating fibrinogen is deficient, so the fibrin mesh over the plug cannot be built

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delta granules are absent, so calcium and serotonin are never released from platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrinogen cannot bridge platelets, so only one or two attach to each vWF molecule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets cannot bind vWF, so no platelet ever reaches the exposed subendothelium

explanation.summary: In Glanzmann thrombasthenia the GpIIb/IIIa defect prevents fibrinogen bridging, so platelets cannot cluster.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abnormality in Glanzmann thrombasthenia is in the GpIIb/IIIa receptors, which prevents fibrinogen from binding platelets together, making it an aggregation problem. The brick explains that plug formation begins, but the patient may only get one or two platelets bound to each vWF rather than a cluster of many, leading to abnormal bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent alpha granules define gray platelet syndrome, a granule secretion disorder rather than a receptor disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is the platelet receptor for fibrinogen, not a shortage of circulating fibrinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absent delta granules define delta-granule deficiency, which impairs release of calcium and serotonin rather than fibrinogen bridging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure of platelets to bind vWF is the GpIb adhesion defect of Bernard-Soulier syndrome, but this patient's platelets adhere normally.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with Bernard-Soulier syndrome is followed for recurrent mucocutaneous bleeding. On routine follow-up he is found to have hematuria, proteinuria, and a rising creatinine. Which of the following nonplatelet complications of his underlying disorder does this most likely represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune thyroiditis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glomerulonephritis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic cirrhosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammatory bowel disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary fibrosis

explanation.summary: Kidney disease in the form of glomerulonephritis is an associated nonplatelet complication of Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond its platelet findings, the brick lists associated nonplatelet complications of Bernard-Soulier syndrome that include kidney disease (glomerulonephritis). Hematuria, proteinuria, and declining renal function fit that glomerular pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune thyroiditis is not described as a complication of this inherited receptor defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic cirrhosis is not among the nonplatelet complications described for this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inflammatory bowel disease is not one of the associated nonplatelet complications listed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary fibrosis is not an association of Bernard-Soulier syndrome in this material.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has a long history of eczema and repeated respiratory infections. A CBC shows thrombocytopenia with unusually small platelets, and his mother reports that two of her brothers had similar problems in childhood. Which of the following disorders is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chediak-Higashi syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gray platelet syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

explanation.summary: Eczema, infections, and microthrombocytopenia in a boy with affected maternal uncles indicate Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder involving mutations in the WASP gene, and the brick lists its signs and symptoms as predisposition to infections, microthrombocytopenia, and eczema. X-linked transmission explains affected maternal uncles, and the syndrome is one of the conditions found together with delta-granule deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome causes giant platelets rather than small ones and is autosomal recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is also a hereditary immunodeficiency linked to delta-granule deficiency, but eczema and small platelets are the Wiskott-Aldrich picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glanzmann thrombasthenia leaves platelet count and size normal and is autosomal recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gray platelet syndrome produces large, empty-appearing platelets and is not characterized by eczema.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow is reviewing peripheral smears from several patients with inherited platelet disorders. Very large platelets are commonly seen in which of the following pairs of disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delta-granule deficiency and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia and delta-granule deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia and gray platelet syndrome

explanation.summary: Very large platelets are typical of Bernard-Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: In its discussion of the peripheral blood smear, the brick states that very large platelets are often seen in Bernard-Soulier and gray platelet syndrome. Bernard-Soulier syndrome is described as one of the giant platelet disorders, a rare group that also includes gray platelet syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome has giant platelets, but Glanzmann thrombasthenia has normal platelet morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delta-granule deficiency has normal platelets, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is characterized by unusually small platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both of these disorders show histologically normal-appearing platelets on the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glanzmann thrombasthenia shows normal-appearing platelets, so only gray platelet syndrome in this pair has large platelets.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with delta-granule deficiency bleeds more than expected after a minor procedure. In addition to low secretion of the factors stored in delta granules, which of the following additional abnormalities may contribute to stunted platelet plug formation in this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased circulating prothrombin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased GpIb receptor density

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased GpIIb/IIIa receptor density

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased von Willebrand factor

explanation.summary: Delta-granule deficiency may also be linked to decreased von Willebrand factor, further stunting plug formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes delta-granule deficiency as a decrease or absence of delta granules leading to low secretion of factors needed for clotting, and adds that it may also be linked to decreased vWF, stunting the formation of platelet plugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prothrombin is a coagulation cascade factor and is not affected in this granule disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased fibrinogen is not described as an accompanying abnormality of delta-granule deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A GpIb abnormality is the defect of Bernard-Soulier syndrome, not of delta-granule deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A GpIIb/IIIa abnormality is the defect of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a separate receptor disorder.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with a hereditary platelet disorder is seen for routine health maintenance. He has required several platelet transfusions in the past. Which of the following preventive measures is specifically recommended for patients with these disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily low-dose aspirin for vascular protection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elective splenectomy in early adulthood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term iron chelation therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scheduled ibuprofen for musculoskeletal pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccination against hepatitis B

explanation.summary: Supportive care for hereditary platelet disorders includes hepatitis B vaccination, NSAID avoidance, correction of iron deficiency, and dental hygiene.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because these patients often receive blood products, the brick states that they may require vaccination against hepatitis B, along with avoidance of NSAIDs, correction of iron deficiency, and proper dental hygiene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspirin impairs platelet function and would worsen bleeding rather than protect this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenectomy is not part of the routine management outlined for hereditary platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency is to be corrected in these patients; chelation removes iron and is not part of this plan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are specifically to be avoided in these patients.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with Glanzmann thrombasthenia has heavy, prolonged bleeding with her first menstrual periods that is not controlled by local measures. Which of the following therapies is most appropriate to stop the excessive bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antimicrobial prophylaxis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryoprecipitate infusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: High-dose estrogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant factor VIIa

explanation.summary: High-dose estrogen can stop excessive bleeding during menarche in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the specific treatments listed in the brick, Glanzmann thrombasthenia may benefit from hematopoietic stem cell transplant if symptoms are recurrent and severe, and high-dose estrogen can also help stop excessive bleeding during menarche.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is used for delta-granule deficiency associated with immune deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryoprecipitate replaces clotting factors, which are not deficient in a platelet receptor disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GM-CSF therapy is offered in delta-granule deficiency with immune deficiency, not for menstrual bleeding here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIIa is listed as a specific treatment for Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man with Glanzmann thrombasthenia has had recurrent severe hemorrhages requiring hospitalization despite transfusion support and avoidance of NSAIDs. Which of the following offers the best chance of definitive correction of his platelet defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic high-dose corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term thrombopoietin agonist therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scheduled prophylactic platelet transfusions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy with postoperative vaccination

explanation.summary: Glanzmann thrombasthenia may benefit from hematopoietic stem cell transplant when symptoms are recurrent and severe.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a specific treatment for Glanzmann thrombasthenia if symptoms are recurrent and severe, because it replaces the megakaryocyte precursors that carry the defective GpIIb/IIIa receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids address immune-mediated platelet destruction, not an inherited receptor defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombopoietin agonists are listed for Bernard-Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome, and raising the count would not correct defective receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Repeated transfusions risk antiplatelet and HLA antibodies that limit the usefulness of later transfusions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not among the treatments described for Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with delta-granule deficiency associated with an immune deficiency has been hospitalized twice this year for bacterial pneumonia. In addition to antimicrobial prophylaxis, which of the following therapies may benefit her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Indefinite warfarin anticoagulation therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intermittent high-dose estrogen therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long-term intravenous iron chelation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scheduled recombinant factor VIIa infusions

explanation.summary: Delta-granule deficiency with immune deficiency is managed with antimicrobial prophylaxis and may benefit from GM-CSF therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that delta-granule deficiency associated with immune deficiency requires antimicrobial prophylaxis and that patients may benefit from GM-CSF (granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor) therapy. Hematopoietic cell transplant is also an option for this disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Warfarin is an anticoagulant and would aggravate bleeding in a platelet disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High-dose estrogen is used to control excessive bleeding at menarche in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron chelation is not part of management here; iron deficiency is instead corrected when present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recombinant factor VIIa is a listed treatment for Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

questions.stem: A man with Bernard-Soulier syndrome and his partner are planning a pregnancy. Genetic testing shows that she carries no copy of the affected gene. Which of the following best describes the risk for their children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 25% will have the syndrome and 75% will be unaffected

choices.label: B
choices.text: 50% will be carriers and 50% will be unaffected noncarriers

choices.label: C
choices.text: 50% will be carriers and 50% will have the syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: All will be carriers and none will have the syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: All will have the syndrome because the father is affected

explanation.summary: With an affected father and a genetically normal mother, every child inherits one affected copy and is a carrier, but none is affected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is autosomal recessive, so two copies of the affected gene are needed to produce disease. An affected father transmits one copy to every child; because the mother is genetically normal, each child receives only that single copy, giving a 100% chance of being a carrier and a 0% chance of having the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 25% affected risk applies when both parents are carriers, not when one parent is affected and the other is genetically normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An affected father is homozygous, so he passes an affected copy to every child rather than to half of them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is the outcome when the mother is a carrier, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Disease would require two copies; a single paternal copy makes the child a carrier only.

questions.stem: Two teenagers with lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding are evaluated. Which of the following findings on the complete blood count and peripheral smear would favor Bernard-Soulier syndrome over Glanzmann thrombasthenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased platelet count with abnormally large platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased platelet count with normal-sized platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased platelet count with normal-sized platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal platelet count with abnormally small platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal platelet count with normal platelet morphology

explanation.summary: Bernard-Soulier syndrome shows a decreased platelet count with abnormally large platelets; Glanzmann thrombasthenia shows a normal count and normal morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's comparison table gives a decreased platelet count and abnormally large platelet appearance for Bernard-Soulier syndrome, versus a normal count and normal appearance for Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Severity is variable in both, so only the count and morphology separate them on routine testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal-sized platelets do not fit Bernard-Soulier syndrome, whose platelets are characteristically giant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An increased platelet count is not the pattern described for Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small platelets point toward the microthrombocytopenia of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal count with normal morphology is the Glanzmann thrombasthenia pattern in the table.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with a known hereditary platelet disorder has bleeding from the gums after a fall. A trainee suggests giving cryoprecipitate. Which of the following is the best reason this product is not indicated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be given to children under five years of age

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reliably induces antiplatelet and HLA antibodies on first exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replaces clotting factors, which are not deficient in this patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: It would falsely normalize the platelet function analyzer result

choices.label: E
choices.text: It would raise the platelet count too quickly and cause thrombosis

explanation.summary: Cryoprecipitate is used for clotting factor deficiencies, and the coagulation cascade is intact in platelet disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hereditary platelet disorders the platelets, not the coagulation cascade, are abnormal, so the PT and PTT are normal. The brick states there is no need for cryoprecipitate in such a patient because that product is used for clotting factor deficiencies, not platelet disorders; platelet transfusion is the product used for severe bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no age restriction of this kind on the product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiplatelet and HLA antibodies arise after repeated platelet transfusions, not predictably on a first exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The platelet function analyzer reflects platelet function and is not the reason to withhold this product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cryoprecipitate supplies clotting factors and does not raise the platelet count at all.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old is being worked up for a suspected inherited platelet adhesion disorder. Which of the following groups of tests is used initially, with the understanding that the results are basic but nondiagnostic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy, spleen ultrasound, and HLA typing

choices.label: B
choices.text: D-dimer, fibrinogen level, and mixing study

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electron microscopy, platelet aggregation studies, and genetic testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum B12, serum ferritin, and reticulocyte count

explanation.summary: Platelet count, PT, and PTT are the basic but nondiagnostic initial tests for inherited platelet adhesion disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time as the basic but nondiagnostic tests used to initially diagnose inherited platelet adhesion disorders. They establish that the cascade is intact and frame the abnormal platelet function that follows.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow biopsy, imaging, and HLA typing are not the basic screening set for these disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D-dimer, fibrinogen, and mixing studies evaluate thrombosis and factor problems rather than screening for platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Electron microscopy, aggregation studies, and genetic testing are the more specific tests that follow an abnormal platelet function result.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B12, ferritin, and reticulocyte count address anemia and nutritional issues rather than platelet disease.

questions.stem: A group of patients with different hereditary platelet disorders all have complete blood counts drawn. Which of the following statements about the platelet count in these disorders is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be measured accurately when platelets are dysfunctional

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is decreased in every hereditary platelet disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is increased in every hereditary platelet disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is normal in every hereditary platelet disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It may be decreased, normal, or increased depending on the disorder

explanation.summary: Across the hereditary platelet disorders the platelet count can be decreased, normal, or increased.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that on the complete blood count, platelet counts can be decreased, normal, or increased in these disorders. Bernard-Soulier syndrome typically shows a low count while Glanzmann thrombasthenia shows a normal one, which is why the count alone cannot exclude a platelet disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Automated counting still yields a count; the abnormality lies in platelet function, not in measurability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia characteristically has a normal platelet count, so a decrease is not universal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated count is only one of several possible results, not the rule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome commonly show thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with mucocutaneous bleeding has a normal platelet count, normal PT and PTT, and an abnormal platelet function analyzer result. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in establishing a specific diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin empiric platelet transfusions and observe the response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measure serum ferritin and total iron binding capacity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obtain a D-dimer and fibrinogen level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proceed to histologic and genetic testing of the platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time

explanation.summary: An abnormal platelet function test prompts more specific histologic and genetic testing to identify the disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that abnormal platelet function will prompt more specific histologic and genetic testing for diagnosis. The screening set of platelet count, PT, and PTT is basic but nondiagnostic, so the specific disorder is identified with studies such as smear morphology, electron microscopy, aggregation patterns, and genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion treats bleeding but does not identify which hereditary platelet disorder is present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron studies address a supportive-care issue rather than the specific diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D-dimer and fibrinogen evaluate fibrin turnover and clotting proteins, not platelet structure or genetics.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeating normal cascade tests adds nothing, since these are expected to be normal in platelet disorders.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy has nosebleeds three or four times a week. His CBC is entirely normal including the platelet count, PT and PTT are normal, and the platelet function analyzer result is increased. He is diagnosed with Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Which of the following statements best explains his condition to his parents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has enough platelets, but they cannot clump together to plug a damaged vessel

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has too few platelets, so there are not enough to cover a damaged vessel

choices.label: C
choices.text: His blood vessels are fragile, so they break even when his platelets work normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: His platelets are destroyed by his immune system faster than they are produced

choices.label: E
choices.text: His platelets are normal, but a missing clotting protein keeps the clot from forming

explanation.summary: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a functional defect: platelet number is adequate but the platelets cannot aggregate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case explains that platelets are cells that plug the hole of a damaged blood vessel by clumping together, and that this child has an inherited condition in which his platelets are unable to do this. He has enough of them, but they do not do their job well, which is why the count is normal while the platelet function test is abnormal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The platelet count is normal in this patient, so a shortage of platelets does not explain the bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The defect lies in the platelets themselves, not in the structure of the vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune destruction would lower the platelet count and is not the mechanism of this inherited receptor defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal PT and PTT indicate the clotting proteins are intact; this is a platelet problem.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman with gray platelet syndrome asks which over-the-counter medications she may use for headaches. Which of the following classes of drugs should she be advised to avoid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral iron supplement tablets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral proton pump inhibitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Second-generation antihistamines

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical corticosteroid creams

explanation.summary: Avoidance of NSAIDs is part of routine care for patients with hereditary platelet disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Along with hepatitis B vaccination, correction of iron deficiency, and proper dental hygiene, the brick lists avoidance of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as part of managing patients with hereditary platelet disorders, because these agents further impair already defective platelet function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron is actually supplied when needed, since correction of iron deficiency is recommended.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proton pump inhibitors are not part of the avoidance advice described for platelet disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihistamines are not identified as agents to avoid in these patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical corticosteroids are not among the medications these patients are told to avoid.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with a hereditary platelet disorder arrives with spontaneous gastrointestinal bleeding and a falling hemoglobin. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate now?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arrange outpatient genetic testing before any therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Begin a thrombopoietin agonist and reassess in two weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start antimicrobial prophylaxis and observe

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse platelets or blood products

explanation.summary: Clinically severe bleeding or a low platelet count in any of these disorders may require platelet or blood transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that treatment depends on the specific disorder and bleeding severity, and that in any of these disorders patients with clinically severe bleeding or low platelets may require platelet or blood transfusion. Transfusion is frequently needed to control spontaneous or severe bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NSAIDs are specifically avoided because they further impair platelet function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genetic testing refines the diagnosis but cannot wait ahead of controlling severe bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombopoietin agonists raise counts over time and do not address active severe hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antimicrobial prophylaxis addresses infection risk in delta-granule deficiency, not acute bleeding.

questions.stem: A student is comparing the four hereditary platelet disorders. For which of the following is the underlying defect and inheritance pattern described as poorly understood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and delta-granule deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia and delta-granule deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gray platelet syndrome and delta-granule deficiency

explanation.summary: The granule disorders, gray platelet syndrome and delta-granule deficiency, have poorly understood defects and inheritance.
