explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's summary states that in gray platelet syndrome and delta-granule deficiency the inheritance patterns and underlying defects are poorly understood, in contrast to the two receptor disorders whose defective glycoproteins and autosomal recessive inheritance are well defined.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome does not belong in this pair, since its defect and inheritance are established.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both of these have a defined glycoprotein defect and established autosomal recessive inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is well characterized as an autosomal recessive GpIb defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a defined autosomal recessive GpIIb/IIIa defect.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 30-year-old man has a routine complete blood count performed at a wellness visit. His hematologist notes that in adults the normal platelet count ranges from 150,000 to 400,000 cells/uL. Below which of the following platelet counts is a patient, by definition, considered to have thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10,000 cells/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: 50,000 cells/uL

choices.label: C
choices.text: 100,000 cells/uL

choices.label: D
choices.text: 150,000 cells/uL

choices.label: E
choices.text: 400,000 cells/uL

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia is defined as a platelet count below 150,000 cells/uL, the lower limit of the normal adult range.
explanation.whyCorrect: The normal adult platelet count is 150,000 to 400,000 cells/uL, so any count below 150,000 cells/uL meets the definition of thrombocytopenia. Lower thresholds mark increasing severity but are not the defining cutoff.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Below 10,000 cells/uL is a hematologic emergency with risk of spontaneous bleeding, not the definitional threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Below 50,000 cells/uL marks the point at which serious bleeding risk and skin signs appear, but it is not the definition of thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 100,000 cells/uL is below normal but is not the definitional cutoff; a count below 150,000 already qualifies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 400,000 cells/uL is the upper limit of the normal range, not a threshold for thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with hypertension and COPD is admitted for pneumonia and subsequently develops a deep venous thrombosis. She is started on several medications. Five days after admission, a complete blood count shows that her platelet count has dropped from 250,000 to 70,000 cells/uL. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaminophen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Albuterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Azithromycin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lisinopril

explanation.summary: A significant platelet drop 5-10 days after starting heparin for a venous thrombosis is classic for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) develops when a circulating antibody complexes heparin with platelet factor 4, leading to platelet destruction and paradoxical thrombosis. It typically occurs 5-10 days after heparin exposure, which matches this patient treated for a DVT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaminophen is not a recognized cause of the acute platelet drop seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Albuterol is used for COPD and is not an established cause of thrombocytopenia in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Azithromycin treats the pneumonia; drug-induced thrombocytopenia from it is far less likely than from heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lisinopril is an outpatient antihypertensive and is not a typical cause of acute thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the skin findings of a patient with thrombocytopenia. Both petechiae and purpura are present. Which of the following best differentiates petechiae from purpura?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Petechiae appear on the abdomen while purpura appears only on the legs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Petechiae are caused by inflammation while purpura are caused by bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Petechiae are more numerous than purpura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechiae are red while purpura are purple

choices.label: E
choices.text: Petechiae are smaller than purpura

explanation.summary: Petechiae and purpura are distinguished chiefly by size: petechiae are less than 3 mm, whereas purpura are 3 to 10 mm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Petechiae are nonblanchable superficial macules smaller than 3 mm, while purpura are larger lesions of 3 to 10 mm. Both result from extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin, so size is the key distinguishing feature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Location does not differentiate the two; both can occur at the same sites.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both petechiae and purpura share the same etiology of subcutaneous bleeding, not inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relative number is not a defining distinction between petechiae and purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Color overlaps (both are red to purple) and is not the reliable distinguishing feature.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 8,000 cells/uL. He has no bruising, petechiae, or active bleeding, and platelet clumping has been excluded. According to standard practice, prophylactic platelet transfusion is generally indicated once the platelet count falls below which of the following values in a non-bleeding patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5,000 cells/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10,000 cells/uL

choices.label: C
choices.text: 30,000 cells/uL

choices.label: D
choices.text: 50,000 cells/uL

choices.label: E
choices.text: 100,000 cells/uL

explanation.summary: In a patient who is not actively bleeding, prophylactic platelet transfusion is generally given once the count is below 10,000 cells/uL.
explanation.whyCorrect: A platelet count below 10,000 cells/uL carries a high risk of spontaneous bleeding, so patients at or below this level should receive transfusion even without active bleeding. Actively bleeding patients with low counts are also transfused, with a goal above 50,000 cells/uL for most patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5,000 cells/uL is lower than the accepted trigger; transfusion is indicated before the count falls this far.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 30,000 cells/uL is not the standard prophylactic transfusion threshold for a non-bleeding patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50,000 cells/uL is the general post-transfusion goal and the surgical safety threshold, not the prophylactic trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Above 100,000 cells/uL is a post-transfusion goal for patients bleeding into the central nervous system, not a prophylactic transfusion threshold.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a complete blood count as part of a pre-employment physical. The CBC is normal except for a platelet count of 8,000 cells/uL. She feels well, and no bruises, petechiae, or purpura are found on examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in working up her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coagulation studies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver function tests

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal function tests

explanation.summary: A markedly low platelet count in a completely asymptomatic patient suggests artifactual (pseudo)thrombocytopenia, which is investigated first with a peripheral blood smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: Such a low count with no bleeding signs is suspicious for pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping in the EDTA specimen. A peripheral smear can reveal the clumps; if present, a repeat CBC in a citrate tube gives an accurate count. Pseudothrombocytopenia should be excluded before further workup or treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow biopsy is a last resort, generally reserved for confirmed low counts with pancytopenia, not for a possible lab artifact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulation studies are part of the broader workup but should follow confirmation that the platelet count is truly low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Liver function tests are useful once real thrombocytopenia is established, not as the immediate next step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal function tests belong to the later workup and do not address the likely clumping artifact.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with infectious mononucleosis is found to have a platelet count of 95,000 cells/uL. He has no bleeding symptoms, and his hemoglobin and white blood cell count are normal. On examination he has a palpably enlarged spleen. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow infiltration by leukemic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune destruction of platelets by autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased splenic sequestration of platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet consumption within microthrombi

explanation.summary: An enlarged spleen from mononucleosis sequesters an increased fraction of platelets, producing mild thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally about one-third of platelets are sequestered in the splenic sinusoids. When the spleen enlarges (hypersplenism), a greater proportion is trapped there and unavailable to the circulation, lowering the measured platelet count. Infection such as mononucleosis is a recognized cause of splenomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no heparin exposure, so HIT antibodies are not the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no pancytopenia or abnormal cells to suggest marrow infiltration by leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune destruction (ITP) is not indicated here; the splenomegaly points to sequestration rather than autoantibody-mediated destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There are no schistocytes or coagulation abnormalities to indicate consumption within microthrombi.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman develops petechiae on her lower legs and gum bleeding two weeks after a viral upper respiratory illness. She feels otherwise well. Her CBC shows an isolated platelet count of 18,000 cells/uL with a normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count. The peripheral smear shows reduced but otherwise normal-appearing platelets and no schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression from leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypersplenism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

explanation.summary: Isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well patient, often after a viral illness, is characteristic of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).
explanation.whyCorrect: ITP is a common acquired autoimmune cause of thrombocytopenia in which autoantibodies destroy platelets in the spleen. It typically presents as isolated thrombocytopenia with normal other cell lines and can follow infections; the smear shows reduced but morphologically normal platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow suppression from leukemia would typically cause pancytopenia with abnormal cells, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC shows schistocytes, prolonged PT/PTT, and a critically ill patient, none of which are present here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIT requires recent heparin exposure and characteristically causes thrombosis, not this post-viral isolated thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypersplenism would be expected to produce splenomegaly and often affects multiple cell lines rather than isolated platelets.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man in the ICU with gram-negative sepsis develops oozing from his intravenous catheter sites and around his gums. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 40,000 cells/uL, prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, and schistocytes on the peripheral smear. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa defect)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA clumping

explanation.summary: Sepsis with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation times, and schistocytes indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In DIC, derangement of the coagulation cascade drives rapid platelet consumption as microthrombi form, producing thrombocytopenia. The associated microangiopathic damage generates schistocytes, and simultaneous consumption of clotting factors prolongs both the PT and PTT. Prolonged coagulation studies are the exception in thrombocytopenia and point specifically to DIC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a hereditary platelet aggregation defect with a normal platelet count, not consumptive thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIT characteristically produces thrombosis rather than diffuse bleeding, and it does not typically prolong the PT/PTT or produce schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT/PTT and no schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pseudothrombocytopenia is a lab artifact in a well patient and would not cause real bleeding or abnormal coagulation studies.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 35 weeks of gestation presents with right upper quadrant pain and malaise. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 60,000 cells/uL, elevated liver transaminases, and evidence of hemolysis on the peripheral smear. Which of the following best explains her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune thrombocytopenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic sequestration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

explanation.summary: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets in a pregnant woman define HELLP syndrome, a microangiopathic consumptive process.
explanation.whyCorrect: HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) occurs in pregnancy and causes rapid platelet consumption within microthrombi, a form of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The combination of pregnancy, right upper quadrant pain, transaminase elevation, and hemolysis is characteristic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIT requires heparin exposure and causes thrombosis, not the hemolysis and liver findings seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ITP produces isolated thrombocytopenia without hemolysis or elevated liver enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sequestration causes mild thrombocytopenia from an enlarged spleen and does not explain hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy but classically presents with neurologic changes and renal involvement rather than the liver-enzyme elevation of pregnancy-related HELLP.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man reports several weeks of fatigue and is noted to be pale. His CBC shows a platelet count of 35,000 cells/uL, a hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, and a white blood cell count of 2,000/uL. The peripheral smear shows abnormal-appearing cells across multiple cell lines. Platelet clumping has been excluded. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coagulation studies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal function tests

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat CBC in a citrate tube

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia with abnormal cells on smear indicates possible marrow failure or neoplasia, which is evaluated with a bone marrow biopsy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The concurrent presence of thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia defines pancytopenia and points to pathology in the bone marrow. A bone marrow biopsy is indicated to distinguish marrow toxicity from hematopoietic neoplasia and to identify a neoplasm such as leukemia if present.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulation studies do not explain pancytopenia or identify a marrow disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfusion may be needed for symptoms but is not a diagnostic step and does not establish the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal function tests would not explain pancytopenia with abnormal cells across cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clumping has already been excluded, so a citrate-tube recount for pseudothrombocytopenia is unnecessary.

questions.stem: A hematologist is teaching students how the bleeding pattern of thrombocytopenia differs from that of a coagulation-factor disorder such as hemophilia. Which of the following findings most strongly suggests a platelet problem (thrombocytopenia) rather than a coagulation-factor disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prolonged PTT with a normal platelet count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deep bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deep intramuscular hematomas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delayed bleeding that begins hours after injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superficial mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia causes superficial mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae, unlike the deep tissue bleeding of coagulation-factor disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleeding in thrombocytopenia is superficial, presenting as petechiae, purpura, and mucous membrane bleeding from the gums and nose. This contrasts with hemophilia and other coagulation disorders, in which bleeding is deep, such as into joints and muscles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A prolonged PTT with a normal platelet count reflects a coagulation-cascade abnormality, not thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemarthrosis is a hallmark of coagulation-factor disorders such as hemophilia, not thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deep intramuscular hematomas indicate a coagulation-factor disorder, not a platelet disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delayed bleeding hours after injury is typical of coagulation-factor defects rather than platelet problems.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man treated with heparin for 6 days develops a 60% drop in his platelet count along with a new arterial clot. A heparin-PF4 antibody test is positive. Heparin is stopped immediately. Because he still requires anticoagulation for his thrombosis, which of the following is the most appropriate next agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Argatroban

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspirin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restart heparin at a lower dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin started alone immediately

explanation.summary: After stopping heparin in HIT, anticoagulation is continued with an alternative agent such as the direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban.
explanation.whyCorrect: In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, stopping heparin is the first step, and the next is starting an alternative anticoagulant. Direct thrombin inhibitors such as argatroban or bivalirudin, or direct factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban or apixaban, are appropriate choices to treat the ongoing thrombotic risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent and provides inadequate anticoagulation for an active HIT-related thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet transfusion can fuel further thrombosis in HIT and does not address the anticoagulation need.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restarting heparin would reintroduce the offending agent and worsen the antibody-mediated process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin should not be started alone in acute HIT because of thrombotic risk; a nonheparin anticoagulant is used first.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a complete blood count ordered for fatigue that shows a platelet count of 90,000 cells/uL. She has no bruising, petechiae, or mucosal bleeding. Her physician explains that most patients remain free of clinical findings until the platelet count falls further. Below which of the following platelet counts do the clinical signs and symptoms of thrombocytopenia typically begin to appear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10,000 cells/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: 30,000 cells/uL

choices.label: C
choices.text: 50,000 cells/uL

choices.label: D
choices.text: 100,000 cells/uL

choices.label: E
choices.text: 140,000 cells/uL

explanation.summary: Clinical signs and symptoms of thrombocytopenia generally do not appear until the platelet count is below 50,000 cells/uL.
explanation.whyCorrect: A count below 50,000 cells/uL places a patient at risk for serious bleeding, and signs of bleeding in the skin such as easy bruising, petechiae, and purpura begin to develop. Because findings are absent above this level, most cases of thrombocytopenia are discovered incidentally on a complete blood count ordered for another reason.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Below 10,000 cells/uL the patient is at risk for spontaneous bleeding, which is a hematologic emergency rather than the point at which findings first appear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Below 30,000 cells/uL there is increased risk of bleeding after minor trauma, but bruising, petechiae, and purpura have already appeared above this level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patients with counts near 100,000 cells/uL are generally asymptomatic and may at most experience easy bruising.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A count of 140,000 cells/uL is only mildly below the normal range and is expected to be asymptomatic.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma has a platelet count of 24,000 cells/uL. He has scattered petechiae on his shins but no active bleeding and normal vital signs. Which of the following best describes his current bleeding risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has no added bleeding risk until the count falls below 10,000

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is at increased risk of bleeding following minor trauma

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is at risk for deep bleeding into joints and muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is expected to bleed spontaneously without any trauma

choices.label: E
choices.text: He should be asymptomatic apart from occasional easy bruising

explanation.summary: A platelet count below 30,000 cells/uL confers an increased risk of bleeding following minor trauma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleeding risk tracks with the severity of thrombocytopenia. Counts of 30,000 to 50,000 cells/uL produce easy bruising, petechiae, and purpura, and once the count drops below 30,000 cells/uL bleeding after minor trauma becomes likely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleeding risk rises progressively well before the count reaches 10,000 cells/uL, and he already has petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deep bleeding into joints and muscle characterizes coagulation factor disorders such as hemophilia, not thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spontaneous bleeding without trauma is the hazard of counts below 10,000 cells/uL, which is considered a hematologic emergency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Patients are asymptomatic or have only easy bruising when the count is closer to the lower end of normal, not at 24,000 cells/uL.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a chronic hematologic disorder has required repeated platelet transfusions over several months and will likely need additional therapy. Her hematologist counsels her that platelet transfusions should be used sparingly rather than routinely. Which of the following is the main reason for this caution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Repeated transfusions may induce immune resistance to future transfusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeated transfusions promote platelet clumping in the specimen tube

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfused platelets accelerate destruction of her own platelets in the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfused platelets predispose to antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfused platelets suppress megakaryocyte production in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Too many platelet transfusions can induce immune resistance to future transfusions, so they are given with caution in chronic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelet transfusion is important for patients with severe symptoms, but repeated exposure to foreign platelet antigens can generate an immune response that renders later transfusions ineffective. This matters most when the underlying condition is chronic and more therapy will be needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet clumping is a laboratory artifact of blood anticoagulated with EDTA and is unrelated to transfusion history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic destruction of a patient's own platelets is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenia, not a consequence of transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex are generated by heparin exposure, not by platelet transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion does not suppress megakaryocytes; decreased megakaryocyte production results from marrow suppression by drugs, toxins, or neoplasms.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with a bleed in the central nervous system has a platelet count of 22,000 cells/uL and is being transfused platelets. Which of the following post-transfusion platelet counts should be targeted in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More than 10,000 cells/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: More than 30,000 cells/uL

choices.label: C
choices.text: More than 50,000 cells/uL

choices.label: D
choices.text: More than 100,000 cells/uL

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 150,000 cells/uL

explanation.summary: Patients with central nervous system bleeding are transfused to a platelet count above 100,000 cells/uL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The usual post-transfusion goal is more than 50,000 cells/uL, but bleeding into the central nervous system is far less forgiving, so the target is raised to more than 100,000 cells/uL. The same higher threshold is used for patients undergoing neurosurgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A count of 10,000 cells/uL is the threshold below which transfusion is triggered in a non-bleeding patient, not a post-transfusion goal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A count above 30,000 cells/uL is not used as a transfusion goal and would leave this patient at risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: More than 50,000 cells/uL is the goal for most patients but is insufficient when the bleed is intracranial.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion is not pushed to a fully normal platelet count of 150,000 cells/uL.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia has a platelet count of 22,000 cells/uL and bleeding from her gums. Her liver and kidney function are normal and no schistocytes are seen on the smear. Coagulation studies are ordered. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolongation of both the prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolonged partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolonged prothrombin time with a normal partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shortened prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times

explanation.summary: Coagulation studies are normal in thrombocytopenia because PT and PTT reflect the coagulation cascade rather than platelet number.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged PT and PTT are not typical of thrombocytopenia. The notable exception is disseminated intravascular coagulation, in which thrombocytopenia and prolonged coagulation studies occur together; nothing in this patient suggests that process.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prolongation of both studies alongside thrombocytopenia would suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isolated prolonged partial thromboplastin time reflects a coagulation cascade abnormality rather than low platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An isolated prolonged prothrombin time points toward chronic liver disease, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia does not shorten coagulation times.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with thrombocytopenia has several flat, nonblanchable purple lesions on his forearm. His physician documents them as ecchymoses rather than purpura. Lesions larger than which of the following sizes are termed ecchymoses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 mm

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 mm

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 mm

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10 mm

choices.label: E
choices.text: 20 mm

explanation.summary: Cutaneous bleeding lesions larger than 10 mm are called ecchymoses, or bruises.
explanation.whyCorrect: Skin findings in thrombocytopenia are graded by size: petechiae are less than 3 mm, purpura are 3 to 10 mm, and lesions larger than 10 mm are ecchymoses. The bruising of thrombocytopenia is superficial rather than the deep bleeding of a coagulation disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1 mm lesion falls well within the size range of a petechia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lesions larger than 3 mm are classified as purpura until they exceed 10 mm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 5 mm lesion sits within the 3 to 10 mm range that defines purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lesions become ecchymoses once they exceed 10 mm; 20 mm is not the cutoff.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a platelet count of 26,000 cells/uL is found to have multiple 1- to 2-mm red, flat dots from midshin to ankles. The lesions are nontender and do not blanch with pressure. Which of the following best explains how these lesions form?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutination of platelets within dermal capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of iron pigment within dermal macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrin microthrombi occluding dermal arterioles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inflammatory infiltration of the walls of small dermal vessels

explanation.summary: Petechiae are nonblanchable, nonpalpable macules less than 3 mm caused by extravasation of blood from small vessels into the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: In thrombocytopenia the capillaries leak because there are too few platelets to seal them, and blood escapes into the skin. Because the blood lies outside the vessels, the lesions do not blanch when pressure is applied, which distinguishes them from dilated vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelet agglutination occurs in the specimen tube and causes a falsely low laboratory count, not skin lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pigment deposition does not explain acute nonblanching red macules appearing with a low platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occlusion of arterioles by microthrombi would produce ischemic skin changes rather than petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inflammation of vessel walls is not the mechanism by which thrombocytopenic petechiae arise.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with severe thrombocytopenia is counseled about what could happen if her platelet count is not corrected. Which of the following is the rare but most serious complication she should be warned about?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolonged gum bleeding after brushing the teeth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recurrent epistaxis from the nasal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous bleeding into the brain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superficial bruising over the extremities

explanation.summary: Spontaneous intracranial bleeding is the rare but potentially fatal complication of severe thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most bleeding in thrombocytopenia is superficial and mucocutaneous, but spontaneous bleeding into the brain can occur and may lead to stroke, coma, or death. This possibility is what drives urgent correction of very low platelet counts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heavy or long menstrual bleeding is a common manifestation in women with thrombocytopenia, not the rare life-threatening one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gum bleeding is a frequent presenting complaint rather than a rare severe complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epistaxis is one of the typical mucous membrane bleeding sites and is usually not life-threatening.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superficial bruising is an expected skin finding once the count is low.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate is obtained from a patient being evaluated for thrombocytopenia, and the pathologist points out two large cells that give rise to circulating platelets. Platelets are released into the bloodstream from the breakdown of which of the following cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythroid precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphoblasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Megakaryocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myeloblasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma cells

explanation.summary: Platelets are produced in the bone marrow from megakaryocytes, which break down and release platelets into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like the other blood cell lines, platelets are made in the bone marrow. The much larger megakaryocytes fragment within the marrow to release platelets into the bloodstream, and they are only rarely seen on a peripheral blood smear. Anything that decreases megakaryocyte number or function causes thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythroid precursors give rise to red blood cells rather than platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoblasts are immature lymphoid cells and do not produce platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myeloblasts are precursors of granulocytes, and their accumulation characterizes acute myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are antibody-producing cells of the lymphoid lineage.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has a platelet count of 62,000 cells/uL, a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL, and a white blood cell count of 2,800/uL. A bone marrow biopsy shows hematopoietic cells with abnormal, dysplastic morphology. His physician notes that this condition may later transform into acute myeloid leukemia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypersplenism from liver failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelodysplastic neoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

explanation.summary: Cytopenias with dysplastic hematopoietic cells that may progress to acute myeloid leukemia define a myelodysplastic neoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myelodysplastic neoplasms are hematologic cancers in which patients present with low blood counts and hematopoietic cells of abnormal morphology. They suppress and infiltrate the marrow, reducing platelet production, and can eventually progress to acute myeloid leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia infiltrates the marrow but is not characterized by dysplastic maturation of hematopoietic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute myeloid leukemia is the disease this condition may transform into, not the current diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypersplenism sequesters platelets and would not produce dysplastic marrow morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an inherited thrombocytopenia present from birth, not a new marrow disorder of an older adult.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a long history of poor nutrition has a platelet count of 88,000 cells/uL along with anemia. He takes no medications and has no exposure to toxins. Deficiency of which of the following is most likely suppressing his bone marrow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron and copper

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thiamine and niacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B12 and folate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin D and calcium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K and vitamin C

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency suppress the bone marrow and can cause thrombocytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bone marrow can be suppressed by chemotherapy, radiation, toxins such as benzene, adverse drug reactions, and nutritional deficiencies. Among vitamin deficiencies, B12 and folate are the ones that reduce marrow output and lower the platelet count, typically alongside anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron deficiency causes anemia without suppressing megakaryocytes, and copper is not identified as a cause here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thiamine and niacin deficiencies cause neurologic and dermatologic disease rather than thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin D and calcium deficiency affect bone mineralization, not marrow platelet production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency impairs the coagulation cascade rather than platelet production, and vitamin C deficiency is not a listed cause of marrow suppression.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has bilateral absence of the radii and a platelet count of 40,000 cells/uL. The mother's platelet count is normal, and there is no evidence of congenital infection. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the infant's thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal drug consumption in pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia with absent radii at birth is the inherited disorder known as TAR syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inherited thrombocytopenias are congenital disorders associated with specific genetic mutations that produce a decreased platelet count at birth. Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome pairs the low platelet count with the skeletal defect seen in this infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congenital infection is the most common cause of neonatal thrombocytopenia overall, but the stem excludes it and it does not cause absent radii.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal drug consumption can lower neonatal platelet counts but would not produce a limb defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia results from maternal antibody against fetal platelet antigen and causes no skeletal malformation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is also an inherited thrombocytopenia but is not associated with absent radii.

questions.stem: A term neonate is found to have a platelet count of 65,000 cells/uL on the second day of life. The pediatric team considers the possible etiologies before ordering tests. Which of the following is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in neonates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inherited platelet disorders

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal antibodies to fetal platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal drug consumption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration

explanation.summary: Infection is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in neonates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Not all thrombocytopenia in babies is inherited. Infections such as rubella, cytomegalovirus, varicella, and hepatitis are the leading cause, followed by maternal drug consumption and maternal antibodies directed at fetal platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inherited thrombocytopenias such as TAR and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome are uncommon relative to infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal antibodies to fetal platelets cause neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, which is rare though potentially severe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal drug consumption is a recognized cause but ranks behind infection in frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration from hypersplenism is not the usual explanation for a low platelet count in a newborn.

questions.stem: A woman in her first pregnancy delivers a healthy-appearing term infant who develops widespread petechiae within hours of birth. The infant's platelet count is 18,000 cells/uL and the mother's count is normal. Testing shows that the infant's platelets carry the HPA-1a antigen, which the mother lacks. Which of the following best explains the infant's thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited mutation has decreased platelet production since birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal antibody crossed the placenta and destroyed fetal platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal platelets crossed the placenta and were destroyed by the fetal spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets were consumed by microthrombi formed during delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: The infant's own autoantibodies are destroying platelet surface proteins

explanation.summary: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia occurs when maternal antibody against a fetal platelet antigen crosses the placenta and destroys fetal platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: The baby's platelets carry an antigen, usually HPA-1a, that the mother lacks. The mother develops an antibody to that antigen, and the antibody crosses the placenta to cause destruction of platelets in the fetal spleen. Unlike hemolytic disease requiring prior sensitization, this can occur in the first pregnancy, and treatment is transfusion of platelets lacking the antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inherited production defect would not be explained by the antigen mismatch between mother and infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibody, not maternal platelets, crosses the placenta in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Consumption in microthrombi occurs in disseminated intravascular coagulation and other microangiopathies, which are not suggested here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoantibodies against one's own platelets describe immune thrombocytopenia, whereas here the antibody is of maternal origin and directed at a foreign antigen.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease has easy bruising and bleeding from his gums. His platelet count is mildly reduced and the blood urea nitrogen and creatinine are markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains the platelet abnormality produced by uremia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies form against uremic toxins bound to platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelet aggregation is decreased and adhesiveness is impaired

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelets are consumed by microthrombi in renal capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets are lost in the urine through damaged glomeruli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets are sequestered within an enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Uremic toxins primarily cause decreased platelet aggregation and impaired platelet adhesiveness.
explanation.whyCorrect: In reduced kidney function, unexcreted toxins build up in the blood and some of these decrease platelet function and production. The mechanism is multifactorial but results chiefly from decreased platelet aggregation and impaired adhesiveness, which produces bleeding that can be out of proportion to the platelet count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uremia is not an immunologic cause of thrombocytopenia and does not act through autoantibody formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Consumption in microthrombi characterizes microangiopathic processes such as hemolytic uremic syndrome rather than uremia itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets are not filtered or lost through the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is the mechanism of hypersplenism, which is not a feature of chronic kidney disease.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with liver failure from chronic alcohol use has a platelet count of 78,000 cells/uL. He has no splenomegaly on imaging and his marrow is not infiltrated. Reduced hepatic production of which of the following most directly accounts for his low platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrinogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prothrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombopoietin

explanation.summary: Liver failure lowers the platelet count because the liver no longer produces adequate thrombopoietin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombopoietin is made in the liver and drives platelet production. Liver failure, particularly from chronic alcohol use, leads to thrombocytopenia through the loss of this hepatic hormone; hypersplenism from portal hypertension can add to the problem but is excluded here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low serum albumin is a marker of chronic liver disease but does not itself reduce platelet production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin drives red cell production and is not the hepatic factor governing platelet number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinogen participates in clot formation but does not regulate platelet production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deficient prothrombin prolongs the prothrombin time without lowering the platelet count.

questions.stem: A student asks why an enlarged spleen lowers the circulating platelet count even when platelet production is normal. In a healthy adult, approximately what proportion of circulating platelets is normally sequestered within the splenic sinusoids?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all

choices.label: B
choices.text: One-half

choices.label: C
choices.text: One-tenth

choices.label: D
choices.text: One-third

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two-thirds

explanation.summary: About one-third of circulating platelets are normally held in the splenic sinusoids and are unavailable to the circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because a third of the platelet pool already sits in the spleen at baseline, any condition that enlarges the spleen markedly increases the number sequestered. Hypersplenism therefore leaves a smaller percentage in the circulation and produces thrombocytopenia without any defect in production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sequestering nearly all platelets is incompatible with a normal circulating count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Half of the platelet mass is more than is normally sequestered in a healthy spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One-tenth understates the normal splenic pool and would make splenomegaly a trivial cause of thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two-thirds would leave too few platelets in the circulation under normal conditions.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with chronic epigastric pain has an isolated platelet count of 32,000 cells/uL with a normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count. Testing for Helicobacter pylori is positive; HIV and hepatitis serologies are negative and the spleen is not enlarged. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial toxins directly lyse circulating platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic gastric blood loss depletes the platelet pool

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross reaction produces autoantibodies against platelet surface proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic enlargement from infection sequesters circulating platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism infiltrates and suppresses marrow megakaryocytes

explanation.summary: Infections such as H. pylori, HIV, and hepatitis cause immune thrombocytopenia through an immunologic cross reaction that generates antiplatelet autoantibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immune thrombocytopenia can be idiopathic, associated with autoimmune disease such as lupus or antiphospholipid syndrome, or triggered by infection. The underlying mechanism in the infectious cases is an immunological cross reaction that produces autoantibodies against proteins on the platelet surface; the antibody-coated platelets are then destroyed in the spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct lysis of platelets by bacterial toxins is not the mechanism of infection-associated immune thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood loss does not produce an isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sequestration requires an enlarged spleen, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow infiltration would be expected to depress other cell lines as well, producing pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman develops petechiae and a platelet count of 21,000 cells/uL one week after starting a new medication for nocturnal leg cramps. She has received no heparin, has no splenomegaly, and her smear shows no schistocytes. Which of the following medications most likely caused her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albuterol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Azithromycin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lisinopril

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quinine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warfarin

explanation.summary: Quinine is a classic cause of drug-dependent antibodies that destroy platelets and lower the count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain medications, including heparin, abciximab, quinine, gold salts, penicillin, vancomycin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and valproic acid, lead to production of drug-dependent antibodies that destroy platelets. Quinine is used for leg cramps and fits both the exposure and the timing here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albuterol treats chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is not a recognized cause of thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Azithromycin is used for pneumonia and is a far less likely culprit than quinine in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is an outpatient antihypertensive and is not among the agents that generate drug-dependent antiplatelet antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is an anticoagulant that can cause bleeding but is not a cause of thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man receiving heparin for 7 days has a platelet count that has fallen from 240,000 to 90,000 cells/uL. A heparin-PF4 antibody is detected. Which of the following complications is he most likely to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow failure with pancytopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deep bleeding into joints and muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: New venous or arterial thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe epistaxis requiring transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous bleeding into the gastrointestinal tract

explanation.summary: In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, clotting is more common than bleeding despite the falling platelet count.
explanation.whyCorrect: A circulating autoantibody complexes heparin with platelet factor 4, leading both to destruction of platelets by macrophages and to platelet aggregation with thrombosis throughout the body. This is why HIT is life-threatening: the dominant hazard is new venous or arterial clot, not hemorrhage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HIT destroys circulating platelets peripherally and does not cause marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deep bleeding into joints and muscle is the pattern of coagulation factor disorders such as hemophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucosal bleeding occurs with severe thrombocytopenia generally, but it is not the characteristic complication of HIT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excess bleeding is less common than clotting in HIT, and the count here is not in the range of spontaneous hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who completed a course of heparin two months ago is given heparin again after hip surgery. Within 18 hours her platelet count falls from 260,000 to 95,000 cells/uL and a heparin-PF4 antibody test is positive. Which of the following best explains the unusually rapid onset?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies from the earlier heparin exposure are already circulating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparin suppresses marrow megakaryocytes directly, without antibody involvement

choices.label: C
choices.text: The postoperative specimen clumped inside the collection tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spleen enlarges acutely after heparin is administered

choices.label: E
choices.text: The surgical procedure consumed platelets within microthrombi

explanation.summary: HIT usually appears 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure but can occur within 24 hours when antibodies persist from recent prior heparin use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The delay in typical HIT reflects the time needed to generate antibody against the heparin-PF4 complex. A patient treated with heparin in recent months already has circulating antibody, so re-exposure triggers platelet destruction and aggregation almost immediately.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Heparin lowers the platelet count by immune-mediated peripheral destruction, not by marrow suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet clumping is an artifact of EDTA specimens and would not be accompanied by a positive heparin-PF4 antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin does not cause acute splenomegaly or sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Consumption in microthrombi occurs in disseminated intravascular coagulation, which would also prolong the coagulation studies.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man being treated with heparin for 6 days has had a 20% fall in his platelet count. He has no venous or arterial thrombosis, and he has gram-negative sepsis that could readily account for the change. His 4T score is low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue heparin without further testing for HIT

choices.label: B
choices.text: Send the heparin-PF4 antibody immunoassay for screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stop heparin and start an argatroban infusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop heparin and start warfarin anticoagulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop heparin and transfuse a unit of platelets

explanation.summary: A low 4T score means heparin can be safely continued without HIT testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 4T score weighs the degree of thrombocytopenia (a drop of 50% or more), the timing (usually 5 to 7 days of heparin), thrombotic complications, and other causes of thrombocytopenia. This patient has a modest fall, no thrombosis, and an obvious alternative explanation in sepsis, so the score is low and heparin can be continued. Screening is reserved for moderate or high scores.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The screening immunoassay is performed when the 4T score is moderate or high, not when it is low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stopping heparin and starting a direct thrombin inhibitor is the management of confirmed or strongly suspected HIT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Warfarin is not the alternative anticoagulant used when HIT is suspected, and there is no indication to change agents here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion is reserved for severe thrombocytopenia or active bleeding, neither of which is present.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a platelet count of 45,000 cells/uL has a peripheral blood smear showing markedly enlarged platelets. Red blood cell morphology is normal, no schistocytes are present, and the white blood cells appear normal. Which of the following does the platelet size most likely indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of megakaryocyte production in the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased platelet turnover and destruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microangiopathic damage to small blood vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet clumping within the specimen tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of platelets in an enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Large platelets on the peripheral smear point to increased platelet turnover and destruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The smear helps determine etiology by showing platelet size and morphology. Large platelets are newly released and indicate that the marrow is compensating for rapid peripheral destruction, whereas schistocytes would instead point to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia or intravascular hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow production failure reduces platelet output and is typically accompanied by abnormalities in other cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microangiopathy is identified by red cell fragments called schistocytes, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clumping appears as aggregates of platelets on the smear and causes an artifactually low count rather than large individual platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration lowers the count without changing platelet size.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic man has a platelet count of 12,000 cells/uL on a routine complete blood count drawn into an EDTA tube. He has no bruising, petechiae, or bleeding, and the peripheral smear shows clumps of agglutinated platelets. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Admit him for immediate platelet transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Order coagulation studies and liver function tests

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the count on a specimen collected in citrate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start corticosteroids for immune thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Platelet clumping in an EDTA specimen is pseudothrombocytopenia, and the count should be repeated in a citrate tube.
explanation.whyCorrect: Artifactual thrombocytopenia is a falsely low count caused by agglutination of platelets in blood anticoagulated with EDTA. It is a laboratory artifact and is not occurring in the patient, which fits his complete absence of findings. Drawing a specimen into a citrate tube gives an accurate count, and pseudothrombocytopenia must be excluded before any work-up or treatment begins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusing on the basis of an artifactual count would expose him to risk without benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for confirmed thrombocytopenia with pancytopenia suggesting marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulation, liver, and renal studies belong to the work-up only after the low count is confirmed to be genuine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treating immune thrombocytopenia presumes a real low platelet count, which has not been established.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Her antiplatelet antibodies have bound to glycoproteins on the surface of her platelets. Which of the following best explains how these antibody-coated platelets are removed from the circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of complement causes intravascular lysis of the platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrophages in the spleen phagocytose the platelets via Fc receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural killer cells recognize and destroy the platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bone marrow stops releasing platelets into the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver sequesters and stores the platelets long-term

explanation.summary: In ITP, IgG-opsonized platelets are cleared by splenic macrophages through Fc receptor binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies (usually IgG) coat the platelets in a process called opsonization. Macrophages in the spleen then bind the Fc portion of these antibodies via their Fc receptors, phagocytose the antibody-coated platelets, and remove them completely from the circulation, lowering the platelet count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes platelet loss to splenic phagocytosis, not to complement-mediated intravascular lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction is carried out by splenic macrophages, not natural killer cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow production is actually increased in ITP (increased megakaryocytes); platelets are destroyed peripherally, not held back by the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is splenic macrophages that engulf the platelets; the liver does not simply store them.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia undergoes a bone marrow biopsy as part of an atypical workup. Which of the following findings would most likely be seen in her marrow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent megakaryocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diffuse infiltration by blasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive marrow fibrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased megakaryocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Markedly hypocellular marrow

explanation.summary: ITP marrow shows increased megakaryocytes because platelet destruction is peripheral, not a production problem.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because platelets are destroyed peripherally in the spleen, the marrow compensates by making more, so it shows increased megakaryocytes. A bone marrow biopsy is not required to diagnose ITP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Megakaryocytes are increased, not absent; production is intact and even ramped up.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blast infiltration suggests leukemia, not ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow fibrosis is a feature of myelofibrosis, not ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The marrow is not hypocellular; the megakaryocyte line is expanded.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with isolated thrombocytopenia is suspected of having immune thrombocytopenia. Aside from the reduced number of platelets, which of the following best describes her peripheral blood smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marked leukocytosis with circulating blasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Occasional large platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prominent red blood cell anisocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocytes and helmet cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small, gray, agranular platelets

explanation.summary: ITP shows isolated thrombocytopenia; platelets are normal or occasionally large, with normal red and white cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The smear in ITP demonstrates isolated thrombocytopenia: platelets are decreased in number while red and white blood cells look normal. The platelets themselves appear normal, though some may be larger than normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukocytosis with blasts suggests leukemia, not the isolated thrombocytopenia of ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell anisocytosis points to an anemia (e.g., iron deficiency), not ITP, in which red cells are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes indicate a microangiopathic process, not ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gray, agranular platelets suggest gray platelet syndrome, a hereditary disorder, not ITP.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is being evaluated for a low platelet count, and immune thrombocytopenia is being considered. Which of the following additional findings, if present, would most strongly argue against a diagnosis of ITP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recent viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks earlier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Concurrent anemia and leukopenia on the complete blood count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased megakaryocytes on bone marrow examination with normal other lineages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Petechiae on the lower extremities and oral mucosa

explanation.summary: ITP requires an isolated thrombocytopenia; involvement of other cell lines points away from ITP.
explanation.whyCorrect: ITP is diagnosed only when the thrombocytopenia is isolated, meaning the red and white blood cells are normal in number. Coexisting anemia and leukopenia mean the thrombocytopenia is not isolated, so another cause (such as a marrow or systemic disorder) is more likely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal PT and PTT are expected, since ITP is a platelet problem, not a coagulation factor problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A recent viral infection is a recognized secondary trigger of ITP and does not argue against it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased megakaryocytes are the expected marrow finding in ITP and support, rather than exclude, the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Petechiae are a typical presenting sign of ITP and are consistent with the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A clinician evaluating a patient with suspected immune thrombocytopenia considers ordering an antiplatelet antibody test to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following is the best reason this test is not relied upon for diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It detects only IgM antibodies, which are not involved in ITP

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has low sensitivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is positive in nearly all healthy people

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is prohibitively expensive and rarely available

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires a bone marrow biopsy to perform

explanation.summary: Antiplatelet antibody tests are not used because their sensitivity is low.
explanation.whyCorrect: The antibody tests have a very low sensitivity: about half of patients with ITP have a negative result. This makes the test unreliable for confirming the diagnosis, which is why ITP remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibodies in ITP are usually IgG, and the problem with the test is poor sensitivity, not the antibody class it detects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick cites low sensitivity (false negatives), not universal positivity in healthy people.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cost and availability are not the reasons given; the issue is the test's low sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The antibody test does not require a bone marrow biopsy; marrow biopsy is not needed for ITP at all.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to clinic with the sudden appearance of a petechial rash and bruising two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. He otherwise looks and feels well, and his labs show an isolated thrombocytopenia. Which of the following is the most likely course of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a lifelong chronic disease requiring continuous therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is self-limited

choices.label: C
choices.text: It typically progresses to acute leukemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: It usually causes fatal intracerebral hemorrhage within days

choices.label: E
choices.text: It will require urgent splenectomy to prevent death

explanation.summary: Acute ITP in children follows a viral illness, is self-limited, and usually resolves within months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute ITP is most common in children and usually follows a viral illness. Although the onset is abrupt, the child typically looks and feels well, the disease is self-limited, generally requires no treatment, and most children recover completely within a few months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lifelong chronic course is characteristic of chronic ITP in adults, not acute childhood ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute ITP is self-limited and does not progress to leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Life-threatening bleeding such as intracerebral hemorrhage is rare; the child usually looks and feels well.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is a third-line therapy reserved for refractory chronic ITP, not a routine step in self-limited childhood ITP.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with petechiae and an isolated thrombocytopenia and is diagnosed with chronic immune thrombocytopenia. Which of the following statements best characterizes chronic ITP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is always self-limited and resolves within a few weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is most common in adult females younger than 40

choices.label: C
choices.text: It nearly always presents with life-threatening bleeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs exclusively in children following a viral illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: It results from decreased production of megakaryocytes

explanation.summary: Chronic ITP most often affects adult women under 40 and may be primary or secondary to disorders like lupus, HIV, or CLL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic ITP presents most commonly in adult females younger than 40 years. It may be primary or secondary, occurring in the setting of conditions such as lupus, HIV infection, or chronic lymphocytic leukemia, with a gradual onset and common recurrences.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A brief, self-limited course is characteristic of acute childhood ITP; chronic ITP tends to recur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In most chronic ITP, bleeding is relatively minor, and life-threatening bleeding is rare.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occurring in children after a viral illness describes acute ITP, not chronic ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ITP is caused by peripheral antibody-mediated destruction, and megakaryocytes are actually increased.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man develops isolated thrombocytopenia and petechiae. His history is notable for a chronic viral infection, and his clinician suspects secondary immune thrombocytopenia due to molecular mimicry. Which of the following is a recognized secondary cause of ITP by this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Factor V Leiden

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatitis C infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypothyroidism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Viral infections such as hepatitis C can cause secondary ITP through molecular mimicry.
explanation.whyCorrect: In viral illness, antibodies generated to fight the virus cross-react with the patient's platelets, a process called molecular mimicry. Cited examples include HIV, hepatitis C, CMV, varicella, and coronavirus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor V Leiden is an inherited thrombophilia, unrelated to antiplatelet antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypothyroidism is not listed as a secondary cause of ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes anemia, not antibody-mediated platelet destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and is not a molecular-mimicry trigger for ITP.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with symptomatic chronic immune thrombocytopenia and a very low platelet count is started on treatment. Which of the following is the usual first-line therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corticosteroids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rituximab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenectomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombopoietin agonists

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids such as prednisone are the usual first-line therapy for ITP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The goal of treatment is to keep the platelet count at a safe level to prevent severe bleeding. Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) are the usual first-line therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusions are generally avoided because the transfused platelets are destroyed just as quickly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab is typically the first choice for relapse after a steroid taper, not initial therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy is now a third-line option reserved for corticosteroid failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TPO agonists are used for recurrence after a steroid taper, not as first-line treatment.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia has a severely low platelet count and active bleeding, and her platelet count must be raised quickly. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate to rapidly raise her platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laparoscopic splenectomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral prednisone monotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rituximab infusion therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists

explanation.summary: IVIG rapidly raises the platelet count in ITP, though its effect is transient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) is used to rapidly raise the platelet count, although the effect is transient. It is useful in the setting of significant bleeding or as pre-operative treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenectomy is a third-line surgical option, not a rapid pharmacologic measure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids are first-line therapy but do not raise the platelet count as rapidly as IVIG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rituximab is used for relapse after steroid taper and does not act rapidly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TPO agonists are used for recurrence and act by stimulating production over time, not rapidly.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with refractory immune thrombocytopenia that has failed medical therapy is scheduled for splenectomy. Which of the following is most important to do before the procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer high-dose iron supplementation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arrange a bone marrow transplant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Begin lifelong warfarin therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunize him against encapsulated bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse platelets to achieve a normal count

explanation.summary: Patients undergoing splenectomy must be immunized against encapsulated bacteria beforehand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenectomy removes the site of platelet destruction and can be effective, but because the spleen is important for defense against encapsulated organisms, patients must be immunized against encapsulated bacteria before the procedure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron supplementation treats iron deficiency anemia and has no role in preparing for splenectomy in ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow transplant is not part of ITP management; marrow production is already intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ITP is a bleeding disorder; anticoagulation with warfarin would be harmful and is not indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfused platelets are destroyed as fast as the patient's own, so routine transfusion to a normal count is not the priority.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia and mild petechiae asks why she cannot simply receive a platelet transfusion to normalize her count. Which of the following best explains why platelet transfusions are generally avoided in ITP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transfused platelets are destroyed just as rapidly as the patient's own platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transfused platelets cause iron overload that damages the liver and heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfused platelets reliably trigger fatal anaphylaxis in patients with this disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfusion permanently increases antiplatelet antibody production by the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion transmits the virus that caused the ITP to household contacts

explanation.summary: Platelet transfusions are avoided in ITP because the transfused platelets are destroyed as fast as the patient's own.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ITP, the antiplatelet antibodies destroy transfused donor platelets just as fast as the patient's own platelets, so transfusion is generally avoided. It may be used only in patients with severe thrombocytopenia and significant bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron overload is a concern with chronic red cell transfusion, not the reason platelets are avoided in ITP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaphylaxis is not the reason transfusions are avoided in ITP; rapid destruction of the platelets is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe transfusion as permanently boosting antibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion is avoided because the platelets are quickly destroyed, not because it transmits a causative virus.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman reports easy bruising, and a complete blood count is ordered. Her physician explains that thrombocytopenia is defined by a platelet count below a specific threshold. Below which of the following values is a platelet count typically considered thrombocytopenic?

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia is an abnormally low platelet level, typically below 150,000/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets, typically below 150,000/mm3. Counts in ITP can then range anywhere from very minor reductions to profoundly low values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A count under 10,000/mm3 is an example of very severe thrombocytopenia, not the threshold that defines the condition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 50,000/mm3 is well within the thrombocytopenic range but is not the defining cutoff.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 250,000/mm3 is a normal platelet count and would not be called thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 450,000/mm3 is above the normal range and represents an elevated, not low, platelet count.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to clinic because of a rash on her shins. Examination shows numerous discrete red-purple dots, each measuring 1 to 3 mm and often described as pinpoint. Which of the following terms best describes these skin lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ecchymoses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Petechiae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Purpura

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telangiectasias

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicles

explanation.summary: Petechiae are the smaller, 1-3 mm pinpoint areas of bleeding into the skin; purpura are larger.
explanation.whyCorrect: Petechiae and purpura are both focal or diffuse areas of bleeding within the skin, ranging from discrete red-purple dots to confluent areas. Petechiae are the smaller lesions, 1-3 mm and often described as pinpoint, while purpura are larger.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ecchymoses are bruises, the larger areas of bleeding seen with easy bruising rather than pinpoint dots.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Purpura are the larger lesions of skin bleeding, not the 1-3 mm pinpoint dots described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Telangiectasias are dilated small vessels that blanch, not areas of bleeding into the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vesicles are fluid-filled blisters and are unrelated to bleeding from a low platelet count.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia is found to have autoantibodies directed against a platelet surface protein. Which of the following is the usual target of these antibodies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Actin filaments of the platelet cytoskeleton

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contents of the platelet alpha granules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fc receptors expressed on the platelet surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phospholipid on the inner membrane leaflet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet membrane glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

explanation.summary: Antiplatelet antibodies in ITP usually bind platelet membrane glycoproteins such as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ITP, patients make antibodies that bind their own platelets. Usually those antibodies bind to platelet membrane glycoproteins, such as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, coating the platelet surface and marking it for removal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoskeletal actin is intracellular and is not the surface target described for these antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha granule contents are stored inside the platelet and are not the antibody binding site.
