explanation.summary: Normal platelets respond to every agent, so the pattern of response across agents is what narrows the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal platelets will respond to every aggregating agent. In certain platelet disorders, however, the platelets do not respond normally to every agent, and the pattern of response to the different agents is helpful in narrowing down a diagnosis, since many congenital platelet defects have specific pattern responses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single agent does produce a measurable fall in turbidity when the platelets clump together.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aggregation studies assess platelet responses, not the activity of individual coagulation factors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal platelets respond to every one of the agents, which is exactly what makes a selective failure informative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clumping in the specimen is a problem for automated counting, not a reason to add more agonists.

questions.stem: A patient has decreased platelet function of uncertain cause, and the clinician wants to know whether a platelet membrane glycoprotein complex is decreased. Which of the following studies is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flow cytometry using whole blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manual review of platelet morphology

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet function assay (PFA-100)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Willebrand antigen assay

explanation.summary: Flow cytometry using whole blood assesses platelet membrane markers such as the glycoprotein complexes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the specialized tests that further narrow the cause of poor platelet function are flow cytometry studies using whole blood. These can assess platelet membrane markers such as the glycoprotein (Gp) complexes, which may be decreased in some disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bleeding time measures primary hemostasis overall and reveals nothing about specific receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Morphology reveals size, shape, and granulation but cannot quantify membrane glycoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PFA-100 shows that function is impaired but does not identify which membrane protein is involved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The von Willebrand antigen assay measures the vWF level, which is low in von Willebrand disease, not a platelet membrane marker.

questions.stem: A clinician reviewing a hematology report notes that the mean platelet volume and the platelet count were both generated on a flow cytometer. Which of the following does the mean platelet volume provide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plasma level of von Willebrand factor available to platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proportion of circulating platelets that lack granules

choices.label: C
choices.text: The response of the platelets to biochemical aggregating agonists

choices.label: D
choices.text: The size of the platelets, which need not reflect how well they work

choices.label: E
choices.text: The time the platelets require to form a plug over an aperture

explanation.summary: Mean platelet volumes and platelet counts reveal the size and number of platelets, which are not necessarily reflective of platelet function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mean platelet volumes and platelet counts are measured on a flow cytometer, and they reveal the number and size of the platelets. Neither value is necessarily reflective of the actual functioning of the platelets, which is why the PFA-100 rather than the mean platelet volume is the preferred measure of platelet function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vWF level requires a specialized von Willebrand factor assay.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granule content is judged on a stained smear, where agranular platelets appear gray.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Responses to aggregating agonists are measured in platelet aggregation studies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plug formation over a standardized aperture is what the PFA-100 measures.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with recurrent epistaxis and prolonged bleeding after a forearm laceration has a normal platelet count but a platelet function assay showing decreased platelet function. Aggregation is normal with collagen, adenosine diphosphate, and epinephrine but absent with ristocetin, and his von Willebrand factor level is low. Which of the following is most important to discuss with him as part of his ongoing care?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His bleeding risk with any surgery he may have in the future

choices.label: B
choices.text: His inability to generate fibrin during secondary hemostasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: His risk of ischemic events from sludgy, slowly flowing blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: His risk of spontaneous bleeding once his count falls below 10,000/mm3

choices.label: E
choices.text: The need for serial platelet counts to detect thrombocytosis

explanation.summary: Once von Willebrand disease is diagnosed, treatment and the bleeding risk of future surgery are the central counseling points.
explanation.whyCorrect: Decreased platelet function with an isolated loss of ristocetin-induced aggregation plus a low von Willebrand factor level establishes von Willebrand disease. Management includes explaining the diagnosis and discussing treatment, especially with regard to the risks for any surgery he might have in the future.

whyWrongByChoice.B: His defect lies in primary hemostasis, and fibrin generation by the coagulation cascade is not implicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ischemic events from sludgy blood belong to thrombocytosis, and his platelet count is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spontaneous bleeding below 10,000/mm3 is a concern in severe thrombocytopenia, which he does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.E: His problem is platelet function; there is no indication that his platelet count will rise.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with several days of bloody diarrhea, vomiting, and decreased urination. Her family lives in a community where romaine lettuce was recently recalled. Her complete blood count shows anemia and thrombocytopenia, and the peripheral smear shows numerous schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A defect in complement regulatory factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: An autoantibody against a phospholipid-binding protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficiency of the enzyme ADAMTS13

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overactivation of the coagulation cascade from sepsis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga toxin from Escherichia coli O157:H7

explanation.summary: Diarrhea-associated HUS in a young child is most often caused by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common type of HUS is acquired and associated with an infectious diarrheal illness due to a toxin-producing gut bacterium. The most common HUS-causing toxin is Shiga toxin, usually from E. coli O157:H7, which is absorbed through the gastrointestinal mucosa and alters endothelial cells, leading to platelet activation and microthrombi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A complement factor defect causes only a rare genetic form of HUS, not the common diarrhea-associated form suggested by the lettuce recall and bloody diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies against a phospholipid-binding protein describe antiphospholipid syndrome, not diarrhea-associated HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP, which is seen mostly in young adults and characteristically involves neurologic findings rather than a preceding diarrheal illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Overactivation of the coagulation cascade describes DIC, which would prolong the PT and aPTT and typically occurs with systemic infection or trauma.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who was previously healthy presents with fever, confusion, and easy bruising. Laboratory studies show anemia, a low platelet count, schistocytes on the smear, and a mildly elevated creatinine. Which of the following features most strongly favors thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura over hemolytic-uremic syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A preceding diarrheal illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurologic abnormalities such as confusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocytes on the peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Neurologic involvement is characteristic of TTP and is unusual in HUS.
explanation.whyCorrect: In TTP, but not HUS, the brain may be involved because of microthrombi leading to strokes and cerebral ischemia, producing confusion, headache, dysarthria, seizures, or coma. HUS is characterized by the same findings as TTP except that neurologic findings are unusual and fever is less common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A preceding diarrheal illness points toward HUS rather than TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is a shared feature of all thrombotic microangiopathies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes reflect microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and are present in both TTP and HUS, so they do not distinguish the two.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia occurs in both TTP and HUS from platelet consumption and is not distinguishing.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Her disease stems from deficiency of the enzyme ADAMTS13. Which of the following best describes the direct consequence of this enzyme deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complement is activated in an unregulated fashion, injuring endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrin is deposited excessively because the coagulation cascade is overactivated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet production in the bone marrow is impaired

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cells are destroyed by autoantibodies directed against membrane antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers are not cleaved

explanation.summary: ADAMTS13 normally cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; its deficiency lets platelets adhere to these multimers and form thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: ADAMTS13 normally inhibits thrombosis by cleaving ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers into smaller multimers that are less likely to form clots. In TTP, ADAMTS13 deficiency prevents this cleavage, so circulating platelets adhere readily to the large multimers, leading to formation of thrombi in small blood vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unregulated complement activation describes the rare genetic form of HUS, not TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess fibrin from an overactivated coagulation cascade describes DIC; TTP thrombi are platelet-rich with minimal fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombocytopenia in TTP results from platelet consumption in clots, not impaired marrow production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TTP does not involve autoantibodies against red cell membrane antigens; RBC damage is mechanical, from shearing by microthrombi.

questions.stem: A hematologist reviews the peripheral blood smear of a patient with suspected thrombotic microangiopathy and identifies fragmented red cells that are small, lack central pallor, and have pointy edges. Which of the following statements about these cells is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are a normal finding when the bone marrow is healthy

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are frequently artifactual and should be disregarded

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are nuclear remnants seen in patients with asplenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are specific for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: They indicate a coexisting glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

explanation.summary: Schistocytes are specific for MAHA and never appear on a normal or artifactual smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: When RBCs travel through small vessels, they are sheared by microthrombi, producing fragmented cells called schistocytes. They are identifiable by their small size, lack of central pallor, and pointy edges, and are specific to MAHA; schistocytes never appear on a normal blood smear and are never artifactual.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Schistocytes are never seen on a normal smear, regardless of marrow health.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Schistocytes are never artifactual; their presence is a genuine and meaningful finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nuclear remnants are Howell-Jolly bodies seen with asplenia, not schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bite cells, not schistocytes, are associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura has widespread microthrombi and a very low platelet count, yet the prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) are normal. Which of the following best explains these normal coagulation results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies inhibit the thromboplastin reagent used in the assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coagulation cascade is overactivated, rapidly consuming clotting factors

choices.label: C
choices.text: The liver compensates by increasing synthesis of all clotting factors

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thrombi are composed largely of platelets with minimal fibrin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin K deficiency prevents activation of the assay

explanation.summary: In TTP and HUS the thrombi are platelet-rich with minimal fibrin, so coagulation factors are not consumed and the PT and aPTT stay normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In TTP, HUS, and most secondary causes of TM, the intravascular thrombi result from platelet aggregation rather than activation of the coagulation cascade. The thrombi are composed largely of platelets with minimal fibrin, so coagulation factors are not excessively consumed, and the PT and aPTT are not prolonged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reagent inhibition by antibodies describes the prolonged aPTT of antiphospholipid syndrome, not the normal values in TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Overactivation of the cascade with factor consumption occurs in DIC, where the PT and aPTT become elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal coagulation times reflect that factors are not consumed, not increased hepatic synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency would prolong, not normalize, the coagulation studies and is unrelated to TTP.

questions.stem: An adult woman is admitted with fever, disorientation, petechiae, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes on the peripheral smear. Coagulation studies are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fresh frozen plasma to replace consumed clotting factors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supportive care with intravenous fluids only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urgent plasmapheresis (plasma exchange)

explanation.summary: TTP is a medical emergency treated with urgent plasmapheresis, often with corticosteroids.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has TTP, which is a medical emergency managed with urgent plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) to clear and replace the defective ADAMTS13. Systemic corticosteroids are used alongside plasmapheresis, and drugs such as rituximab may also be used.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not useful in most cases of thrombotic microangiopathy, including TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors for bleeding from factor consumption, which is not the mechanism in TTP; plasma exchange is required.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet transfusion is not the treatment for TTP and does not address the underlying ADAMTS13 problem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Supportive care with fluids is the mainstay for HUS, not the definitive treatment for TTP.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops hemolytic-uremic syndrome after an episode of bloody diarrhea. He has hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-dose antibiotics to eradicate the causative bacterium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate splenectomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term warfarin anticoagulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supportive care with correction of electrolytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urgent plasmapheresis and corticosteroids

explanation.summary: HUS is managed primarily with supportive care, including fluids, electrolyte correction, and renal support.
explanation.whyCorrect: HUS treatment is primarily supportive care. Because most patients present with diarrhea, electrolyte abnormalities, and AKI, management means correcting electrolytes, supporting renal function, and providing intravenous fluids as needed. Antibiotics are not useful in most cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not useful in most cases of HUS and are not the mainstay of therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenectomy has no role in the treatment of HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Long-term anticoagulation is not the management of HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urgent plasmapheresis with corticosteroids is the treatment for TTP, not the primarily supportive approach to HUS.

questions.stem: A patient with a thrombotic microangiopathy has laboratory studies performed to characterize the hemolysis. Which of the following combinations of serum findings is most consistent with the intravascular hemolytic anemia of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High conjugated bilirubin, low LDH, and high haptoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: High haptoglobin, low bilirubin, and low reticulocyte count

choices.label: C
choices.text: High unconjugated bilirubin, high LDH, and low haptoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low LDH, low reticulocyte count, and high haptoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal bilirubin, normal LDH, and normal haptoglobin

explanation.summary: Intravascular hemolysis produces high unconjugated bilirubin, increased LDH, and low haptoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum studies in TM are typical of intravascular hemolytic anemia, showing high unconjugated bilirubin, increased LDH, and low haptoglobin because of RBC lysis. Reticulocytes also rise as the marrow tries to make more RBCs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemolysis raises unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin and LDH and lowers haptoglobin, the opposite of this option.
whyWrongByChoice.B: High haptoglobin and low bilirubin are inconsistent with hemolysis; haptoglobin falls and bilirubin rises.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low LDH and high haptoglobin argue against hemolysis, and the reticulocyte count typically rises.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Entirely normal values would not reflect the active intravascular hemolysis of a thrombotic microangiopathy.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and hypertension. Laboratory studies show hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, a low platelet count, and schistocytes on the smear. Which of the following secondary causes of thrombotic microangiopathy best explains her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcineurin inhibitor toxicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Malignancy with micrometastases to vessel walls

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a pregnancy-associated secondary TM with hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets) is a secondary cause of TM in which pregnant patients develop MAHA and low platelets similar to TTP, causing abdominal pain and hypertension. It can progress to placental abruption and organ failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcineurin inhibitors cause drug-induced TM through direct endothelial injury and are used for transplant rejection, not in this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC would prolong the PT and aPTT and usually arises with systemic infection or trauma rather than the pregnancy-specific picture described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stem cell transplantation causes TM through associated radiation therapy or chemotherapy, which does not fit a pregnant patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Malignancy-associated TM results from micrometastases to vessel walls and is not suggested by this obstetric presentation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a blood pressure of 230/125 mm Hg. Laboratory studies reveal anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and a rising serum creatinine. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his hematologic and renal findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ADAMTS13 deficiency causing platelet microthrombi

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited complement factor defect causing HUS

choices.label: C
choices.text: Malignant hypertension causing vessel injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: March hemolysis from repetitive impact on the soles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga toxin-mediated endothelial injury after diarrhea

explanation.summary: Malignant hypertension is a secondary TM that can cause MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malignant hypertension, defined as a blood pressure above 220/100 mm Hg, is a secondary cause of TM that can cause vessel injury, often leading to MAHA, low platelets, and AKI with a rising serum creatinine. Secondary causes such as this should be considered and excluded before diagnosing HUS or TTP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP, which is not defined by severe hypertension and is a primary rather than secondary TM.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A complement factor defect causes a rare genetic form of HUS, which does not explain the markedly elevated blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: March hemolysis is a rare cause of MAHA from RBC fragmentation in the soles of the feet and does not involve severe hypertension or AKI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin causes diarrhea-associated HUS in young children, not a hypertensive emergency in an older adult.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Which of the following is the most common mechanism responsible for the ADAMTS13 deficiency in her form of the disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An autoantibody that inhibits ADAMTS13

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inactivating mutation in the ADAMTS13 gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumption of ADAMTS13 by widespread fibrin thrombi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased hepatic synthesis from vitamin K deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga toxin-mediated destruction of ADAMTS13

explanation.summary: Acquired TTP is most often caused by an autoantibody that inhibits ADAMTS13.
explanation.whyCorrect: The deficiency of ADAMTS13 can be inherited or acquired. Acquired cases, which are more common, mostly result from an autoantibody directed against ADAMTS13. Some acquired cases occur late in pregnancy, when ADAMTS13 levels drop.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An inactivating gene mutation causes the inherited form of TTP, which is less common than the acquired autoantibody-mediated form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TTP thrombi are platelet-rich with minimal fibrin, and the enzyme deficiency is not due to consumption by fibrin thrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency affects clotting factor synthesis, not ADAMTS13 levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin causes HUS and has no role in the ADAMTS13 deficiency of TTP.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes has an uncertain diagnosis after routine testing, and the clinician wants to confirm immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. A special assay is ordered. Which of the following results would best confirm this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: ADAMTS13 activity under 10% with a detectable antibody inhibitor

choices.label: C
choices.text: An elevated D-dimer level, as seen in most thrombotic states

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased fibrin degradation products, as in many thrombotic states

choices.label: E
choices.text: Schistocytes and a low platelet count on the peripheral smear

explanation.summary: Immune TTP is confirmed by ADAMTS13 activity under 10% and/or a detectable inhibitor against ADAMTS13.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the cause of a suspected TM remains unclear, special assays can confirm TTP from ADAMTS13 deficiency. These suggest immune TTP if the ADAMTS13 activity is under 10% and/or an antibody inhibitor against ADAMTS13 is detected. Because results may take several days, treatment should not be delayed to wait for them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A prolonged PT points toward DIC; in TTP the PT is characteristically normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated D-dimer is nonspecific and elevated in most forms of thrombosis, so it does not confirm TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrin degradation products are elevated in many thrombotic states and do not confirm a diagnosis of TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Schistocytes and thrombocytopenia are seen in all thrombotic microangiopathies and cannot by themselves distinguish immune TTP.

questions.stem: A pediatrician reviews the frequency of hemolytic-uremic syndrome before counseling families in a community affected by a foodborne outbreak. Which of the following best approximates the incidence of hemolytic-uremic syndrome in the United States?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 case per 10 million people

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 cases per 1,000 people

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 cases per 100,000 people

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4 cases per 1 million people

choices.label: E
choices.text: 40 cases per 100,000 people

explanation.summary: HUS occurs at about 2 cases per 100,000, making it an uncommon illness in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: HUS is seen mainly in young children, mostly after bacterial infections, with an incidence of 2 cases per 100,000. That makes it an uncommon illness in the United States, comparable in frequency to rheumatic fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One case per 10 million understates the frequency; HUS is uncommon but not that rare.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two cases per 1,000 would make HUS a common childhood illness, which it is not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Four cases per 1 million is the reported frequency of TTP, which is rarer than HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Forty cases per 100,000 overstates the frequency of HUS by roughly twentyfold.

questions.stem: The classic description of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a pentad of fever, neurologic abnormalities, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Which of the following best describes the proportion of patients with this disease who present with all five elements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 75%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About one half

choices.label: C
choices.text: About one third

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fewer than 5%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly all patients

explanation.summary: Fewer than 5% of patients with TTP present with all five elements of the classic pentad.
explanation.whyCorrect: In its full-blown form TTP presents as a pentad of fever, neurologic abnormalities, MAHA, immune thrombocytopenia, and AKI, but fewer than 5% of patients present with all five elements. Most patients are therefore diagnosed with some combination of the pentad rather than the complete set.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Seventy-five percent would describe a typical presentation rather than the rare complete pentad.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Half of patients presenting with all five findings would make the complete pentad the usual presentation, which it is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One third greatly overstates how often the complete pentad is present at presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Almost no patients show all five elements, so the pentad cannot be required for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is diagnosed with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and his family asks about the risk of stroke-like symptoms. Approximately what proportion of patients with this disease develop brain involvement from microthrombi?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 25%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 75%

explanation.summary: Brain involvement from microthrombi, causing strokes and cerebral ischemia, is seen in about 25% of patients with TTP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In TTP, but not HUS, the brain may be involved because of microthrombi leading to strokes and cerebral ischemia, and this is seen in about 25% of patients. Symptoms vary and can include confusion, headache, dysarthria, numbness, weakness, and seizures, and some patients may even develop coma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Five percent understates the frequency of neurologic involvement in TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ten percent is too low; roughly a quarter of patients have brain involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Half of patients would overstate the frequency of cerebral microthrombi in TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three quarters would make neurologic involvement nearly universal, which it is not.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy hospitalized with hemolytic-uremic syndrome has had markedly decreased urine output for 2 days. He now complains of chest pain, and a friction rub is heard on auscultation. Which of the following best explains this new finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding into the pericardial space from thrombocytopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct invasion of the pericardium by Escherichia coli O157:H7

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microthrombi in the coronary circulation causing myocardial ischemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shiga toxin binding directly to cardiac myocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uremia resulting from his severe acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: Severe AKI in a thrombotic microangiopathy produces uremic symptoms such as confusion and pericarditis with chest pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: AKI in TM occurs from microinfarcts in the kidney caused by microthrombi obstructing the vascular supply, and it is usually asymptomatic and found on lab testing. Patients with more severe AKI can have decreased urine output and develop uremic symptoms such as confusion or pericarditis with chest pain, which is exactly why the name hemolytic-uremic syndrome was coined.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pericardial bleeding would produce tamponade physiology rather than the uremic pericarditis expected with severe AKI.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The organism stays in the gut; it is the absorbed Shiga toxin, not bacterial invasion, that produces disease at distant sites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coronary microthrombi with myocardial ischemia are not a described feature of HUS, and a friction rub with oliguria points to uremia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shiga toxin acts by altering endothelial cells, leading to platelet activation, not by binding cardiac myocytes.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with hemolytic-uremic syndrome has had several days of bloody diarrhea and severe vomiting, and her serum creatinine is rising. In addition to obstruction of the renal microvasculature by toxin-injured endothelium and platelet aggregates, which of the following most likely contributes to her reduced glomerular filtration rate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of immune complexes within the glomeruli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct tubular toxicity of unconjugated bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of the ureters by blood clots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prerenal volume depletion from her gastrointestinal losses

explanation.summary: Vomiting causes volume depletion, which lowers the GFR on top of the microvascular obstruction of the kidney.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some types of TM, especially HUS and TTP, bacterial toxins and platelet aggregates damage the endothelium of the renal vasculature and obstruct the blood supply to the kidney. Additionally, vomiting leads to volume depletion, which also reduces the GFR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane are not part of the renal injury in a thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli is not how HUS injures the kidney; the injury is vascular and ischemic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unconjugated bilirubin rises from hemolysis but is not described as a cause of the reduced GFR in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ureteral obstruction by clot is a postrenal process and is not a described mechanism of AKI in HUS.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury without any preceding diarrheal illness. Genetic testing reveals a defect in a complement regulatory factor. Unregulated activation of which of the following is most directly responsible for his endothelial damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The alternative complement pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: The classical complement pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contact activation pathway of coagulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fibrinolytic pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lectin complement pathway

explanation.summary: The rare genetic form of HUS arises from complement factor defects that permit unregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: A rare genetic form of HUS is caused by a defect in complement factors, which leads to unregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway. The result is endothelial damage and thrombus formation, producing the same microangiopathic picture without the diarrheal prodrome of the common acquired form.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The classical pathway is antibody-triggered and is not the pathway left unregulated in genetic HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The contact activation pathway belongs to the coagulation cascade, whose overactivation characterizes DIC rather than genetic HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinolysis dissolves clot rather than injuring endothelium, so its activation would not produce this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lectin pathway is not the one implicated in the complement factor defects that cause genetic HUS.

questions.stem: Shiga toxin is the toxin most often responsible for hemolytic-uremic syndrome, and it usually comes from Escherichia coli O157:H7. Which of the following organisms is the next most common source of this toxin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Campylobacter jejuni

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salmonella typhi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shigella species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yersinia enterocolitica

explanation.summary: After E. coli O157:H7, Shigella is the next most common source of the Shiga toxin that causes HUS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common HUS-causing toxin is Shiga toxin, usually from Escherichia coli O157:H7, with Shigella next most common. The toxin is released by bacteria in the gut and then absorbed through the gastrointestinal mucosa into the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni causes diarrheal illness but is not the second most common source of Shiga toxin in HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis and is not a Shiga toxin producer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Salmonella typhi is not listed among the toxin-producing gut organisms responsible for HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yersinia enterocolitica is not a described source of the Shiga toxin that triggers HUS.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is reviewed for fragmented red cells. Which of the following is a recognized type of schistocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helmet cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spherocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cell

explanation.summary: Helmet cells and triangulocytes are the named types of schistocyte seen in MAHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistocytes are identifiable by their small size, lack of central pallor, and pointy edges. Types of schistocytes include helmet cells, which are crescent-shaped cells that resemble football helmets, as well as triangulocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bite cells are typically seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency rather than as a form of fragmented cell in MAHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickle cells are the crescent-shaped red cells of sickle cell anemia, a different mechanism of hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes are not among the fragmented cell types produced by shearing through microthrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target cells, with a dark ring surrounding a clear center, are most commonly seen in thalassemia.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with a thrombotic microangiopathy has an elevated reticulocyte count reported with her complete blood count. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fragmentation of red cells by microthrombi produces these immature-appearing forms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immature red cells accumulate because they cannot pass through clotted capillaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marrow increases erythropoiesis to compensate for the ongoing hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The marrow releases immature white cells in response to systemic inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen releases stored immature red cells as it sequesters damaged cells

explanation.summary: Reticulocytes rise because the healthy bone marrow increases red cell production in response to hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most patients with TM have anemia with a low hemoglobin and hematocrit, and schistocytes are seen on the peripheral smear along with reticulocytes as the bone marrow tries to make more RBCs to correct for the hemolysis. Reticulocytosis is expected in any form of hemolytic anemia as long as the marrow is healthy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragmentation produces schistocytes, which are distinct from reticulocytes and reflect shearing rather than new production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reticulocytes are not trapped by capillary thrombi; their rise reflects increased marrow production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, not white cells, and are unrelated to an inflammatory leukocyte response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reticulocytes come from the marrow's increased output, not from splenic release of stored cells.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis is found to have anemia, an elevated LDH, and fragmented red cells on his peripheral smear. His platelet count, renal function, and coagulation studies are all normal. Which of the following best explains his findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against red cell membrane antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial injury produced by absorbed Shiga toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Traumatic shearing of red cells by the prosthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uncleaved von Willebrand factor multimers from ADAMTS13 deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unregulated complement activation on the endothelial surface

explanation.summary: Prosthetic heart valves cause MAHA by mechanically shearing red cells even though they are not small vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most, but not all, MAHA is due to thrombus formation. Rarer causes include MAHA from prosthetic heart valves, in which there is mechanical shearing of RBCs. Although heart valves are not located in small vessels, they are still considered a cause of MAHA because the result to the RBCs is the same.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies against red cell membrane antigens cause autoimmune hemolysis, which does not fragment cells into schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Shiga toxin causes diarrhea-associated HUS with thrombocytopenia and renal injury, neither of which is present here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes TTP, which would also produce thrombocytopenia rather than the isolated hemolysis described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unregulated complement activation causes the rare genetic form of HUS, which would include low platelets and kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man who runs 60 miles each week is found to have a mild hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells on his peripheral smear. His platelet count, renal function, and coagulation studies are normal, and he takes no medications. Which of the following best explains his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumption of red cells by widespread platelet-rich microthrombi in the kidneys

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragmentation of red cells in the small vessels of the soles of the feet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidative injury to red cells during periods of sustained exertion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of red cells within an enlarged and congested spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shearing of red cells across a prosthetic mechanical heart valve

explanation.summary: March hemolysis occurs when repetitive impact fragments red cells in the tiny vessels of the soles of the feet.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the rarer causes of MAHA is the unusual march hemolysis, in which people who log many miles either running or marching develop hemolytic anemia due to fragmentation of RBCs as they pass through the tiny vessels in the soles of the feet. The normal platelet count, renal function, and coagulation studies argue against a primary thrombotic microangiopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Widespread microthrombi would consume platelets and injure the kidneys, neither of which is present in this runner.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidative red cell injury produces bite cells, as in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, not fragmented cells from mechanical trauma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sequestration does not fragment red cells, so it would not produce schistocytes on the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prosthetic valve is a recognized cause of mechanical hemolysis, but this patient has no valve prosthesis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago and takes tacrolimus develops anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and a rising creatinine. Her PT and aPTT are normal. Which of the following best describes how her medication produces this syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct injury to endothelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune injury mediated by drug-dependent antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of hepatic ADAMTS13 synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotic injury to cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus cause thrombotic microangiopathy through direct endothelial cell injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the medications that cause secondary TM, the calcineurin inhibitors used for transplant rejection, such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus, as well as interferon and vascular endothelial growth factor inhibition, cause direct endothelial cell injury. Vessel wall injury then activates the process that consumes platelets and shears red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune injury is the mechanism attributed to quinine rather than to tacrolimus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drug-induced TM in this setting comes from endothelial damage, not from reduced ADAMTS13 production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osmotic injury to cells is the described mechanism for extended-release oxycodone, not for a calcineurin inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia here results from platelet consumption in microthrombi rather than from marrow suppression.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man taking extended-release oxycodone for chronic pain develops microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug causes a thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct inhibition of ADAMTS13 activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune injury mediated by drug-dependent antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotic injury to cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway

explanation.summary: Extended-release oxycodone is described as causing thrombotic microangiopathy through osmotic injury to cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medications are an important secondary cause of TM, and each drug class injures the vasculature differently. Extended-release oxycodone can cause osmotic injury to cells, which is distinct from the direct endothelial injury of calcineurin inhibitors and the immune injury of quinine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of ADAMTS13 in acquired TTP comes from an autoantibody rather than from an opioid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune injury from drug-dependent antibodies is the mechanism assigned to quinine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: VEGF inhibition causes direct endothelial cell injury and is a property of a different class of agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unregulated alternative complement activation underlies the rare genetic form of HUS, not drug-induced TM.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection is admitted with fever, anemia with schistocytes, and thrombocytopenia. His PT and aPTT are normal, ADAMTS13 activity is normal with no inhibitor detected, and he takes no medications associated with vessel injury. Which of the following best explains his thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inhibitory autoantibody directed against ADAMTS13

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct viral injury to the vessel walls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelial injury from prior radiation therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Micrometastases seeding the vessel walls

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga toxin absorbed through the gastrointestinal mucosa

explanation.summary: Infections such as HIV are a secondary cause of thrombotic microangiopathy through direct injury to the vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infections are listed among the secondary causes of TM because they can lead to direct injury to the vessels; examples include HIV, cytomegalovirus, aspergillosis, and malaria. Secondary causes such as this should always be considered and excluded before diagnosing HUS or TTP, which are less common overall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ADAMTS13 inhibitor would establish immune TTP, but his ADAMTS13 activity is normal and no inhibitor was found.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radiation-associated TM is described after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which this patient has not undergone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Micrometastases to the vessel walls explain malignancy-associated TM, and this patient has no malignancy described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga toxin causes diarrhea-associated HUS in young children rather than this adult's infection-related picture.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with widely metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma develops anemia with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. Her PT, aPTT, and thrombin time are all normal. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inhibitory autoantibody directed against ADAMTS13

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diffuse activation of the clotting cascade with fibrin thrombi

choices.label: C
choices.text: Micrometastases seeding the vessel walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotic injury to endothelial cells from her analgesics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway

explanation.summary: Malignancy-associated thrombotic microangiopathy is often due to micrometastases to the vessel walls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many malignancies are associated with TM, sometimes due to micrometastases to the vessel walls. Because secondary causes should be considered and excluded before diagnosing TTP or HUS, an advanced cancer with MAHA and thrombocytopenia points to the malignancy itself as the cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ADAMTS13 inhibitor would make this immune TTP, but a secondary cause is present and should be excluded first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diffuse cascade activation describes DIC, which would prolong the PT, aPTT, and thrombin time rather than leaving them normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osmotic injury is attributed to extended-release oxycodone, and no such medication is described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unregulated alternative complement activation causes the rare genetic form of HUS, typically in children.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute leukemia develops microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Which of the following aspects of his treatment most likely caused this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor lymphocytes reacting against his red cell antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: The intravenous immunoglobulin given for prophylaxis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The packed red cell transfusions given during his admission

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prolonged neutropenia that followed the transplant

choices.label: E
choices.text: The radiation therapy and chemotherapy given with the transplant

explanation.summary: Thrombotic microangiopathy after stem cell transplantation is attributed to the associated radiation therapy or chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for the treatment of leukemias and lymphomas is a listed secondary cause of TM, arising from either the associated radiation therapy or the chemotherapy. These injure the vessel wall, which is the common initiating event in all causes of TM.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An alloimmune attack on red cell antigens would not fragment cells into schistocytes or consume platelets in microthrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous immunoglobulin is not described as a cause of thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell transfusion is not among the secondary causes of thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia itself does not injure the vasculature or produce a microangiopathic picture.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis develops anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and a rising creatinine. Her coagulation studies are normal. Which of the following best explains her thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorption of a bacterial toxin through the gastrointestinal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of coagulation factors from diffuse cascade activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct injury to the blood vessel walls by her rheumatologic disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excessive cleavage of von Willebrand factor multimers by ADAMTS13

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shearing of red cells across a stenotic native heart valve

explanation.summary: Rheumatologic disorders such as systemic sclerosis directly injure blood vessel walls and cause secondary TM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatologic disorders are a secondary cause of TM: systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and antiphospholipid syndrome can directly injure blood vessel walls. Vessel wall injury is the shared first step in all causes of TM, after which platelets aggregate and red cells are sheared.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Toxin absorbed from the gut causes diarrhea-associated HUS, which is not suggested by this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor consumption from diffuse cascade activation describes DIC, which would prolong her coagulation studies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excess ADAMTS13 activity would reduce, not promote, thrombus formation; TTP arises from deficiency of the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mechanical shearing across a valve is a rarer cause of MAHA and would not produce thrombocytopenia and kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with gram-negative sepsis has anemia with schistocytes and a platelet count of 38,000/uL. Which of the following sets of coagulation results would most support disseminated intravascular coagulation rather than another thrombotic microangiopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Normal aPTT, normal PT, normal thrombin time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal aPTT, prolonged PT, normal thrombin time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal thrombin time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolonged aPTT, prolonged PT, prolonged thrombin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shortened aPTT, shortened PT, prolonged thrombin time

explanation.summary: DIC is the thrombotic microangiopathy in which the aPTT, PT, and thrombin time are all increased.
explanation.whyCorrect: In TTP, HUS, and most secondary causes of TM, the aPTT, PT, and thrombin time are normal because the thrombi are platelet-rich and coagulation factors are not consumed. DIC is the exception: its thrombi result from overactivation of the coagulation cascade, so factors are consumed and all three assays become prolonged while platelets fall and schistocytes appear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Entirely normal coagulation studies are the pattern of TTP, HUS, and most secondary causes, not of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An isolated prolonged PT with an otherwise normal panel does not match the DIC pattern of uniformly elevated assays.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isolated prolonged aPTT does not reflect the global factor consumption of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shortened clotting times are not a feature of DIC, in which factor consumption prolongs the assays.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, and secondary causes of thrombotic microangiopathy have been excluded. Which of the following best describes how the distinction between hemolytic-uremic syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is usually made?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By the clinical history and the physical examination

choices.label: B
choices.text: By the degree of elevation of LDH and the depression of haptoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: By the number of schistocytes counted on the peripheral smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: By the results of the prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: E
choices.text: By the severity of the thrombocytopenia on the complete blood count

explanation.summary: HUS and TTP cannot be separated by routine laboratory testing; the distinction is made clinically.
explanation.whyCorrect: When secondary causes are excluded, the clinician evaluates for TTP and HUS, which are less common. The distinction between HUS and TTP is not made by lab tests but is usually made by the clinical history and exam, such as a preceding diarrheal illness versus neurologic findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum studies of hemolysis are typical of intravascular hemolysis in all forms of TM and cannot distinguish between causes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Schistocytes are present in every thrombotic microangiopathy and cannot distinguish among the causes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PT and aPTT are normal in both HUS and TTP; they separate DIC from the others, not HUS from TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are decreased in both disorders, so the degree of thrombocytopenia does not separate them.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion, anemia with schistocytes, and a platelet count of 15,000/uL. Coagulation studies are normal and secondary causes have been excluded. An ADAMTS13 activity and inhibitor assay is sent, and the laboratory reports that results will take several days. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin plasma exchange now without waiting for the assay results

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give intravenous fluids alone and repeat the smear in 48 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting the results

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfuse platelets and reassess when the assay returns

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withhold specific therapy until the ADAMTS13 results return

explanation.summary: Treatment for suspected TTP must start immediately because the ADAMTS13 assay takes days to return.
explanation.whyCorrect: Special assays can confirm TTP from ADAMTS13 deficiency, but the results usually are not available for several days, and treatment for TTP has to start as soon as possible. Because TTP is a medical emergency managed with urgent plasmapheresis, the clinician cannot wait for these results before deciding whether to start treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluids alone form the supportive approach to HUS and do not treat a patient with suspected TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibiotics are not useful in most cases of thrombotic microangiopathy and would not treat TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet transfusion does not address the underlying ADAMTS13 problem and is not the treatment for TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Withholding therapy for several days in a medical emergency risks progressive microthrombotic organ injury.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man hospitalized with COVID-19 and respiratory failure is found to have microthrombus formation. His platelet count is normal, he has no anemia or schistocytes, and his ADAMTS13 level is not decreased. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and needs urgent plasma exchange

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has disseminated intravascular coagulation triggered by his infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has hemolytic-uremic syndrome caused by a viral toxin

choices.label: D
choices.text: He has inherited thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura from an inactivating ADAMTS13 mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: His findings do not represent true thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

explanation.summary: COVID-19-associated microthrombi are not true TTP because ADAMTS13 is normal and the hematologic findings of TTP are absent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cases of microthrombus formation have been described in patients with COVID-19 and respiratory failure. They do not appear to be true thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, however, since ADAMTS13 levels are not decreased and patients usually have normal platelet counts and lack hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired TTP requires ADAMTS13 deficiency with thrombocytopenia and MAHA, none of which he has.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC consumes coagulation factors and platelets, whereas his platelet count is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HUS follows a toxin-producing bacterial diarrheal illness and includes hemolytic anemia and low platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inherited TTP also produces ADAMTS13 deficiency, which has been excluded by his normal level.

questions.stem: A hematologist is counseling a patient about conditions that raise the risk of developing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asplenia after splenectomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Advanced chronic kidney disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term cigarette smoking

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male sex in middle adulthood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus

explanation.summary: TTP usually strikes previously healthy people, but underlying autoimmune disease such as SLE, female sex, pregnancy, and obesity raise the risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: TTP usually presents in previously healthy people, though some have underlying autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus. Other risk factors include female sex and conditions such as pregnancy and obesity; the reasons for these associations are not known.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asplenia is associated with Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear and is not a risk factor for TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic kidney disease is not listed among the risk factors for developing TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smoking is not among the described risk factors for TTP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Female sex, not male sex, is the risk factor associated with TTP.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman who has been taking quinine for nocturnal leg cramps develops microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discontinuation of the offending medication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: For a secondary thrombotic microangiopathy, the main treatment is removing the causative drug or treating the underlying condition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Quinine is a listed medication cause of TM, producing an immune injury to the vasculature. TMs are always treated in consultation with a hematologist, and for a secondary cause the main treatment is removing the causative drug or treating the underlying condition such as hypertension or cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not useful in most cases of thrombotic microangiopathy and would not reverse a drug effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet transfusion does not treat the underlying vascular injury in any thrombotic microangiopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rituximab is used alongside plasmapheresis in TTP and does not address an offending medication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urgent plasmapheresis with corticosteroids is the treatment of TTP, a primary TM, rather than a drug-induced secondary TM.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is evaluated for a deep venous thrombosis of the calf, and the clinician contrasts it with the thrombotic microangiopathies. Which of the following features best distinguishes the thrombotic microangiopathies from this patient's deep venous thrombosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clot formation requires the participation of platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple clots form in small vessels throughout the body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red cells are destroyed within the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clot obstructs blood flow through the involved vessel

choices.label: E
choices.text: The disorder is always caused by an inherited enzyme defect

explanation.summary: Thrombotic microangiopathies are defined by diffuse, multiple clots in small vessels, unlike a single localized clot such as a DVT.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microangiopathy means small vessel disease and thrombotic means the problem has to do with excessive blood clotting, so these diseases are characterized by the excessive formation of multiple clots in small vessels throughout the body. It is this diffuse systemic nature that distinguishes them from disorders in which a patient makes a single clot, like a deep venous thrombosis in the calf.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelets participate in clot formation in both situations, so this does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell destruction in TM is mechanical shearing within small vessels rather than splenic destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Obstruction of flow through the involved vessel occurs in a deep venous thrombosis as well.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most thrombotic microangiopathies are acquired, including the common forms of TTP and HUS.
